At least 30 people were killed and 15 injured after a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring road in Egypt on Wednesday, the country's health ministry said. The blaze broke out in Giza's Al-Warraq district, on a highway connecting key routes across Greater Cairo.
The vehicle overturned before catching fire, triggering the deadly blaze. The fire broke out above a tunnel, the health ministry said.
Local media reported that firefighters had brought the blaze under control. Emergency services responded to the incident, while the injured were taken for medical treatment.
The ring road is a major transport route connecting the governorates of Cairo, Giza and Qalyubia. It links several key highways across the Greater Cairo region.

Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious charges against Netanyahu
- Published
Judges in Israel have suggested prosecutors drop bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially handing the caretaker prime minister a boost as he fights for his political survival.
The judges told the attorney general that there was little chance of conviction in the first of three cases he is facing, in which he is accused of granting government favours in exchange for positive media coverage.
They also questioned whether his actions amounted to criminal conduct in a second corruption case, and suggested prosecutors seek a plea deal in a third.
Netanyahu has consistently denied the allegations against him and called on Wednesday for the trial to be ended "immediately".
"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my family, my son," he said in a televised statement.
"Ten years of incitement to hatred that wounds the soul."
Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, but court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.
The case now under serious doubt, known as Case 4,000, concerns an alleged "reciprocal arrangement" between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder in Israel's biggest telecoms company. Both denied any wrongdoing.
In a highly unusual step, a judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court summoned Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara on Wednesday to express their concerns.
"The chances of conviction are low – to an extent that warrants reconsidering the matter," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told her, Israeli media reported.
The judges also cast doubt on whether Netanyahu's actions, which are subject to a second case – concerning another alleged quid-pro-quo with another media baron, known as Case 2,000 – met the threshold for criminality.
While they left open the possibility of a conviction in the third case: Case 1,000, which alleges Netanyahu acted for the benefit of an Australian billionaire after being gifted cigars and champagne by him.
- Netanyahu: What are the corruption charges? 
  - Published22 May 2020
However, the judges told the attorney general that, in the public interest, there needed to be a "rethink" in how the trial should move forward, Israeli media report.
Baharav-Miara said she would consider the judges' recommendations.
It has been six years since Netanyahu became Israel's first sitting prime minister to face a criminal trial.
He has always claimed to be the victim of a political witch-hunt and said on Wednesday that the "fabricated cases" against him were now falling apart.
The cases have continued to progress in court while Netanyahu remained in power throughout the war in Gaza, though judges agreed to reduce the number of hearings due to security concerns around the conflict.
The accusations against him have rocked Israeli politics, fuelling already deep divisions. His trial has coincided with controversial, far-reaching judiciary reforms by Netanyahu's government.
For his opponents, Netanyahu's fear of prison has distorted his decision-making as prime minister and made him especially dependent on his far-right coalition partners to remain in power.
This latest development will give a boost to Netanyahu, whose political opponent Gadi Eisenkot is currently attempting to form a coalition government after an inconclusive general election last month.
While Netanyahu's parliamentary bloc won more seats than that of his rival, both fell short of an outright majority. Israel's president has offered Eisenkot the first chance to form a new administration.
Netanyahu remains subject to an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, which he also denies.

As far as trailblazers go, Kadambini Ganguly will figure right on top of several lists. She was a pioneering woman physician, the first to practise successfully in India, a gynaecologist and a social reformer who, equally efficiently, managed a large family as well. The story of Kadambini Ganguly is one of extraordinary achievement, and if told widely, will continue to inspire the young women of today.
In a profile published in Cureus in 2024, the authors point to the influence of the progressive Bramho Samaj movement, initiated by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, that helped Kadambini emerge from the shackles of conservative orthodoxy that might have stiffled her immense talent. “This environment, which championed the values of education and gender equality, contributed significantly to shaping her exemplary career and lifelong dedication to social justice,” the article reads. Records of her life acknowledge that she was partly recognised during her lifetime, but also mercilessly criticised and defamed for being a progressive, working woman. The full recognition of her contributions in medicine and the social sector came much later, only in recent decades.

New Delhi, Nov 25: The Union Cabinet, chaired by the Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the "Scheme for Enhancement of Construction and Infrastructure Equipment (CIE) Manufacturing Ecosystem" with a financial outlay of Rs.11,000 crore. The Scheme, to be implemented by the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI), aims to incentivize domestic manufacturing of CIE and its components and to establish a dedicated CIE testing facility in the country, thereby enhancing self-reliance and positioning India as a key player in the Global CIE market.
India's CIE industry is currently the world's third largest, after China and the United States, with a market size of around Rs.97,500 crore in FY2024-25. Driven by accelerated growth in infrastructure (roads and ports) and housing, the industry is projected to increase more than double, reaching a market size of around Rs.2,28,100 crore by FY2029-30.
Driven by rapid growth in the construction and infrastructure sector, the scheme aims to incentivize manufacturing of technologically advanced equipment such as Ship-to-Shore Cranes, Tunnel Boring Machines, Hydraulic Excavators, Off-Highway Trucks, etc. The scheme has also provision of establishment of state of art dedicated CIE testing facility in the country.
The scheme with duration of eight years from FY2026-27, comprise of a two-year gestation period (FY2026-27 to FY2027-28) for setting up manufacturing facilities, followed by a five-year incentive disbursement period (FY2028-29 to FY2032-33), and a final year (FY2033-34) for settlement of incentives on incremental sales of FY2032-33.
The scheme has two components:
Sales-linked Incentive – Incentives will be provided on the Incremental Sales Value of eligible CIE equipment and components to approved applicants across two categories – eligible OEMs and Component Manufacturers. Graded Incentive rates range from 13% to 8% of incremental sales value over a five-year period.
Grant for CIE Testing Facility – A grant of up to Rs.375 crore, in the nature of Viability Gap Funding, for setting up a dedicated CIE testing facility.
This initiative by the Government of India is a landmark step towards strengthening the domestic Construction and Infrastructure Equipment manufacturing ecosystem and enhancing competitiveness in the global markets. By fostering indigenous capabilities in manufacturing of CIE, the scheme will ensure supply chain security, increase opportunities for employment and promote Atmanirbhar Bharat. It embodies the Government’s unwavering commitment to build a technologically self-reliant, globally competitive and sustainable industrial base, in line with the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.

Improve your Starlink Wi-Fi speed with this app setting
Is your Starlink Wi-Fi slower than it should be? A simple change in the app can help, though it comes with a few trade-offs worth knowing first.
While Starlink has had a lot of bad press in 2026 — mostly because of reported slowdowns in Ukraine and its general association with Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — there's no denying that for some people, it may be their best or only internet option. That's because Starlink satellites have wide global coverage, reaching areas inaccessible not just to landline connections but potentially competing cellular and satellite services as well.
There are a variety of ways Starlink can be optimized, an obvious one being dish placement. Less obvious, though, is controlling how your system broadcasts Wi-Fi. You'd think the hard part would be capturing signals from space, after all, not bouncing them a few more feet to your laptop or TV.
What we're specifically talking about here is splitting your Wi-Fi into separate 2.4 and 5GHz networks in the Starlink app. We'll explain what that means, why it can be beneficial and when you may want to stick with the normal unified setting.
Why splitting your Starlink Wi-Fi might provide a speed boost
If you already know why you'd want to split Wi-Fi, let's cut to the chase. All you have to do is find and select the Add Network option, then toggle Split Network. You'll be asked to name the two new networks, which should probably include "2.4" and "5" so you can tell which network your devices are connecting to.
For everyone else, it helps to know that most Wi-Fi routers are dual-band, broadcasting over two main frequency bands, 2.4 and 5GHz. Starlink's bundled hardware doesn't currently support the newer 6GHz band, even when it's equipped with Wi-Fi 7. The reason a split might help is that 5GHz is inherently faster than 2.4GHz. Shorter wavelengths translate not just into higher potential speeds but more non-overlapping channels. Overlap can result in congestion and interference. For devices that support 5GHz, then, forcing them to use the band all the time may result in noticeable speed boosts. As with any Wi-Fi network, exact performance figures are going to depend on a variety of factors, including not just your router but the range and kinds of devices connecting to your network.
As if that weren't enough, some low-power devices, such as many Wi-Fi smart LED light bulbs, are 2.4GHz-only. If they're competing with devices that could be on 5GHz, they might be encountering unnecessary congestion of their own.
When splitting your Starlink Wi-Fi can cause problems
The first potential issue here is range. The 2.4GHz band offers the greatest reach of any Wi-Fi band, typically up to 150 feet (45 meters) indoors, versus 5GHz's 50 to 75 feet (15 to 25 meters). It also offers better penetration through walls and other obstacles. In some scenarios, then, limiting devices to 5GHz may result in a flaky signal or none at all where things were previously stable. Under a unified network, devices can flip between bands automatically as needed.
The other major concern is that devices on one network ID might not be able to talk to those on the other. They should be able to on paper, and naturally, that won't matter if all they have to do is communicate with the internet. But if you do encounter this issue, it can wreak havoc, particularly with a mix of smart home accessories that require specific bands. You may not be able to configure them all to work together, let alone trigger complex automations.
One final problem is convenience. Reassigning a bunch of devices to new networks can be a hassle, and to deal with range, you may have to manually switch some mobile devices every time you take them into a particular room. If you're not encountering any performance barriers with your existing setup, you might want to leave Starlink untouched.

How to watch every 2026 NFL Thanksgiving game on streaming
Cutting cable should never stop a tradition.
Death, taxes and vegging out on the couch to watch Thanksgiving football are three givens in America. This year's holiday slate is jam-packed with major storylines, including division rivals, star players, big-name halftime performers and, for the first time, an extra matchup on Thanksgiving Eve.
With games spread across both streaming services and TV networks, knowing how, where and when to stream the NFL has become a sport of its own, but we've got you covered.
Where to stream on Thanksgiving Eve
Today, you can stream Packers at Rams exclusively on Netflix, kicking off at 8:15PM ET/5:15PM PT. If you don't have an active subscription, you can sign up for the ad-supported tier at $8.99/month. Signing up today will also get you access to this year's Christmas Day games.
Since this is the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game, the league is bringing out a big name for halftime: U2 will perform at SoFi Stadium fresh off the release of its new album, Carnaval De Luz. Unlike 2014's Songs of Innocence, it didn't show up on your iPhone overnight, so you may have missed it.
Where to stream on Thanksgiving
On Turkey Day itself, the action kicks off at 1PM ET/10AM PT with Bears at Lions, airing on CBS and streaming on Paramount+. You can get Paramount+ starting at $8.99/month to watch the game and see Wu-Tang Clan swarm the stage for a halftime show executive produced by Michigan-bred icon Eminem.
Next on the docket is Eagles at Cowboys, starting at 4:30PM ET. The game airs live on Fox, but it's the one matchup you can stream at no cost on Tubi. It's also available on the Fox One streaming service for $19.99/month. Texas native Miranda Lambert is set to perform at this year's Salvation Army Red Kettle Kickoff Halftime Show, marking 30 years of the annual tradition.
Then, two of the league's premier quarterbacks, Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, face off to close out the night with Chiefs at Bills. This matchup airs live on NBC and streams on Peacock at 8:20PM ET. You'll need the Premium tier to watch on Peacock, which starts at $12.99/month. Like the prior game, the NFL tapped a local act, the Goo Goo Dolls, to headline halftime in Buffalo.
If you cut cable a while ago but don't want to sign up for individual subscriptions, you can watch these three NFL games on live TV streaming services, including YouTube TV (starting at $49.99/month for the Sports tier), Hulu + Live TV (starting at $99.99/month) or DIRECTV (starting at $94.99/month). Eagles at Cowboys and Chiefs at Bills will also be available to stream on Sling TV Select ($19.99/month) or a higher tier.
Where to stream on Black Friday
On Black Friday, you can stream Broncos at Steelers on Prime Video at 3PM ET. If you're not a Prime subscriber, you can score a standalone subscription for $8.99/month. This matchup will not feature a halftime performance, but two of the league's top teams should suffice.

For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.
Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.
The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.
That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.
The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.
The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.
The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.
Those differences help explain why the two governments are building different walls. Beijing’s proposal shields cell and gene therapy from outside entities, areas where they have a demonstrated or aspirational determination to lead the world. Platforms must remain domiciled in China while individual products can be marketed abroad. That is a coherent industrial strategy, and it is paying off well. Chinese financial regulators report that foreign deals for Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion through August 2026, up more than a third from the year before.
Washington’s proposal works differently. The Treasury Department proposal prevents American investors from punting on a piece of Chinese biotech and yet still allows American companies to pay for Chinese molecules. In areas where China now leads, the combined effect would seem at best to be a division of labor. As my co-author and I pointed out in our earlier STAT article, China increasingly invents and owns while American firms are more prone to take licenses, complete late stage development, and pay royalties.
To be fair, biotechnology raises real national security questions, from genomic privacy to research that could be misused for nefarious purposes. Imposed limits on capital flows are a legitimate tool. I am certainly not arguing that U.S. investors should fund Chinese state-linked companies without scrutiny. Nor do our data indicate that all Chinese products are comparable in terms of quality or originality. Higher counts may overstate the number of genuine breakthroughs.
Nonetheless, a decision to cut off scientific and/or economic engagement would seem detrimental to both nations.
Restriction is a defensive move. It does not put a single new medicine into the clinic. It treats “biotech” — which comprises drugs, devices, diagnostics, ag-tech, and many other areas — as one thing. Each of these competitive races is being run at different speeds and with entirely different players, outcomes, and pole positions.
The fundamental problem is the one described in our December 2025 article. American output of new experimental drugs has been flat since 2018. In our earlier study, China’s public sector, including universities and state-linked enterprises, contributed more than twice as many new drugs in 2024 as their American counterparts. All the while, the U.S. universities that built our lead in nucleic acids and gene therapy face shrinking federal research support as has been highlighted by STAT.
A competitor lacking fuel will lose the race even if regulators try to slow the opposition.
Three steps would accomplish more than walls ever can.
First, subject matter experts should take advantage of the public comment period the Treasury Department has opened through Dec. 7.
Those comments should press Treasury on several points. If it does impose restrictions, and it is not obvious that it should, they should be aimed narrowly at transfers of platforms and capabilities rather than at all investment. More clarity is also needed to address “NewCo” deals, in which a Chinese licensor takes a stake in a new U.S. company. Importantly, the regulator should set a date and objective criteria to review whether any new rules are working as intended.
Second, policymakers should prioritize and incentivize investment in areas where America leads or could lead. Nucleic acid and gene therapies depend on academic discovery and specialized manufacturing. Stable funding for proven models such as translational research by the National Institutes of Health, ARPA-H, and domestic manufacturing is the most obvious and reliable way to protect a declining margin. In cell therapy, policymakers should ask candidly why so many early trials now start in China (regulation, investment, technology, or combinations thereof), and how we might alleviate domestic hurdles.
Third, Washington should measure the race in a more nuanced way, such as by drug or disease type. The totals of new experimental drugs, such as those we have previously emphasized, can hide more meaningful long-term outcomes, such as FDA approvals as well as market and public health improvements. Federal agencies could start by tracking first-in-human trials by drug type and sponsor country. As this will take time, it should become a long-term indicator, ignoring annual variations. Policy aimed at the aggregate and/or based solely on short term measures will miss key details.
Walls are what you construct when you think you are under attack or are losing. In the technologies that will define the next generation of medicines, from RNA drugs to gene editing, American institutions still lead. The biggest threat does not come from abroad but from changes in domestic policy, such as cutting biomedical research. Our current lead in these fields was built with reliable investments by the public and private sectors, not barriers.
Michael S. Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

The Indian women’s hockey team has achieved its highest-ever ranking (5th) in FIH, surpassing its previous best of 6th in 2022 and 2023.
India has now won 12 matches in a row and is undefeated in 13, including convincing victories in the ongoing Women’s Asian Champions Trophy.

The last time India lost a competitive match was back in August, when it lost 0-2 to the Netherlands in the World Cup. India’s only other loss of the year was in March, when it lost 0-2 to England.
The team has had an impressive year, in which it has won 21 out of its 27 matches, drawing four and losing only two. This has led India to win both the gold at the Asian Games in September/October and the Nations Cup in June.

SpaceX said Tuesday that it will give one share of its stock to every active Trump Account.
Elon Musk, SpaceX's CEO, will also personally match the number of shares donated by the AI and rocket company, SpaceX said. Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and chief operating officer, also pledged more than 2 million SpaceX shares.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
In July, the Trump administration launched Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for children born between 2025 and 2028. Once an account is opened, the US Treasury Department will make a one-time $1,000 contribution.
The Treasury Department has said that the accounts are designed to help families build long-term financial security.
SpaceX joins a growing number of companies that have decided to invest in Trump Accounts. Dell, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Charles Schwab, and BlackRock have also pledged contributions to the accounts.

We weren't able to confirm, as of this writing, precisely how many barrels of lead azide would be exploded.
In mid-November, a rumor spread online that the U.S. Army had plans to set off two detonations to destroy an old cache of lead azide — a highly explosive compound — in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 20.
"The Army found 68 barrels of the explosive that had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years," one Facebook post read (archived). "Lead azide becomes more unstable as it ages and can detonate with slight movement or friction, making it unsafe to move off site."
The claim spread across other platforms, with several Snopes readers also contacting us for answers.
In short, the claim is true. Here's what we know:
Army confirms explosions will take place
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant launched a campaign to inform the public about the upcoming explosions, including an open house on Oct. 15 and a notice (archived) on Nov. 15 warning people in the affected area to evacuate and inviting residents to shelter at the Armed Forces Reserve Center during the explosions if needed.
In a document titled "Keeping Our Community Safe," the Army described how plans to reduce harm from the explosion by using specialized water misters and cleaning and removing affected soil and debris once the operation ceases.
(U.S. Army)
The public warnings issued by the Army to residents in the area were as follows:
- Consider avoiding the affected area.
- If you are inside of the affected areas, avoid outdoor air by staying indoors.
- Keep windows and doors closed.
- If it is safe to do so, set heating and cooling systems to "recirculate" to minimize outdoor air exposure and maximize indoor air filtration until the plume passes by your community.
- Avoid unnecessary travel through impacted areas.
- After the US Army determines the air exposure period has ended, consider cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces such as play surfaces for children and windowsills.
- If your car was parked outside, consider washing your car at a car wash to minimize your contact with potentially exposed surfaces.
Is the circulated 'blast zone' map accurate?
In the circulated map shown in the Facebook post above, the blast zone appears to stretch approximately 100 miles northeast from the blast site. We compared this map to maps the Army released ahead of the planned detonations and found they aligned.
(Facebook user Live Storm Chasers and U.S. Army)
As Nov. 20 draws closer, the Army's maps will be updated. Residents in the area were encouraged to regularly check for updates.
What is lead azide and how did it get there?
According to the Environmental Protection Agency, lead azide is a "hazardous waste that exhibits the characteristic of reactivity (energetic) and exhibits the characteristic of toxicity for lead." In a public notice (archived) Nov. 16, the EPA wrote:
The recrystallization of the stored lead azide has increased the material's sensitivity to friction and shock, and disturbing the containers of lead azide could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation. The Army's evaluation of a range of potential alternatives for the treatment of lead azide culminated in the secretary of the Army selecting in-place, controlled, intentional detonation for the treatment of lead azide.
The material is used to initiate munitions, according to a Q&A document the Army published.
It's unclear precisely how the lead azide stores came to be stored at that underground location. While a number of media outlets reported that 68 barrels would be detonated, we were unable to confirm that amount. We contacted the Army seeking more context and information about the history of the lead azide stores and will update this story if we receive a response.
In March, the Army announced that experts were conducting a safety review for the "safe removal of a chemical compound currently at the plant."
On Nov. 17, local ABC affiliate KCRG reported that local activists were planning a "peaceful demonstration" against the planned detonations.
Group organizers were reportedly demanding:
- An immediate halt to the Nov. 20 lead azide detonation, at minimum until affected communities have had an adequate opportunity to review the risks and alternatives.
- Full transparency regarding the potential environmental and public health consequences.
- Independent environmental experts to review the proposed disposal method and evaluate safer alternatives.
- A comprehensive plan for independent air, soil, and surface testing in potentially affected communities.
- A commitment to clean up and remediate any lead contamination resulting from this operation, at no cost to affected residents and property owners.

The battery in your Fitbit Edge is replaceable, but it's not as easy as you'd think
You can get a manual from iFixit for free to guide you through the process.
After a brief period of people worrying that Google that was abandoning Fitbit devices in favor of the Pixel Watch, the company recently assuaged those fears by releasing two new devices, led by the Fitbit Edge. It's an obvious successor to the Charge series, albeit without Google Pay, or EDA scans for measuring stress.
An enhancement that might've caught your attention is the product's user-replaceable battery. The dirty secret of most fitness trackers (and smartwatches, for that matter) is that while they can last for years, if their batteries aren't replaced, their capacity will inevitably shrink until it becomes unusable. In theory, as long Google maintains app support and compatible batteries are still in warehouses, an Edge can last indefinitely.
This isn't quite like replacing the AAs in a flashlight, however, or even the coin battery you might find in an analog watch. You need specialized gear, and the process is delicate enough that there's a risk of sabotaging your Fitbit if you make a mistake.
What makes the Fitbit Edge battery replacement so complicated
Google's partner on this is iFixit, which provides a free PDF manual once you've signed into their website. Before you begin, however, you need to buy specialized parts and tools, including not just a fresh battery, but replacement screws for the surrounding equipment. That might seem strange, but iFixit says that these replacement parts can only be used once, a claim which may or may not say anything about the original parts as well.
Where things get risky is after you've managed to pry open the Edge's case. Its O-ring can fall out, and you'll need to reassemble that if you want your device to retain any water resistance. You'll also need a pair of tweezers, and needless to say, poking circuits could accidentally break something, as could static shock. iFixit recommends precautions like a grounding mat, and even avoiding any clothing that could build up a static charge, such as fleece.
For some owners, the major hurdle is going to be the scale of the operation. The screws and connectors involved are tiny, even by the standards of most electronics. If your hands aren't steady, this process could prove frustrating or outright impossible, speaking as someone who's hand-assembled desktop PCs.
Are there any alternatives to Google's procedure?
Officially, no. If you don't want to perform the procedure yourself, Google doesn't offer a paid replacement service. The company might conceivably perform a free swap if you've got a defective battery and you're still under warranty, but you're otherwise expected to handle things yourself. If you do qualify for a battery fix, there's a chance that Google will simply send you a replacement Edge.
As time goes on, third-party options might arrive, yet Google cautions against using unofficial parts, stating that "a non-qualified battery and improper disposal may present a risk of fire, explosion, leakage, and/or other hazards." The company is, of course, covering itself legally — but there's a grain of truth in that there's no telling what the quality of a generic part may be. Lithium-ion batteries can burst into flames if they're damaged or defective. Even with Google's official parts, you should be prepared to dispose of a battery in a fireproof container.
All this helps to explain why more wearables haven't gone the replaceable route. Companies don't want to be on the hook for their customers' mistakes, and it remains to be seen how many people will actually take advantage of the option. By the time an Edge's battery wears out, you might be more inclined to buy a newer device than resuscitate last-gen hardware.

When medical student Emmanuel Oyebadejo went to watch his friend's American football game, he had no idea he would end up being scouted himself for a sport he had never even played.
He wasn't even interested in it. In fact, while still at school in Manchester he'd delivered a speech titled 'I have a dream' in which he outlined plans to do "very well in basketball, return from the NBA and be the prime minister of the United Kingdom".
But now, four years later, he is being tipped to become the first Briton to be a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.
It is a rapid rise for the 22-year-old, who had to learn the game from scratch and win over his parents who "begged" him not to play and instead focus on his medical studies.
His biggest challenge at the start, though, was finding a pair of boots big enough for his size 16 feet.
It was 6ft 6in Oyebadejo's physique that had caught the eye of the coaching staff at Exeter Demons when he was a spectator for his friend's university game that was taking place at the club's home ground, The Crumb.
"I was talking to one of the other coaches, Jack Mullins, and we sort of turned around [and thought] 'that guy's freaking huge! We should go talk to him'," Lydon Ward-Best, one of the Demons' coaches, tells BBC Sport.
Oyebadejo had been a talented basketball player, playing for Manchester Magic - one of England's top junior clubs - from the age of 11 to 18. But by the time he was at the University of Exeter he was no longer playing competitively.
Lydon Ward-Best persuaded him to give a new sport a go.
"He started coming to training and just had the most ridiculous intro to American football I think I've ever seen," the coach adds.
A straight-A pupil, who had also learned the piano, guitar and drums while studying medicine, Oyebadejo had always been a quick learner.
"I always say that American football is kind of like violent chess," says Mullins, the Demons' current head coach.
"[Emmanuel] got the violent bit pretty quickly. He was fine at that - 'I am much bigger than you, watch me go'.
"The chess bit took a little longer because there's all these things that you have to think about."
But as Ward-Best puts it, "he's not just a big sort of jock athlete, he's a smart guy. He is so dedicated and disciplined with everything."
Oyebadejo played for the Demons at the end of the 2022-23 season, before the team went unbeaten in his first full season, 2023-24. When back home he also played for the Manchester Titans and helped them win the Britbowl in September 2023.
By December 2023, he decided he wanted to take things further. Could he make it in the United States? Would college teams be interested if he sent them videos of his highlights?
Coach Ward-Best told Oyebadejo it would be "tough", adding: "You know the percentages are not on your side here, but you are 6ft 6in and 280 pounds (20 stone), so you've got a better chance than most.
"I wanted to be realistic with him," he adds. "But I said I'd do whatever I could to help get him out there."
Emmanuel's father Oladini says he thought it was a "joke" and that he did not support him playing this "dangerous" game, explaining: "He had never played this game before. He'd only done it for a few months, so why would anybody from America want him?"
But they did.
There was interest from several colleges and Oyebadejo ended up at Jacksonville State, where he would study biology and play under legendary college coach Rich Rodriguez, having managed to win his parents round thanks to the influence of an uncle who lived in Dallas and understood the sport.
His first season was hit by injury but, despite coming up against players who have played American football since they were young children, his second was a big success.
As a defensive end, Oyebadejo's job is to get past the offensive linemen trying to block him and tackle the ball carrier or claim a sack - when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
He recorded 4.5 sacks, forced two fumbles and had 41 total tackles during the 2025 season.
Now the big college teams were paying attention.
College football is America's most passionate sporting pastime. While the NFL plays on Sundays, the college game dominates Saturdays during the autumn months.
And Oyebadejo transferred to the University of Florida to play for one of college football's biggest teams in the most prestigious conference, the Southeastern (SEC).
The Florida Gators are three-time national champions, have about 50 former players currently in the NFL and get home crowds of 90,000 at 'The Swamp'.
Oyebadejo was undaunted as he burst on to the scene. He had 2.5 sacks in a win at rivals Auburn in September and followed that up by impressing in big wins over Mississippi and Texas, the latter in front of 103,989 people.
After barely being on the radar of NFL scouts at the start of the season, Oyebadejo's form has propelled him into contention to be an early-round draft pick in 2027.
NFL teams do not have youth systems or academies. Almost all players have come through the US college system and they are recruited via the NFL Draft when they graduate.
One of the biggest events in the American sporting calendar, the NFL Draft takes place over three days in April, with the 32 teams taking turns to select players across seven rounds.
First-round picks in April will be guaranteed a rookie contract of at least $19.1m (£14.4m) and they are often fast-tracked into starting roles. The contract values decrease in a sliding scale so, for example, a third-round pick (top 96) will be guaranteed $7.3m (£5.5m).
Among the latest prospects, ESPN's veteran draft analyst Mel Kiper has ranked Oyebadejo as the fifth-best edge rusher (defensive end). That is regarded as the sport's second-most important position behind quarterback - and therefore the second-best paid in the NFL.
The reason is that Oyebadejo has everything needed to be a starting defensive end in the NFL. Firstly, his height and weight are ideally suited for the grappling battle required in what is known as 'the trenches'.
He has very long arms (7ft wingspan), perfect for winning a wrestling match against the kind of enormous opponent he faces, and unusually for a man as big as him, he's extremely quick. That's the money-making trait.
Although he now weighs about 300lbs (more than 21 stone), it is believed he has a remarkable body-fat percentage of about 12%. All his measurables are seen as ideal for a defensive end, if not better.
There are simply very few people with Oyebadejo's physical talent, and given the fast-tracked nature of his rise in American football, he does not look as raw as you might expect.
"He's British and has only played the sport for three [full] seasons," says his mentor and former coach Ward-Best. "You'd therefore think he must be very green, but he doesn't look that way.
"The physical qualities are clearly there but he's worked a lot on mastering aspects of the position as well."
Menelik Watson, also from Manchester, holds the record for being the highest-drafted British player. He was the 42nd pick in 2013 and spent six years in the NFL, earning a total of $16.4m (£13.7m).
London-born Osi Umenyiora, the 56th pick in 2003, enjoyed an illustrious 12-year career - winning two Super Bowls with the New York Giants.
"I have spoken to Osi, he's a really cool guy," says Oyebadejo, who is also of Nigerian heritage.
"To be a first-round pick out of the UK, it would be amazing. It would do so much for the American football community back home."
Oyebadejo impressed again in an upset win at Kentucky on Saturday and has 4.5 sacks with two regular-season games left. Florida could then play in a 'bowl' game, an end-of-season exhibition.
After that, Oyebadejo is expected to participate in a physical-testing event called the 'scouting combine', where he will be assessed by representatives of all 32 teams in March.
The draft then begins in Washington DC on 27 April, and if Oyebadejo hears his name called, he will complete an unlikely journey and make his now fully supportive parents very proud.
"It's mad," says Ward-Best. "I've been doing this for 20 years and I've never seen anything like this. We almost have to pinch ourselves."
Oyebadejo has stayed in touch with his former coaches in Exeter. The Demons hold watch parties for Florida games and there is a real sense of pride over where his journey began.
"It was just complete chance that he wanted to wander up to The Crumb and watch a game, just being there for his mate," says coach Mullins.
"If those things didn't happen, we wouldn't be having this conversation. He would be four years into his medical degree."

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to prime minister Narendra Modi seeking a ban on releasing the Pakistani series “Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo” on Netflix India on December 4, 2026. The body has also demanded a "strong, permanent law" to keep Pakistani content off Indian television, OTT platforms and cinema. The letter, dated November 24 and signed by AICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta, was shared by news agency ANI on X. It is copied to information and broadcasting minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and to Netflix India. AICWA’s four demands are listed below: that the series is not released or streamed in India on December 4 or any other date that all OTT and streaming platforms strictly comply with the May 8, 2025 advisory that the permanent law be enacted that platforms be made to understand that commercial interest can never come before national security and the sentiments of the martyrs' families The letter also appeals to Netflix India and other OTT platforms to state clearly in their social media posts that such content will not be shown in India. It ends with the line: "No Pakistani face, voice or story has a place on Indian screens." Netflix is yet to issue a statement on this. Inc42 has reached out to the company and the story will be updated based on their response. AICWA claimed that the series stars Pakistani actors — Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan and Hania Aamir — have spoken against India at times of high tension between the two countries. The association said its letter speaks for the "140 Cr people" of the country. The letter's central argument is that Netflix's release would run directly against the government's stance. AICWA pointed to the information and broadcasting ministry's May 2025 advisory, which asked OTT platforms and streaming services to stop streaming Pakistan-origin web series, films, songs and podcasts. Back then, the ministry said that several terrorist attacks in India have been established to have cross-border linkages with Pakistan-based state and non-state actors. ICWA highlighted that the government itself had banned Pakistani artists from working in the Indian film industry after the recent Pulwama attack. Notably, this pattern of cancelling things associated with Pakistan is not only limited to content. Last year, trade body CAIT asked the government to ban Pakistani flags and merchandise on ecommerce platforms. The Central Consumer Protection Authority then issued notices to Amazon, Flipkart, Etsy and three other platforms over the sale of such products.

Deepavali, the festival of lights, left a trail of dark smoke across large parts of India’s northern plains, especially around the national capital, Delhi, where 80 million people, particularly infants and the elderly, are struggling to breathe. The Air Quality Index (AQI) at several locations in the National Capital Region (NCR) had touched 400, indicating the severity of the conditions. Other cities and towns in the north, south, east and west, though better off than the NCR because of favourable weather and geographical advantages, do not have pristine air either. Air in most Indian cities contains pollutants, including particulate matter, at levels about eight times higher than the threshold set by the World Health Organization. The worst part of the problem is its dire predictability, except for concessions from the weather. The costly lessons from the capital have implications for the entire country.
The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) swiftly moved up the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) from Stage I to Stage III within 15 days. The Commission, a statutory body established as an emergency response to toxic air conditions, has been cracking down on farm fires in Punjab, with its teams visiting fields to check incidents of stubble burning. PAVAN-I3C, the CAQM’s new Integrated Command and Control Centre, seeks to capture non-compliance in industries, traffic and transport systems and trigger immediate action against pollution spikes. Construction and demolition (C&D) activities have been halted until the 20th of this month. Inspections of construction sites and checks of Pollution Under Control Certificates (PUCC) are also vigorous. Last week, in an unprecedented move, CAQM directed Delhi and other NCR States to plan reduction of annual pollution levels by 15-20% forthwith.
Regulatory moves, however essential, are not enough. Fines and work stoppages offer only partial deterrence, while obstructions and congestion on roads are an outright failure of enforcement. Institutional compliance, enforcement and monitoring by agencies are paramount, but civic behaviour is equally critical.
The asks of people are not any great sacrifices, but some lifestyle retuning: use public transport and minimise use of personal vehicles, work from home, avoid construction activities for a few weeks, clean air filters at homes and in vehicles, avoid activities which generate dust, heat and smoke, and avoid open burning of solid waste and biomass. It would be unimaginable in many other countries for vehicle owners to be reminded of the pollution caused by their vehicles only during the months when the air becomes unbreathable. If clean air is part of the right to life, citizens also have a charter of duties to follow.
The causes of pollution are well known. These straddle sectors, including industry, roads and buildings, vehicles, agriculture, shrinking green cover, municipal waste and urban living. However, citizens and their behaviour, in their varied roles as farmers, car and house owners, builders, contractors, and urban residents, remain at the centre. People complain and curse, and even silently suffer sickness from foul air, but sensitive and responsive behaviour remains elusive. The expansion of metro services and the availability of more public transport have not persuaded private car owners to switch. The Supreme Court went the extra mile by allowing firecrackers this Deepavali, while imposing justifiable restrictions on their toxic content and duration of use. Yet, citizens’ responses have not remotely matched the severity of the problem. It might seem contradictory, but many would like to reap all the dividends of GRAP without complying with its requirements.

Duran Duran founding member and original guitarist Andy Taylor has died.
His passing comes “following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer,” according to a statement from his old band members “Andy passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November.” Having left the New Romantic band years ago, Taylor was 65.
He is survived by his wife Tracey and their three children Andrew, Isabelle, Bethany and Georgina.
In a statement posted online, Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor (who recently stepped back as the band’s drummer himself due to tinnitus) paid tribute to the six-stringer.
“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” the quartet wrote of their early 1980s years in England’s north. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.” The remaining members of Duran Duran added of the rocker: “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”
Watch on Deadline
In a statement of her own, Tracey Taylor said of her husband: “To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather. He was the rock of our family.”
Riding the mania of the always camera ready group’s mega-stardom in the early 1980s and hit like the Union of the Snake and Hungry Like the Wolf, Taylor left Duran Duran twice. Also a founding member, with bassist John Taylor, of funk rockers The Power Station, Andy Taylor exited Duran Duran in 1986 the first time, and, after the original members reunited for a spell after over a decade, again in 2006.
Born in the working class area of Cullercoats in the UK on February 16, 1981, Taylor was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2018, but didn’t make his condition public until 2022 when he announced he would not be able to join the rest of the band at their Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction. In 2023, Taylor started taking the medication Lutetium-177, which was assumed to be able to help extend his life by several years.
In his blunt 2008 autobiography Wild Boy, Taylor admitted to whole heartedly embracing the rock star lifestyle — until he crashed and burned. In terms of his musical career, besides Duran Duran and Power Station, Taylor put out a solo album, toured with ex-Sex Pistol Steve Jones and went on the other side of the studio to produce. Taylor got back together with his old bandmates in 2023 for Duran Duran for their Danse Macabre album. That same year, Taylor put out his last solo album, Man’s a Wolf to Man.
Thank you, Andy, for giving the world so much joy with your talent. Rest in peace.

In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis
This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen. Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.
But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.
Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.
In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.
Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.
As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.
A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.
On bright screens posted around the store, discount offers flashed: 25% off edibles, read one; 30% off for medical patients, read another. An extra $5 off for bringing in cans of food for the store's holiday drive.
Kelley Vinton, 36, is a regular at The Forest. She's a medical marijuana user and usually sticks to a strict weekly budget, she said. But on Monday, she threw in a few little extras — for the "cousin walk," Vinton said.
"You know, you take a little breaky-poo with your cousins, and we live in the country, so we just walk, usually before dinner," Vinton said. "We smoke a joint, and we get nice and high, and get some munchies and get ready for dinner."
The federal government still classifies recreational marijuana as a Schedule I drug, meaning it is considered to have "high potential for abuse," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. But medical cannabis was reclassified this year to Schedule III, a category shared by drugs like Tylenol with codeine and anabolic steroids.
In 2025, Whitney Economics found, revenue was down across the industry thanks to an oversupply of plant product and declining prices, driven by the discount culture of cannabis retailers.
It was the first year since 2014 — when Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize cannabis sales for recreational use — that the industry saw a dip, according to an analysis by Whitney Economics.
"It's forced a race to the bottom," said Beau Whitney, the founder and chief economist at Whitney Economics. "What this is resulting in is great prices for the consumer, they're spending less and getting the same or more, so that's good for them on an affordability perspective. But it's hurting operators."
Though the industry has seen a slight rebound this year — an increase of about 5% in sales for the same period last year, Whitney's team found — forecasts for the end of 2026 and the outlook for 2027 remain relatively modest.
The biggest reason for this, Whitney said, is customer behavior.
Through the beginning of the 2020s, Whitney said, consumers would typically come into a dispensary with a set amount to spend. Their cannabis budget. If they got a discount, Whitney said, they'd add additional products into their carts to hit their budget.
But that began to change in 2024, as inflation rose and the cost of essentials, like gas, ballooned.
"Behavior changed literally overnight," Whitney said. "What they're doing is they're taking the discounts — and there's a lot of them now — and they're using that money to buy gas and buy groceries. So they're adjusting the amount that they purchase based on what's going on in their own personal economy."
The discount model, he said, has also forced prices down. With legal retailers competing for a pool of customers that has not seen rapid growth in years, discounts help draw people into stores. But they've also created a culture where customers expect them, several cannabis store owners said.
It's why doing well on a week like this one, as customers flood in for Green Wednesday deals, is essential for shop owners like The Forest's Christina Betancourt Johnson.
On Monday, the Baltimore store was stocked — with edibles and pre-rolls and other cannabis products, but also stacks of snacks for customers waiting in longer-than-usual lines, branded giveaways and samples of gummies to try (no weed in those).
A steady flow of customers wandered in. Some for their usual supplies, others for a little holiday shopping.
Employee Thomas Bourne loaded a vape into a paper bag for one of the dispensary's regular customers. That seemed a little light for the holiday, he observed, teasingly.
"Gotta come back for your cousin walk essentials, man," Bourne said. "'Tis the week."
The customer smiled, nodding. He'd be back.

(Bloomberg) -- A rent freeze backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration was cleared by a state judge who dismissed a lawsuit filed by a group of landlords seeking to void the measure, which went into effect last month.
The landlords sued the city’s Rent Guidelines Board in July, arguing that Mamdani improperly influenced the vote and ignored evidence of rising operating costs for building owners. A judge on Wednesday threw out the case, saying the decision to implement the freeze was not “unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious” and must be upheld.
But the judge, Brendan T. Lantry, sharply criticized Mamdani’s campaign promises to freeze the rent. The mayor’s comments were “reckless and irresponsible” because only the board can raise, freeze or adjust the rent of stabilized units in the city, the judge wrote. Correspondence between the mayor’s office and the board about the measure was “troubling” and “puts a dark shadow over the purported ‘independence’ of the board,” but it doesn’t show that the mayor dictated the decision, Lantry said.
“The court recognizes that political candidates routinely comment on prevalent policy issues while running for an elected position, but to guarantee a rent freeze to millions of New Yorkers without the authority to do so, is irresponsible and, quite frankly, invited” the lawsuit, the judge wrote. Still, there is “nothing to suggest the guideline-setting process was an orchestrated ‘sham process,” Lantry said.
In a statement, Mamdani cheered the decision. “This is a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in,” he said. “Because housing is not a luxury. It is a basic necessity. This holiday weekend, more than two million New Yorkers can breathe a little easier.”
Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the landlords and a former deputy mayor in the Giuliani administration who has also challenged the pied-a-terre tax backed by Mamdani, didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.
The suit came weeks after the board voted for the first time ever to freeze rents for both one-year and two-year leases for roughly 1 million stabilized apartments. The last one-year rent freeze was during the pandemic in 2020.
Courts have historically deferred to the Rent Guidelines Board. A state court judge dismissed a challenge by landlords to a 2016 rent freeze. While that lawsuit claimed the board didn’t account for finances of the building, this challenge focused on the mayor’s involvement.
Mamdani made the freeze a centerpiece of his mayoral campaign, contending that tenants squeezed by years of rising housing costs needed immediate relief. After taking office, he appointed a majority of the board’s members. A member of the board who represented landlords, Christina Smyth, resigned in protest hours before the vote.
Tenant advocates hailed the vote as a long-overdue reset after inflation and housing shortages left many renters facing mounting financial pressure. Landlord and housing industry groups have warned that the freeze will make it harder for owners to maintain aging buildings and finance fixes as insurance, taxes and repair costs have surged amid a tight rental market.
The case is Kenilworth Holdings LLC v New York City Rent Guidelines Board, 453580/2026, New York State Supreme Court, New York County.

Nearly three-quarters of consumer companies that declared themselves free of dark patterns to the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) continue to deploy deceptive user-interface practices, despite fresh regulations against such practices set to take effect on January 1. A study commissioned by LocalCircles analysed 354 widely used online platforms across 45 sectors, drawing on consumer complaints, social media reports and the company's AI-powered dark pattern detection engine. The number of companies submitting self-declarations to the CCPA rose to 31 in November from 23 in July. However, platforms operated by 23 of these companies (74%) still contained dark patterns, the study found. Across the broader sample, 94% of platforms, or 334 out of 354, exhibited at least one dark pattern. Only 20 platforms were found to be free of such practices. Listed companies fared no better. Of the 108 consumer-facing platforms operated by companies listed on Indian stock exchanges, 102 (94%) continued to feature dark patterns. In 37 of the 45 sectors examined, not a single platform was found to be compliant. These included online grocery, food delivery, online banking, taxi aggregators, OTT streaming and edtech. B2B business marketplaces were the only category to achieve 100% compliance, followed by car rental platforms, where compliance stood at 25%. Sectors directly covered by anti-dark pattern protections also recorded low compliance rates. Ecommerce platforms had a compliance rate of just 17%, while quick commerce stood at 14%. Forced action was the most prevalent dark pattern, appearing on 237 platforms (67%). Drip pricing was the second most common, at 63%, followed by bait and switch (50%) and interface interference (48%). New Dark Pattern Rules Soon To Come Into Effect The findings come ahead of the implementation of the Consumer Protection (Ecommerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026, notified by the Department of Consumer Affairs in September. The amended rules require ecommerce entities to: Comply with dark pattern guidelines and conduct annual self-audits. Prominently display a 'dark-pattern-free' compliance certificate. Disclose the lowest price offered in the preceding 30 days when advertising discounts. Avoid misleading search manipulation and clearly identify sponsored listings Refrain from bundling fees for unrelated services. Obtain express, affirmative consent for specified uses of consumer data. Disclose product details, including 'best before' or 'use before' dates, along with relevant seller information. Clearly provide return and refund policies, warranty information, delivery terms and payment details. The findings also build on concerns raised during previous festive sales. We had reported last year on how dark patterns proliferated across ecommerce platforms during festive sales, nudging shoppers towards higher spending and purchases without adequate information. Since the introduction of regulations prohibiting dark patterns, the CCPA has penalised several platforms, including IndiGo, Zepto, FirstCry, PhysicsWallah, BookMyShow, SpiceJet and Rapido, for deploying such practices. Sectoral regulators, including the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), have also moved to strengthen consumer protections against dark patterns.

Ben McKenzie promised his wife that he was through with being an activist; that he’d go back to the acting gigs that had made him famous. At the end of his documentary taking on the cryptocurrency industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money,” the former star of The O.C. and Gotham turned to his spouse and fellow actor Morena Baccarin and swore he was done.
Turns out, that scene might need an edit. McKenzie is launching a new nonprofit, The Public Trust and Transparency Project, that not only continues his battle with the crypto business but widens it to fight prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi.
McKenzie tells WIRED he’s worried about “the gamification of the economy and the notion that we're turning everything into gambling—both investments, in the form of cryptocurrencies, and “prediction markets,” which look an awful lot like online casinos.”
“The more gambling gets into our culture, the more people feel like it's somehow a good idea to view these things as legitimate investment strategies,” he says. The prediction markets reject the comparison (although 80 percent of Kalshi’s trades came from sports in September, according to Bloomberg). McKenzie rejects the rejection: “I mean, if your investment strategy is, ‘I'm going to gamble on the Spurs-Knicks,’ like, come on! So there's a real, real problem here.”
John Reed Stark, who spent 18 years in the Securities and Exchange Commission’s enforcement division, will serve as an adviser to the Project. American Kleptocracy author Casey Michel and Tonazin Carmona, who runs economic policy for the left-of-center Century Foundation, will sit on the board.
The group is coming together at a time when regulators and law enforcement officials at every level are looking to rein in prediction markets. Federal regulators have launched new probes into both major prediction markets. The GOP-led House Oversight Committee recently released its investigation into US troops and government insiders trading on insider knowledge on Polymarket and Kalshi. The Senate just passed a bill prohibiting prediction markets for military operations and assassinations. Executives at the markets know they’re in for a rough few months; Kalshi even launched an ad campaign, starring Martha Stewart, reminding its users not to trade on confidential information.
But insider trading is only one concern among many. There’s also the problem you find in old-school gambling houses too: The vast majority of people who use the markets lose their money. A recent Wall Street Journal report shows that .01 percent of accounts take in two-thirds of all of the profits on Polymarket. On Kalshi, unprofitable accounts outpace profitable ones by almost three to one.
Then there’s the corruption angle, which McKenzie says is going to be front-and-center for the Project, especially with it featuring as a top issue in the recent midterm elections. Donald Trump Jr. was, until recently, a paid adviser to Kalshi. Trump Jr.’s venture firm, 1789 Capital, made its latest and biggest in a series of investments in Polymarket over the summer; months earlier, the Trump Justice Department sued the state of Minnesota when it tried to ban the prediction markets in the state. (At a recent conference, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called Trump Jr.’s involvement “heavily overblown. We have all types of investors.”)
Prediction markets have been around for hundreds of years, as a forthcoming book on the subject notes. American academics have been turning to them as teaching tools since the late ’80s. Their advocates note that they can be an effective way to hedge against risk, and a form of trading on sports that’s far more consumer-friendly than the online gambling houses. “I accept that there may be some utility,” McKenzie notes. “I'm not saying these things should not exist. I'm just saying they need to be properly regulated.”
McKenzie’s plan will be to push Congress in that direction, sort of the inverse of how the former actor lobbied publicly and privately against the “Clarity Act,” which would’ve brought cryptocurrencies into the financial mainstream. (The bill was rejected in September.)
That pressure is only bound to increase when Democrats take control of Congress next year. “In the bold new world starting [on the] first Monday in January,” Representative Frank Lucas, an Oklahoma Republican, told Politico, “nobody’s untouchable anymore.”

“Dancing With the Stars” aired its Season 35 finale live coast-to-coast for the first time on Tuesday, and the results were big. A season-best 9.2 million total viewers watched Paralympic track and field athlete Ezra Frech and partner Daniella Karagach take home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, according to Nielsen live+same-day preliminary, panel-only program ratings.
According to ABC, the finale posted a 2.38 rating with adults 18-49, which made it the best number in the demo since Nov. 25, 2014 (coincidentally, the season when now-host Alfonso Ribeiro won the trophy with partner Witney Carson). The finale was also up 11% in the demo vs. last year’s telecast (2.15 rating).
That 2.38 rating makes it TV’s top entertainment telecast with adults 18-49 since the Oscars in March and the highest-rated regularly scheduled entertainment telecast in 18-49 since the April 1, 2020, episode of Fox’s “The Masked Singer.”
In total viewers, the 9.2 million viewers matched last year’s finale.
In other demos, the finale averaged a 2.86 rating with adults 18-34 — the best performance since the Season 12 finale on May 24, 2011. With women 18-34, “Dancing With the Stars” posted a 4.46 rating, which is the best series telecast number in the demo for any network broadcast since the Season 3 premiere of Fox’s “Empire” on Sept. 21, 2016. And the show posted the best teens 12-17 rating (1.18) since “The Masked Singer” on Feb. 27, 2019.
ABC said the finale attracted more than 86 million votes, a new high (up 19% from 72 million in 2025) — the most ever for a single episode. The finale was the No. 1 most social program on television across broadcast and cable on the night and the No. 1 most social episode of any broadcast primetime series, year-to-date.
“Dancing with the Stars” aired live in every U.S. time zone for its special three-hour finale on Tuesday; the finale also re-aired in primetime in the Pacific time zone and started streaming the next day on Hulu.
The five final couples also included Amber Glenn and partner Pasha Pashkov, Maura Higgins and partner Mark Ballas, Connor Wood and partner Rylee Arnold and Tatyana Ali and partner Jan Ravnik.
The three-hour event included an instant dance challenge, where the couples were tested on their ability to improvise; a “judge’s choice” round and a freestyle round. The finale kicked off with an opening number to “One More Time” by Daft Punk. The “Dancing with the Stars: Live!” 2027 tour pros performed a routine to “It’s Not Right but It’s OK (Thunderpuss Mix)” by Whitney Houston, and then all Season 35 couples returned for multiple performances. Season 34 champs Robert Irwin and Witney Carson danced to “Free Bird” by Lynyrd Skynyrd.
“Dancing with the Stars” is co-hosted by Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough. Ballroom judges are Carrie Ann Inaba, Bruno Tonioli and Derek Hough. BBC Studios produces.
“Dancing With the Stars” Season 35 had been building to its finale with some of its strongest ratings in years. For its penultimate episode on Nov. 17, the show hit season highs with 7.64 million total viewers and a 1.68 rating in adults 18-49, based on preliminary Live + Same Day Panel Only data. It was the best ratings for a semifinal telecast in nine years, since Season 25 on Nov. 20, 2017 and Season 24 on May 22, 2017.
Season to date, “Dancing With the Stars” is primetime’s No. 1 entertainment series in adults 18-49 (1.59 rating in live+same day) for the third year in a row. It’s 86% above the No. 2 show, CBS’ “Survivor” (0.86), which ABC said is the largest advantage in Nielsen electronic measurement history.
