Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

Air pollution helps cause dementia by changing the genes that are switched on in microglia, the brain's immune cells, in ways that disrupt their normal functions, a new study has found.
The study, published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation, combined health records from nearly half a million people from the UK Biobank with experiments in mouse models.
"By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain's immune cells," senior author Sanjay Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at the Case Western Reserve University's school of medicine, said.
"These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world's population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it," Rajagopalan said.
Mice were exposed to outdoor Cleveland (US) air for five months. The fine particles in the air, known as particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), were concentrated to levels similar to those found in the world's most polluted cities.
Otherwise healthy mice developed memory problems, a leaky blood-brain barrier and brain inflammation. Their brains also showed a lower chemical balance reflecting its energy status and ability to withstand injury and disease.
The mice's brains also showed an increased death of newborn neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's centre for learning and memory.
The analysis found that people living in the most polluted third of areas are 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease or a related form of dementia than those in the least polluted third.
Further, in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer's, air pollution caused the same harm and also sped up amyloid plaque buildup -- a hallmark of the neurodegenerative disease.
The authors wrote: "These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure."
"We've identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer's disease," co-senior author Andrew Pieper, professor in translational psychiatry at Case Western Reserve University, said.
"This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can't avoid those stressors," Pieper said.

Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.
Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.
As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.
Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an issue with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal says it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this update.

An 18-second-long video has been circulating on social media, which shows Sandeep Khirwar, Special Director General (SDG) of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), making a remark regarding the transportation of the bodies of two Special Police Officers (SPOs) in a dumper truck.
In the viral clip, Khirwar can be heard saying, “All military trucks and vehicles in the area were occupied. So we had no choice but to transport the bodies of our two martyred SPO personnel in a dumper truck. But the real issue is not whether they were transported in a dumper or a garbage truck. Their families received the bodies of their loved ones. What more could they possibly want?”
X user @cutegirlindia21 shared this video and wrote, “Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred Kishtwar Police officers had to be transported in a garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the Indian Army refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police.”
🛑 Heartbreaking 💔 😢
Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred @KishtwarPolice officers had to be transported in a #garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the #IndianArmy refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police. https://t.co/Jm9i7bScN0
— A N U S H I ❤️T I W A R I🇮🇳 (@cutegirlindia21) November 16, 2026
According to an NDTV report published on November 14, the bodies of SPOs Bobby Chand and Rashpal Kumar — who lost their lives in a recent terror attack in the Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir — were transported to their native village Kiyar in a dumper truck without coffins. This incident sparked significant outrage among locals, with many questioning the manner in which the bodies were transported.
Against this backdrop, the purported video of SDG Sandeep Khirwar began to circulate. Several other users on X, including @RedDeFactoIND, @NetaNamax, and @unknownnewss, also shared the video with similar claims.
The video is also circulating on Facebook with similar assertions.
Fact Check
To determine the authenticity of the viral clip, Alt News used relevant keywords to search for information regarding statements made by Khirwar. We did not find any credible news reports or official statements that substantiate the claims made in the viral clip.
We observed that the viral video bears an ANI logo. Performing a ‘reverse image search’ using keyframes from the clip, we found the original video, which was posted by ANI on its official X account on November 16, 2026. In the video, Sandeep Khirwar, SDG of the CRPF’s Jammu & Kashmir Zone, is seen speaking to the media in Srinagar regarding the deaths of two SPOs in Kishtwar.
#WATCH | Srinagar, J&K: On the mortal remains of two missing SPOs recovered in Kishtwar, SDG, CRPF J&K Zone, Sandeep Khirwar says, “Every loss of life to any jawan in the security forces is a huge loss to all of us… We stand with their families, and we will make sure that they get justice.”
— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
While the visuals of the video matches, the audio is different. In the original footage, Khirwar states: “All I can say is that, every loss of life to any Jawan, of any security forces are huge loss to all of us and we owe our utmost respect to all the fallen. And we stand with their family. We will make sure that they get justice, the families get justice.” He does not make any mention of the bodies being transported in a dumper truck, nor did he claim that the families were ‘grateful’ upon the recovery of the bodies.
Further, we found that the Khirwar’s voice and manner of speaking in the viral clip does not match the way he is heard speaking in the ANI footage, indicating that the original audio has been digitally altered or manipulated. We ran the viral clip through AI-detection Hive Moderation, which revealed that it is 98.9% likely to contain AI-generated speech.
On November 17, the official X handle of the CRPF’s Srinagar Sector addressed the viral claim. They stated that the video had been digitally tampered with and that false statements had been attributed to Sandeep Khirwar, clarifying that no such statements were made by him.
This claim is false and misleading. The video was digitally manipulated, with fabricated remarks attributed to CRPF Special DG Sh. Sandeep Khirwar, who is not the Kashmir Police Chief. The original footage contained no such statement. This is an attempt to spread misinformation and create an anti-India narrative.
— Srinagar Sector CRPF 🇮🇳 (@crpf_srinagar) November 17, 2026
Thus, the viral clip has been digitally manipulated using AI, falsely attributing statements about the transportation of SPOs’ bodies in a dumper truck to Sandeep Khirwar. The original footage by ANI does not carry any such comment.
Sajahan Ali is an intern at Alt News.

The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) on Wednesday (local time) said that it was investigating a ‘cybersecurity incident’ involving unauthorised access to some of its systems. According to FinCEN, it had taken certain systems offline as a precaution amid an ongoing investigation into the breach.
Further details, including when the breach occurred, who was responsible, and what data was affected, have not been made public yet. This is the latest in a string of high-profile cyberattacks in the US.
CIA, FBI also targeted
A cybersecurity breach at the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) exposed some unclassified information, US media reported Tuesday.
The New York Times said the recently discovered intrusions targeted an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that sifts through public, unclassified material for insights.
Also Read | NSA outage: National security’s network goes offline amid software patch
NYT, citing US officials and people familiar with the issues, said that classified material was not jeopardized.
Earlier, the Department of Agriculture and the FBI were also targeted in cyberattacks, which many in the US believe may have links to Iran.
Asked about the reported FBI breach on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had only recently learned of it.
"I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he told Fox News.
Iran link
On Monday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US is investigating Iran's potential involvement in dozens of cyberattacks against energy tankers amid concerns that Tehran is widening the war with cyber operations and terror plots against Americans far from the Middle East.
Also Read | US outages: Intelligence chief rules out state-sponsored attack
As many as 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemical products and other explosive substances are believed to have been attacked, the Journal said, citing US officials and others familiar with the matter.
Some ships have also received warnings and bomb threats indicating that the vessels could be blown up, the Journal said, adding that Iran is a primary suspect in the attacks, and Russia is also seen by US authorities as a possible culprit.
Tech disruptions in US
The cyberattacks coincided with a string of technology failures this month that disrupted critical US systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN that Americans should expect more technology outages and disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.
"And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service," Clayton said.

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Following a Yellow Level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

Keralam govt working to resolve decades-old church dispute: CM Satheesan
Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam Chief Minister V D Satheesan on Wednesday said his government was making efforts to resolve the decades-old dispute between the rival Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church and Jacobite Syrian Christian Church, and would adopt only a fair and just approach in dealing with the issue.
Speaking at a press conference here after the weekly Cabinet meeting, Satheesan said the dispute was not a recent development but has been continuing for several decades, and he has been trying to find an amicable settlement.
"The dispute has been there for years. I am someone who has been trying to resolve it. The issue became more intense following the visit of the Patriarch of Antioch . The government's effort is to ensure that the situation does not worsen," he said.
He said the government was trying to prevent further estrangement between the two factions and bring them closer through dialogue.
"That is the government's position. We will take only a fair and just stand. Complaints will be examined seriously and whatever can be done will be done," the CM said.
His remarks came a day after his latest effort to establish peace between the two factions faced a fresh hurdle, with the Orthodox Church leadership expressing strong resentment over recent developments involving disputed churches.
Satheesan on Tuesday visited the Malankara Orthodox Church headquarters at Devalokam in Kottayam and held discussions with its head, Catholicos Baselios Marthoma Mathews III, amid continuing tensions between the two factions over the administration of several churches.
The meeting, which lasted more than half an hour, followed objections raised by the Orthodox Church over recent visits by Moran Mor Ignatius Aphrem II, Patriarch of Antioch and supreme head of the Universal Syriac Orthodox Church, to churches at Manarcad, Kothamangalam and Rakad.
The Orthodox Church alleged that the visits violated court orders and its constitution and said the developments had deeply hurt its members.
Church officials had described Tuesday's discussions with the chief minister as cordial and said they had conveyed their grievances to him.
The dispute between the Orthodox and Jacobite factions has its roots in differences over ecclesiastical authority and the administration of churches under the Malankara Church.
While the Orthodox faction recognises the Catholicos of the East as the head of the Church in India, the Jacobite faction recognises the Patriarch of Antioch as its supreme spiritual head.
The differences have led to prolonged legal battles and disputes over the control of several churches in Keralam.
In its 2017 verdict, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the 1934 Constitution of the Malankara Church, strengthening the Orthodox faction's position in the dispute. However, tensions have persisted in several parishes, with the implementation of court orders frequently triggering fresh confrontations.
Successive efforts to resolve the differences through negotiations have failed to achieve a lasting settlement.
Satheesan recently reiterated his intention to bring peace between the two factions and find an amicable solution to the decades-old dispute. Tuesday's meeting with the Orthodox Church leadership was part of that initiative.

Mental health concerns among refugee communities are linked not only to past trauma, violence and forced displacement but also to legal uncertainty, limited work opportunities, poor living conditions and social isolation in host countries, finds a study of Sri Lankan Tamil and Rohingya communities in India, published in the International Journal of Migration, Health and Social Care.
Titled ‘Building mental health capacity in protracted refugee situations: Empirical pointers from Sri Lankan Tamil and Rohingya populations in India’, the study looks at common mental health concerns and barriers to accessing care. It calls for training community members and health workers to recognise psychological distress, provide basic support and facilitate access to professional mental health services.

Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.
"The Freshman Representative to Leadership would be elected by members of the incoming freshman class and confirmed by the Conference," the letter said. "We intend to request a vote on this proposal."
The letter, first reported by Politico, is signed by California Sen. Adam Schiff, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, and New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim.
The letter nods to the diverse class of incoming freshmen who helped catapult the party to controlling both chambers of Congress.
"These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table."
Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift new voices in the party.
"On election night, people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms.
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW that leadership extends beyond the top post.
"This is a time for new leadership," Booker said, mentioning wanting to see more of incoming Sens. Annie Andrews of South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas. "I want to see them out front, I want to see them taking issues, I want to see them running on the field."
The proposed rule change comes ahead of the leadership election next week. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader.
Senate leadership is comprised not only of the top position of Majority leader but of additional conference officers. Both Van Hollen and Schumer support the idea of adding a position for a freshman to that leadership group.
"Leader Schumer was already planning to do this and is incredibly supportive of the idea," a spokesperson told NPR.
On Tuesday, Van Hollen posted to social media: "There should be a freshman senator on the Senate leadership team. As I've said, we need a new way to organize so we can deliver for the American people."

Nandini curd prices cut by Rs 2 per kg in Karnataka after backlash
Under the revised pricing, the 1 kg pack of Nandini curd, which currently costs Rs 68, will be available for Rs 66. The price of the 500 g pack has also been reduced from Rs 34 to Rs 33. The revised rates will take effect from Sunday, November 29, KMF said in an official statement.
Weeks after raising the prices of Nandini dairy products, Karnataka has ordered a Rs 2 per kg reduction in curd rates, offering some relief to consumers. The revised prices, announced by the Karnataka Co-operative Milk Producers' Federation Ltd (KMF), will take effect from November 29.
Under the revised pricing, the 1 kg pack of Nandini curd, which currently costs Rs 68, will be available for Rs 66. The price of the 500 g pack has also been reduced from Rs 34 to Rs 33. The revised rates will take effect from Sunday, November 29, KMF said in an official statement.
The decision comes less than a month after Karnataka revised the prices of Nandini milk and curd, triggering criticism from consumers, opposition leaders and hotel associations over the increased cost of dairy products.
WHY KARNATAKA GOVERNMENT ORDERED CURD PRICE CUT
According to KMF, the latest reduction follows a direction from the Karnataka government to bring down the selling price of curd by Rs 2 per kg in the interest of consumers. The federation said the earlier revision of milk and curd prices, which came into effect on November 1, was made following a request from the state's milk producers.
However, the government subsequently directed KMF to reduce the price of Nandini curd, resulting in the latest revision.
In its statement, the federation said it operates on cooperative principles and seeks to maintain a balance between the interests of consumers and milk producers across Karnataka.
HOW MUCH WILL NANDINI CURD COST NOW?
With the latest reduction, consumers will pay less for both commonly available Nandini curd pack sizes. The 1 kg pack, earlier priced at Rs 68, will now cost Rs 66, while the 500 g pack will be available for Rs 33 instead of Rs 34.
The reduction follows a sharp increase in curd prices earlier in November. Before the November 1 revision, the 1 kg pack was priced at Rs 54, while the 500 g pack cost Rs 28.
The earlier revision raised the prices to Rs 68 and Rs 34, respectively.
MILK PRICES ALSO WENT UP IN NOVEMBER
The curd price reduction comes against the backdrop of a wider revision in Nandini dairy prices earlier this month.
The Karnataka Cabinet had approved an increase of Rs 8 per litre in Nandini milk prices, effective November 1. KMF also revised curd prices at the time, citing a request from milk producers.
KMF said the Nandini brand has served consumers in Karnataka for decades, supported by processing technology, quality checks and food safety standards. It also highlighted the federation's role in supporting the livelihoods and economic empowerment of lakhs of dairy farmers across the state.
The latest reduction will offer some relief to consumers who had faced higher curd prices following the November 1 revision.

Over a lakh persons belonging to high-risk occupational groups, including animal handlers and dog catchers of local bodies, in all 38 districts will receive Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) against rabies under the Tamil Nadu State Action Plan for Dog-Mediated Rabies Elimination (SAPRE) - Vision 2030.
The State government has given the administrative sanction for implementation of the initiative at a cost of ₹2.22 crore, which will be met from the National Health Mission, Tamil Nadu, an order issued recently said.
The Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine noted that certain occupational groups are routinely exposed to dogs and other animals in the course of their duties. Provision of PrEP to such identified high-risk personnel will provide an additional layer of protection and strengthen the State’s rabies elimination strategy.
The programme aims to provide PrEP to identified personnel of occupational groups having sustained risk of exposure to dogs and other potentially rabid animals.
The main categories include sanitation workers, animal handlers and dog catchers of local bodies and eligible personnel of the Animal Husbandry Department involved in animal handling, dog catching, veterinary and para-veterinary activities.
Eligibility criteria
As per the National Guidelines on Rabies Prophylaxis, eligibility will be determined based on occupational exposure risk and the nature of duties performed. Based on the presently available department data, the preliminary beneficiary estimation was 1,29,009 - 1,21,844 local body sanitation workers, 3,324 local body animal handlers/dog catchers and 3,841 personnel attached to the Animal Husbandry department, the directorate said.
The initiative will be implemented through designated government health facilities, including Primary Health Centres (PHC), Urban PHCs, government hospitals, and medical college hospitals. Identification of beneficiaries and mobilisation will be carried out by the respective local bodies and Animal Husbandry Department.

Russia's own figures show almost 500,000 deaths in war in Ukraine
- Published
At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
How we came to a figure near half a million
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.

Ahead of Thanksgiving, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump spent his first Thanksgiving as president in 2017 with the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Snopes previously reported on this claim in November 2025, when questions about Trump's whereabouts coincided with the House Oversight Committee's release of a trove of documents relating to Epstein, a sex offender who died in a New York City jail cell in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex-trafficking charges.
Trump and Epstein had a well-documented friendship in the early 2000s. The exact circumstances of how the friendship ended remained unclear. Trump reportedly kicked Epstein out of his Mar-a-Lago club in 2007, 10 years before online claims said the pair spent Thanksgiving together.
One Threads user who spread the claim about Epstein and Trump spending Thanksgiving 2017 together wrote, "The NEW 20,000 Epstein Files released yesterday, SHOW TRUMP HAVING THANKSGIVING DINNER WITH EPSTEIN (WHILE IN THE WHITE HOUSE 2017)"
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived).
It appeared to originate with a post on the @TheDemocrats X account, the official account of the Democratic Party. According to screenshots of it (archived, archived), that post claimed an email exchange from the House Oversight Committee release showed that Trump spent Thanksgiving with Epstein in 2017. The post did not appear on the @TheDemocrats X account at the time of this writing.
The email exchange the post referred to between Epstein and Faith Kates, reportedly a fashion management executive, did suggest that Epstein and Trump were both in or near Palm Beach, Florida, during Thanksgiving 2017. At the time, Epstein owned a mansion in Palm Beach. According to Roll Call's public schedule for the president, Trump spent five days at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach from Nov. 21 to 26, 2017. Roll Call is an insider publication that covers all things Capitol Hill.
In the released email exchange dated Nov. 23, 2017, Kates asked Epstein "When are you back in NYC?" suggesting that Epstein was not at his Manhattan townhouse. Later in the exchange, Kates asked, "Who else is down there?" to which Epstein replied, "david fizel, hanson. trump." Given that Roll Call's Presidential Calendar and reports at the time said Trump was in Mar-a-Lago, the email exchange suggested "down there" meant Palm Beach.
While both Epstein and Trump were likely in Palm Beach over Thanksgiving 2017 (the holiday fell on Nov. 23 that year), Epstein did not directly say in the email exchange that he had or would spend time with the president while in Florida. We did not find other reputable reports that Epstein and Trump spent time together during Thanksgiving 2017. Due to the possibility of a private meeting between the two, we leave this claim unrated.
White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson did not reply to an emailed question about whether Trump spent time with Epstein during Thanksgiving 2017. Instead, Jackson said via email when we first investigated this claim in 2025: "These emails prove literally nothing. Democrats and the mainstream media are desperately trying to use this hoax as a distraction to talk about anything other than Democrats getting utterly defeated by President Trump in the [2025 government] shutdown fight."
Snopes reached out to communications staff at the Democratic National Committee, which runs the @TheDemocrats X account, to confirm whether it posted and deleted the X post in question, and why. We also reached out to Kates to confirm her role in the correspondence and whether Epstein told her he spent Thanksgiving with Trump. We reached out again in 2026 and await replies to our queries.
Trump's calendar did not show meeting with Epstein
According to Roll Call and reports at the time, Trump arrived at Palm Beach International Airport the afternoon of Nov. 21, 2017. He had no public events scheduled on Nov. 22, but met with pool reporters in the morning and went to Trump International Golf Club around 9:30 a.m., according to Roll Call. Trump posted (archived) on X on Nov. 22 that he would be "having meetings and working the phones from the Winter White House in Florida (Mar-a-Lago)."
On Thanksgiving, Nov. 23, Roll Call's calendar showed Trump thanked members of the military on a virtual call and visited Coast Guard members at Lake Worth Inlet Station before heading back to Trump International Golf Club around 11 a.m. News reports and official records corroborated the two Nov. 23 engagements in or near Palm Beach.
Trump had no public events scheduled on Nov. 24, 25 or 26, according to Roll Call. He reportedly played golf with professional golfers Tiger Woods and Dustin Johnson on Nov. 24.
Much of the time Trump spent in Palm Beach was unaccounted for in Roll Call's calendar. According to a CNN report at the time that cited White House spokespeople, Trump planned to celebrate the holiday with family at Mar-a-Lago. It was unclear exactly who attended festivities at Mar-a-Lago.
According to a Guardian analysis of the House Oversight Committee's document release, Epstein stayed informed about Trump's travel as it related to his own after the pair fell out. The Guardian reported that Epstein would discuss Trump's travel with employees as both regularly flew in and out of Palm Beach International Airport.
According to the report, Epstein continued to discuss Trump's whereabouts in New York City and Palm Beach and received news articles about Trump more generally from his associates after the two fell out and Trump became president.
Snopes previously reported on the content of the House Oversight Committee's email release, including whether Epstein called Trump "the dog that hasn't barked" or alleged Trump "knew about the girls," referring to victims of Epstein's alleged sex crimes.

The fetishization of mass murderers has been around since long before TikTok.
Bonnie and Clyde were folk heroes. Serial killer Ted Bundy was adored by a legion of female fans. And the mother of Columbine shooter Dylan Klebold reported receiving love letters to her son in the mail written by young girls.
More recently, this phenomenon has manifested in a network known as the True Crime Community, or TCC, a group of mainly young people who lionize mass shooters like Klebold. (This group is distinct from true crime enthusiasts who like to read books or listen to podcasts about unsolved crimes.)
While this community has been around for years, in 2026, it moved en masse to TikTok. There, supercharged by the video-sharing platform's powerful black-box algorithm, the community’s violent, nihilistic worldview expanded its reach dramatically, serving up graphic content to users who had never been exposed before.
Tracking the scale and real-world impact of the network has been difficult, because the coded language, symbols, and memes used within the group are constantly changing to avoid detection by platforms and law enforcement. On TikTok some of the group members most interested in violence began referring to the group as the True Cringe Community. When TikTok blocked that term, they began referring to themselves as the True Larp Community.
But now, for the first time, the National Contagion Research Institute (NCRI), a Princeton, New Jersey–based nonprofit that tracks online extremism, has collated data that shows that attacks and attempted attacks linked to the TCC have exploded by 200 percent over the last two years. The data, shared exclusively with WIRED ahead of publication, shows that the number of annual attacks or attempted attacks have gone from 13 reported in all of 2024 to 30 by mid-October this year.
The footprint of these attacks also expanded globally. Attacks and attempted attacks linked to the TCC were registered in 13 different countries in 2026, with two of every three incidents happening outside the US. And NCRI’s researchers predict that without intervention, the situation is about to get much worse.
“This is heading towards an explosion,” Joel Finkelstein, chief science officer with NCRI, tells WIRED. “That's what the data is suggesting, and the data is unambiguous. It's heading next year to a point where this is going to be happening more than once a week. That's really alarming.”
The TCC is part of a broader online nihilistic violent extremism movement and often overlaps with the extremist crime network known as “The Com,” which incorporates groups like 764 and No Lives Matter,
The TCC’s members, a large proportion of which are teenagers, share content online that references, glorifies, mimics, and simulates school shooters, mass shooters, and serial killers from all over the world. This is done through flattering videos posted on social media, taking pictures replicating the hand signals attackers used during their killing sprees, or wearing the T-shirts worn by mass shooters. The members also use AI to turn videos of mass shootings into cartoons or anime in order to avoid detection by online platforms’ trust and safety teams.
Beyond posting fan fiction about their favorite school shooters, this community also encourages others to carry out their own attacks. If successful, those attackers in turn become part of TCC’s ever-expanding lore and mythology, becoming part of a self-reinforcing cycle.
While writing its report, NCRI researchers documented numerous other attacks linked to the group, including the September 18 shooting at a high school in the Philippines and an October 1 attack at a secondary school in Torreón, Mexico. There was also a shooting on October 12 at a middle school in France and a knife attack on October 13 in South Africa that have also been linked to the TCC community.
While TCC was found on a lot of platforms online, for the first 10 years of its existence, much of its activity was centered on Tumblr. But in January, the site implemented a ban wave that drove much of the community to TikTok, where the platform’s unique algorithm put TCC-related content in front of a much broader audience, according to a report from the Institute of Strategic Dialogue published earlier this month.
“Algorithmically driven engagement has supercharged its spread,” the report’s authors wrote. “Unlike Tumblr, where the fandom is largely isolated, TikTok actively works to expose users to new content through its algorithm, resulting in TCC videos being served to a much larger audience.”
Finkelstein says that while TikTok does remove some of the accounts his team flags to the platform, in general the company is not doing enough to combat the problem.
“[TikTok’s] capacity to manage this is very spotty,” Finkelstein said. “This is an uncontained open wound. Whatever measures they think they're making to manage this are obviously inadequate to deal with the damage that the community is unleashing. If you took TikTok offline for a few weeks, my guess is these attacks would slow down because there's not a permission structure in place that's encouraging vulnerable youth to go out and murder people in order to be famous with their peers because they're so depressed and living in their mom's basement and spending 10 hours a day on social media.”
TikTok, whose US operations are now owned primarily by a group of investors including Oracle, controlled by GOP megadonor and Donald Trump ally Larry Ellison, said it had rules in place to proactively remove TCC-linked content.
“We enforce strict rules against content that promotes violence or glorifies perpetrators of mass violence, and we had already banned a large number of the accounts in this report,” a TikTok spokesperson tells WIRED.
WIRED shared the report with several other researchers who closely track TCC activity online, and all broadly concluded that NCRI’s assessment was accurate. One independent researcher, Ry Terran, pointed out that accurately tracking this movement is difficult given the dense nature of the language they use around attacks.
“When examining perpetrators' social media, I see that they frequently frame threats as a joke, a LARP, or AI-generated,” Terran tells WIRED. “Social media companies should not take these claims at face value, but rather report any credible threats. Without appropriate interventions, TCC-inspired attacks will likely continue to increase.”
Another European-based researcher, who requested anonymity due to fears of retaliation, tells WIRED, “We're panicking here in Europe.” The researcher collaborates with European law enforcement agencies and says they are concerned about the increasing number of attacks taking place globally.
Finkelstein says that US lawmakers and law enforcement need to do more in order to combat this problem. “The FBI seems to want to deal with it by arresting kids. None of this makes any sense,” he says. “We've got to step back and see the scale of this. We should be turning to our law enforcement agencies and our national security apparatus that has the ear of the president and say something's got to be done about this.”
The FBI declined to comment, and the White House did not respond to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security referred WIRED to the FBI.
“The Justice Department remains vigilant against the threat of such violent extremist networks that operate within the United States and around the globe,” Wyn Hornbuckle, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, tells WIRED.

Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
The claim
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
The evidence
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
The bottom line
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit
- Published
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.
It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.
But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.
"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.
Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.
"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.
In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.
"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.
Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.
Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.
Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.
"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.
Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.
Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.
While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

She filmed herself deliberately pressing her breast against a man’s hand while he visibly tried to create distance and protect himself.
If true, this wasn’t an accident. It was a calculated attempt to manufacture a molestation clip — just for views.
One video. One false narrative. And an innocent man’s life, reputation, and freedom put at risk for content.
This is not empowerment. This is weaponizing accusations. When will society stop treating every man as guilty by default?
Innocent until proven guilty — even when the camera is rolling.
#FalseAccusations #DueProcess #MenToo #JusticeForAll
— MenToo (@MenTooSave) November 19, 2026
Men’s rights activist Barkha Trehan shared the same video on her Instagram account (@barkhatrehan16) on November 20. She also claimed the woman was trying to manufacture a molestation video for views, and the incident was from Patna, Bihar.
Social activist Deepika Narayan Bhardwaj (@DeepikaBhardwaj) also shared the video on X claiming the woman was deliberately sticking to the man so that she could “cry molestation”.
Fact Check
A close examination of the video shows that there is a release announcement poster of a film, ‘Janak’ at the end of the video. Below is a screenshot of the last frame of the viral video:
We then searched for the trailer of the movie, ‘Janak’, and found it on the YouTube channel of Marathi Cineyug, where it had been uploaded on October 14, 2026. The trailer contains the visual that is now viral. The same two people, the same background, clothing and movements can be seen at the 0:49-0:50-second mark in the trailer.
In the process, we also found behind-the-scene photos related to the movie shared on Instagram by Anushka Pimputkar, the woman in the viral clip. In one of the photos, she is seen with Avinash Narkar, the actor who is standing next to her in the viral video.
To sum up, the viral video does not show a real incident of a woman trying to record a fake molestation clip on a bus. It is a scene from the trailer of the Marathi film, ‘Janak’. Social media claims presenting the footage as real are false.

Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.
On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.
The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.
Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.
In a statement, the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.
The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."
Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.
Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.
The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."
The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.
More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.
But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.
The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.
Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.
However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.
Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.
The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.
“Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” says Greg Pollock, the director of research at security company UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”
The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.
Exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more important than ever to attackers.
The data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock says.
The China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He says the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.
Pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, says that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.
“Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he says. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”
The larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler says.
“After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how big it was.”
Among the vast trove were email addresses, usernames, passwords, cookies, session tokens, device information, and more. Fowler says it is the largest exposure of credentials he has found in an accessible database, with the file structure and other attributes appearing to be distinct from a collection of more than a billion passwords amassed last year. He adds that he broadly validated the data using sampling methods, but did not comprehensively check for duplicates.
Fowler says there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.
The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims. The details included usernames and logins along with cookies, application and browser data, operating system details, and other “important files” that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.
Fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting company, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.
The enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.
