World chess champion Gukesh Dommaraju insisted he was approaching his first title defense with the mindset of a challenger on Sunday as he and Javokhir Sindarov faced the media ahead of their historic showdown in Geneva, the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title.
The two 20-year-old grandmasters appeared side by side at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva, where they struck a respectful tone before their best-of-14-games encounter begins on Tuesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva.
Pressed on whether defending a world championship was more difficult than winning it the first time, Gukesh politely rejected the premise.
“I don’t think I’m here to defend anything,” the Indian said. “I’m here to win it all over again. That’s the mindset I’m in.”
Sindarov, the fast-rising Uzbek challenger roughly six months older than Gukesh who enters the match as the oddsmakers’ favorite despite being a relative newcomer to the game’s highest level, was similarly reluctant to dole out predictions. Asked to assess his chances of becoming world champion, he put them at a diplomatic 50%.
“It’s a hard match and 14 games,” Sindarov said. “Everything can happen.”
The contest brings together two players whose careers have traced sharply divergent trajectories since Gukesh became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed champion in December 2024.
The Chennai native, who was only 18 when he defeated China’s Ding Liren to shatter the age record previously held by Garry Kasparov, has struggled badly for form since reaching the summit. After climbing to a career-high No 3 in the world that month, he has plummeted to No 26 following an extended string of underwhelming performances, making him the lowest-ranked reigning world champion since Elo ratings were introduced in 1971.
Sindarov, meanwhile, has surged from No 25 a year ago to a career-best No 4 after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup in Goa last November and an unbeaten masterclass at this year’s Candidates Tournament in Cyprus, where he finished with six wins and eight draws against a stacked field including Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri to earn a shot at Gukesh’s title.
The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Sindarov also holds a 2½-½ advantage in their three previous classical meetings, with two wins and one draw.
Yet both men played down the significance of past results on Sunday.
“Whatever has happened till now, I think just gets erased when we sit at the table for Game 1,” Gukesh said. “It’s a completely different match, completely different opponent and different place.”
He acknowledged Sindarov’s sustained run of success, describing the Tashkent-born challenger as one of the world’s strongest players and predicting a formidable assignment.
“Sindarov has just been in very consistent and very good form,” Gukesh said. “It’s for sure going to be a real test.”
Sindarov was equally complimentary about the champion, pointing to his extraordinary performances in winning the title as evidence that his recent difficulties should not be overinterpreted.
“Gukesh’s performance in 2024 is something fantastic,” Sindarov said, adding that he had experienced the Indian’s strength firsthand in January when they played to a 78-move draw at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee. “Sometimes you have some bad periods.”
The two players also revealed contrasting approaches to preparing for the championship. While Gukesh deliberately pared back his tournament schedule this year, Sindarov continued regularly entering competitions against elite opposition, reasoning that he needed more experience at the highest level.
Sindarov added that he had accepted an invitation to the four-month Grand Chess Tour circuit before winning the Candidates and saw little reason to withdraw afterward.
“Even after I won Candidates, I wanted to have more experience because I didn’t play that many strong tournaments in my career,” he said. “I’m happy with my decision.”
Gukesh said the strategy had not surprised him or his team, who expected the challenger to take advantage of his momentum and accumulate experience against the world’s strongest players. The trade-off was that Sindarov’s busy slate also gave Gukesh and his team a wealth of recent games to study for clues about the challenger’s approach.
The preparations have also given Sindarov an appreciation for the peculiar demands of a world title match. He once found it difficult to believe that players could spend three or four months preparing to face a single opponent. Now, having devoted much of the past six months to the task himself, he wonders whether even that is enough.
“I was thinking six months is enough time,” he said. “But maybe even this six months ... is also maybe not enough to prepare for such a hard tournament.”
The Indian, by contrast, can draw on his experience in the pressure-cooker environment of the world championship stage, where the psychological and physical demands of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Gukesh said he had been surfing, running and spending time outdoors, while Sindarov has taken up padel, playing regularly during his training camp.
“If I would be, like, 30, 40, maybe it will be tough,” Sindarov said. “But because I’m young, I think it’ll be not very hard, like, physically.”
Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who helped guide his successful 2024 campaign, as well as South African mental conditioning coach Paddy Upton, who was part of the backroom staff for India’s cricket team when they won the 2011 World Cup and the Indian men’s hockey team when they claimed bronze at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Sindarov revealed he is working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, although neither player has publicly disclosed the full composition of his team of seconds, the trusted advisers responsible for preparing openings and analyzing the opponent.
The match will be staged at the Fondation Martin Bodmer, a museum and research library housing rare manuscripts and books, including a Gutenberg Bible, a Shakespeare First Folio and a first edition of Isaac Newton’s Principia. Both players inspected the playing hall on Saturday ahead of Monday’s technical meeting.
Unlike most recent world championship tilts, the players will not compete inside a purpose-built soundproof enclosure. Fide has abandoned the familiar transparent cube in order to preserve the atmosphere of the historic venue, relying instead on enhanced security measures and strict limits on the number of spectators and media admitted to the playing hall.
Sindarov admitted that he had expected to play inside the traditional fishbowl, but was impressed by the stage. “The playing hall is really very beautiful,” he said. Gukesh, meanwhile, said he had checked the chairs, lighting and even the floor to ensure he would be comfortable during games that could last four or five hours – and occasionally even longer. As for the rare books surrounding the board, the champion admitted he had barely looked at them. “I don’t think I’ll be reading in between the games,” he joked.
The glass enclosure, designed to shield players from distractions, was first used during Garry Kasparov’s 1995 title defense against Viswanathan Anand at New York’s World Trade Center and has featured in numerous subsequent championships, including Gukesh’s victory over Ding in Singapore two years ago. Sindarov admitted the setting would take some getting used to, having never played a tournament in which there was nobody else competing nearby.
The match carries a $2.5m (£1.9m) prize fund, with $200,000 awarded for each decisive game and the remainder divided equally between the players. Sindarov will open with the white pieces on Tuesday after the drawing of lots at Sunday’s opening ceremony, with the players alternating colors throughout the match. The first to reach seven and a half points will be crowned champion, with rapid and blitz tiebreaks scheduled if the contest finishes level after 14 games. Three of the past five world title matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023.
The winner will join or continue a centuries-spanning lineage stretching back to Wilhelm Steinitz, who became the first official world champion in 1886. Gukesh is seeking to retain the crown he won as a teenager, while Sindarov is attempting to become the first player from Uzbekistan to capture the title.
For now, neither is allowing himself to dwell too much on what victory might mean.
Sindarov, who will turn 21 on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12, said he had made no pledges or wagers about how he might celebrate winning the championship.
“I really want to focus on my next 20 days and try to play my best chess,” he said. “Then we’ll see.”
Gukesh, who celebrated his 2024 triumph by fulfilling a promise to go bungee jumping, was more cryptic when asked whether he had another stunt up his sleeve.
“I have a couple of things in mind,” he said, smiling. “I think you’ll get to know in time, maybe.”

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A
- Published
Max Verstappen triumphed in a thrilling Las Vegas Grand Prix ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.
There were 34 lead changes across the 50 laps of racing as Dutchman Verstappen held off attacks from Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, plus his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar.
Ferrari had to deal with another intra-team battle on track as Charles Leclerc received a 10-second time penalty after colliding with Lewis Hamilton.
Here, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
After Las Vegas, have Ferrari now reached a crossroads? With Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's on-track antics, is their partnership sustainable? Should Ferrari consider a change of direction, potentially bringing Oliver Bearman into the equation? - Michael
The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Ferrari is one that keeps on giving - but not in a way Ferrari would want.
The collision in Las Vegas for which Leclerc was penalised was just the latest flashpoint for the team in a season that has been full of them.
The drivers argued over race strategy in relation to each other in Zandvoort and Singapore.
Hamilton made an aggressive dive down the inside at the first chicane on the first lap at Monza, only for Leclerc to shove him on to the gravel.
Hamilton ignored calls to pit in both Singapore (because he didn't want to just circulate behind Leclerc) and Brazil (because, he said, he had not been given enough information about the weather).
There was the first-lap incident at Turn Four in Mexico in which their fighting led to both going off track and letting in Max Verstappen to win a race Ferrari should have finished one-two.
And now Las Vegas, where first Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty for gaining a position on Lando Norris on track in an incident that also involved Leclerc, then Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for tipping Hamilton into a spin later in the race.
Leclerc was on the receiving end of team principal Frederic Vasseur's ire in Las Vegas - the Frenchman calling the situation "unacceptable". But inside Ferrari they felt both drivers had a degree of culpability for the Mexico situation.
Somehow Vasseur needs to get a handle on this.
Ferrari want to allow them to race. And it's hard to imagine two drivers of such standing would accept anything else.
The problem is that doing so, amid their battle for supremacy within the team, is harming the team's results.
The concern for Ferrari is this is happening when there is relatively little at stake. It's easy to imagine how combustible it could become if Ferrari have a car capable of challenging for the title next year.
Both want to be the driver to deliver that next championship, for very different reasons.
Hamilton would get his eighth, which he feels he was unfairly denied in Abu Dhabi in 2021. And Leclerc would win his first, and complete the journey of being the first Ferrari academy driver to win the world championship for the team.
At the moment, this is not an existential question, but it's easy to see how it could become one, and Ferrari left with a decision of it being one or the other if they can't find a way to race without compromising the team.
But that's not just on Vasseur.
Both drivers have buy into that and, as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have largely done at McLaren, accept there will be days when they have to sacrifice themselves for the greater good of Ferrari while ensuring they are ahead of the other more often than not on speed and fair racing.
It's then up to the team to decide when there comes a point to impose team orders if either or both are in a title fight with another driver.
It remains to be seen whether either of them can fully buy into that in circumstances when they individually end up losing out.
Why does George Russell often feel the need to try mind games and make comments, such as those about Max Verstappen? It often backfires on him and are usually made when he's got nothing to race for. Shouldn't he focus on himself? - Nick
This, as Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff pointed out after the race in Las Vegas, is a rivalry that goes back years.
"They've known each other so long," was Wolff's verdict. "Since karting. I think it's probably been a bit of cat and mouse. Provocations on either side. Another good factor of entertainment."
Verstappen also had a bit of a set-to with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in Mexico practice, which was not dissimilar in some ways.
There, stewards ruled that both had driven in an "unacceptable manner" and both drivers admitted their moves had been unnecessary and clumsy.
There's no question Russell believed what he was saying about Verstappen's driving in final practice at Las Vegas. According to the stewards, he was in the right, as Verstappen was given a warning for his changing direction in the braking zone.
Are these mind games? Or just Russell saying what he thinks? He feels he has a valid point to make.
Making it in public does not seem to affect Verstappen in any way. Does it change anything? Verstappen is a remorseless, ruthless competitor on track whether he is provoked or not.
Yes, he admitted satisfaction when he saw Russell make his late-race error in Las Vegas. But did he race any differently because of the Briton's comments? That's unlikely. Verstappen was just doing what he felt was right to win the race.
Ultimately, it's Russell's career, and it's up to him how he conducts himself, what he chooses to say in public and what he does not.
Track design, cold temperatures, energy deployment strategies or just the unwillingness of one team-mate to hold station behind another. What was the dominant factor in Las Vegas that led to such a hectic race? - Tim
The extraordinary Las Vegas race, with long trains of cars unable to break free of each other, was a combination of technical factors. Nothing to do with the willingness or otherwise of team-mates to hold station.
It was a combination of the track characteristics, particularly the long straights, the energy deployment demands of the engines, which are energy starved, and the cold temperatures and track surface and the effect they had on tyre behaviour.
As Max Verstappen said: "It was just the tow (in) combination with the deployment. Of course, when you are within a second, you have the overtake mode as well, and around here that is powerful. So, you could not pull away."
The tow provided a significant lap time gain of well over 0.5secs a lap. That's why a car in front could not pull away from a car behind even if it was slightly quicker.
The overtake mode provides an extra 0.5MJ of electrical energy per lap for a car following another by under a second. So that's another factor preventing someone pulling away.
Then the batteries were running out before the end of the straights, so a car running in front in free air was suffering from that, too.
On top of that, Las Vegas is a smooth track which is light on tyres. So degradation was almost non-existent. That kept tyre temperatures under control and allowed people to push hard throughout.
If the tyres had shown their usual behaviour of surface overheating leading to sliding, there would have been less action as drivers would have found it much harder to follow each other closely. As is usually the case in F1.
Drivers have been pushing for years for tyres to behave in this way, but so far Pirelli has been unable or unwilling to provide them. It only happens occasionally in specific circumstances.
The flip side of the argument is that so-called zero-deg races are sometimes boring as much as they are sometimes great, because drivers pushing to the limit can means less overtaking. Not in this case, though

With a move to engines with a smaller electrical component in 2030, are F1 cars becoming less relevant to modern road cars? The argument was always that F1 is the test bed for future road car technology. - Paul
The current F1 engines, with a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, were decided upon five or so years ago when the road-car market was slightly different to now.
The push for electrification is still there, and will continue. But consumer take-up of electric cars, especially in the performance market, has not been what manufacturers expected. Hence a slight shift in focus.
That said, it's not as if the current F1 engines are especially road relevant. With a few exceptions, road cars tend to be either full electric, plug-in hybrid, where the electrical element is much less than 50-50, or full internal combustion.
So there is an argument the new engines, with sustainable fuel and a hybrid element that is about 12-13% of total output normally or 25% when on overtake mode, are more relevant to road cars, not less, at least in their fundamental architecture.
The sustainable fuel is key here.
If this can get to a point where it is available to the mass market - and F1 is simplifying the demands on its make-up for the next ruleset in an attempt to help make the fuel more cost-effective for exactly that reason - it could be a game-changer for emissions in the road-car market.
That's because there will inevitably be a lot of legacy internal combustion vehicles on the road globally for many years, even after the new-car market becomes fully electric.
So if emissions from these can be reduced by 80%, as is the ballpark figure for the carbon-impact reduction of sustainable fuels versus fossil fuels, that's a major step.
Don't forget, too, the 2030 rules were the product of talks between the manufacturers and the FIA.
It was the manufacturers who pushed back against FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's initial desire for a naturally aspirated engine with no hybrid element.
And they did that exactly because it made them more road relevant.

Donald Trump’s administration has reached an agreement to let Kilmar Abrego Garcia leave the U.S. voluntarily, ending a nearly two-year legal battle over the fate of a Salvadoran immigrant whose story has been at the center of the president’s mass deportation campaign.
He boarded a commercial flight to Spain on Tuesday night.
Abrego Garcia’s case has been a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s efforts to rapidly arrest and deport tens of thousands of people from the country despite legal safeguards and humanitarian protections that the president has also eroded since returning to the White House.
The administration has spent the last year trying to deport Abrego Garcia a second time — including to Liberia — after the government unlawfully deported him to a brutal prison in his home country, triggering the high-profile legal battle for his return.
“After a protracted fight, Abrego Garcia, on his terms, boarded a flight tonight to Spain,” his legal team said in a statement Tuesday. “We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department. He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
The Independent has requested comment from the Department of Homeland Security.
Abrego Garcia, 31, has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years after fleeing gang violence in El Salvador and entering the U.S. illegally as a teenager. An immigration judge blocked the government from deporting him to his home country in 2019.
But last year, federal agents abruptly deported Abrego Garcia to El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison where he says he endured torture and “severe” abuse for several weeks before he was transferred to a separate jail.
Government officials admitted in court that his removal was due to an “error,” and several federal judges and a unanimous Supreme Court ordered the administration to “facilitate” his return.
The government spent weeks battling those orders while White House officials launched a barrage of public attacks against him and declared that he would never again step foot in the country.
He was returned to the U.S. last June — only to face allegations that he illegally moved other immigrants across the country. He pleaded not guilty.
A federal judge later dismissed the criminal case against him after finding that the administration unlawfully targeted him as part of a smear campaign.
“Objective evidence” has shown that federal prosecutors only brought charges against Abrego Garcia after he won his lawsuit challenging his arrest and removal, the judge ruled.
The administration has, at the same time, tried to deport him to at least five different countries, including four in Africa, and refused to let him leave the country for Costa Rica.
In a memo issued in March, ICE’s then-acting director Todd Lyons argued that sending him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States.”
In April, the administration “analyzed and eliminated all other options” from the table and settled on Liberia as “a final country of removal,” despite his own attempts to voluntarily remove himself to Costa Rica.
Government lawyers argued in court documents that the U.S. has expended significant political capital and entered “high-stakes” and “extensive negotiations” to send him to Liberia.
But the judge overseeing his deportation case had blocked Immigration and Customs Enforcement from re-deporting or detaining him, noting earlier this year that the government has made “one empty threat after another to remove him to countries in Africa with no real chance of success.”
Both sides were scheduled to discuss his case at a hearing in October, but U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis abruptly ended the hearing after she met privately with attorneys in her chambers.
Judge Xinis issued an order in the case on November 20 but it remains sealed.
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who traveled to El Salvador in an attempt to secure Abrego Garcia’s release from prisons there, said his constituent is now “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man — unharmed and with dignity.”
“While the Trump administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar's will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said in a statement Tuesday night.
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this administration’s constant persecution,” he added. “This is a victory for due process and our Constitution.”

US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
- Published
The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.
The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.
The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.
The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.
While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.
Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.
The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.
In the run up to the Shenzhen summit, the US accused China of not fully living up to the terms of what it agreed in October 2025.
Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".
However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.
The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

Children who lived in Brazilian neighbourhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday.
The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world's dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten.
In neighbourhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighbourhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil's severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team.
The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.
“This is really exciting,” said David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn't involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places.
The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s.
Usually in the continental US, dengue is found mostly in people who travelled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa.
Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy.
How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes' ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population.
Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus.
The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease.

Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.
Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.
Build-your-own Medicare menu
Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.
Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
Medicare Advantage
This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
"People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.
The hassle saves money
Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. But that average doesn't tell the whole story. An analysis by KFF, the health policy research nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, found that enrollees who stay in their prescription drug plan will see a 50% increase on average, from $34 to $51. About 10.4 million people could pay higher premiums, not including higher deductibles and coinsurance costs.
Some beneficiaries who didn't have to pay monthly premiums in recent years will begin paying for prescription drug Part D coverage in 2027. While that change follows the 2025 introduction of federal caps on out-of-pocket drug expenses, it comes as the Trump administration is ending temporary federal subsidies that helped keep premiums down. The cap on out-of-pocket expenses for prescription drugs in 2027 will be $2,400, a total enrollees can opt tospread out over the course of the year.
Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said people who don't shop around could be leaving money on the table.
"It is worth it to avoid any unpleasant surprises in the form of either higher premiums or higher cost sharing for covered services in 2027," she said.
Some plans no longer offered
An estimated 4.3 million people now have to look for a new Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plan after private insurers left the market. Those who want to stay in Medicare Advantage must select new coverage, or they'll be moved to traditional Medicare automatically. For those shopping for a new plan, low monthly premiums may be appealing, but it's important to read the fine print and add up the other costs.
"There are going to be, often, increases in cost sharing and copays, increases in out-of-pocket caps, and reductions in the scope of some of the extra benefits that Medicare Advantage plans provide," Lipschutz said.
So ask: Is my prescription covered? Is my pharmacy preferred? Is my doctor in-network? What does the dental benefit actually cover?
And pay attention to the out-of-pocket maximum for the Advantage plans, Cubanski said, so you know how much you might have to shell out in 2027.
"Look at that dollar value specifically," she said.
For those moving to traditional Medicare, it won't come with a drug plan, so enrollees must sign up for a new Part D plan if they want most prescriptions covered. Enrollees who miss that step when they are first eligible may not have drug coverage for the coming year, and they may face a late-enrollment penalty on their monthly premiums for life.
When selecting a drug plan, enrollees must also tell their insurer how they want to pay, either by getting a bill in the mail or by having the cost deducted from their Social Security. If you don't pick a payment plan, you could get dropped from coverage.
If enrollees elect to leave their Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare within their first year of joining Medicare, they have a guaranteed right to buy a Medigap plan, with no health screening. After that, all bets are off: Insurers in most states can turn enrollees down or charge more because of a health condition. Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, and New York are exceptions.
Enrollees whose Advantage plans have not been renewed — and haven't been consolidated into another plan — can switch to traditional Medicare and buy a Medigap policy without a health screening, but they need to act before March.
For shopping help, think "SHIP"
Medicare experts advise enrollees to write down all their prescription drugs, as well as any procedures planned in the next year, such as a joint replacement or dental work, to help them decide which plan will cover their needs. Call a favorite doctor's office to see whether they are in-network for the plans being considered. Remember that brokers might earn commissions, especially on Advantage plans, and might not represent every plan.
For unbiased help, every state has a federally funded State Health Insurance Assistance Program that offers free plan counseling specific to your situation, in person and over the phone. To get help, go to the website at shiphelp.org/open-enrollment, email info@shiphelp.org, or call the SHIP National Technical Assistance Center at 877-839-2675.
A SHIP counselor can also help enrollees apply for benefits that help pay for Medicare premiums and prescription drug costs, such as the Medicare Savings Programs and Medicare Part D Extra Help.

Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.
"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."
A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."
Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.
They say it's theirs.
Land grabs and falsified documents
"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.
After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.
When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.
In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.
He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and, later, became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach. But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlore named Pellumb Petritaj.
The pair has claimed plots of land — including Mocka's family plot — up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Nov. 18, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlore on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land — which does not include Mocka's family plot — confiscated from Shehu last week. The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
Albanian prosecutors say land linked to Kushner may have been "illegally acquired"
The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota, are past the age of 70. On a recent warm and sunny afternoon, the two are resting on benches in the courtyard of the village church after a day of harvesting olives. They nod their heads when asked about Artur Shehu.
"He is from the village of Kanina, far from here and up in the mountains," says Konomi, motioning inland, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings."
Then Kota speaks up. "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "But we've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."
Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the 300-acre parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner.
That transaction, however, is under review.
In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."
A spokesman for Kushner did not respond to NPR's request for comment by the time this article was published. Kushner had previously issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. "Title was reviewed by counsel and verified," the statement says.
Shehu did not respond to NPR's request for comment. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. However, in Tirana, a former lawyer for Shehu was willing to talk.
Oceanfront properties are now claimed by several parties
"The people that Artur [Shehu] has authorized by power of attorney to deal with his family's properties committed a forgery in which they removed the property from the brother of Artur's grandfather and passed it to Artur's grandfather," says Kujtim Cakrani. "That is the whole story of the property."
Cakrani says Shehu's associates forged an inheritance certificate that made it appear that Shehu's grandfather had owned the land, which was then passed to Artur Shehu himself. And then last April, Shehu sold that land to Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, Syrian-born Qatari billionaire brothers who are financial partners of Jared Kushner.
Cakrani says that when he discovered that Artur Shehu was involved in this alleged forgery, he dropped him as his client. "I could no longer continue representing him because of the seriousness of the matter," he says. "It is impossible for me, with these documents that he has, to defend him."
And this is why, Cakrani says, Albanian state prosecutors have put Shehu under investigation and froze his bank accounts. Cakrani says he is now representing a group of 30 relatives of Shehu who he claims to be the rightful owners of this land.
Gentian Mocka, as well as Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota in Zvernec, tell NPR that nobody by the name of Shehu — neither Artur nor his relatives — has any legal claim to what they say is their land, oceanfront property that has now been claimed by several parties, including the son-in-law of the president of the United States.
Wealthy speculators have exploited land in Albania since the fall of communism
Albanian real estate law expert Roden Hoxha says he has seen this kind of land battle many times before. "But now that Kushner is in it," he says, "everybody is freaking out."
He says land ownership in Albania is complicated by decades under a Stalinist regime that stole all the land from private owners and collectivized it. When communism fell in 1991, he says Albania became a land grab free-for-all.
"It was basically chaos," he says. "People started claiming land wherever they threw a stone. It was basically the Albanian version of the U.S.' claiming of the West."
Hoxha describes wealthy speculators keen to exploit the chaos of the moment: locals whose families have farmed the land for generations and well-connected operators like Shehu, who aggressively try to claim that land. "And then on the international level," says Hoxha, most recently, "it exploded because it was Kushner and Trump and Arab money behind it."
And so, Hoxha says, what at first appeared to be yet another Albanian land dispute now has ties all the way to the White House. In the end, an Albanian court will likely decide who the rightful owner of this property is. But for now, it has sparked unprecedented public outrage in Albania. Protesters have taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, every day since May 31, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. But Rama has only vowed to crack down harder on what have become increasingly violent demonstrations against his entire government.
Rama has also vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned, but an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.
When contacted by NPR, Elona Sinaj, Rama's spokesperson, sent a statement saying, "If the seller does not have legitimate ownership of the property, the money will remain within the Republic of Albania, and certainly it will be used for anyone who proves that his claim over the property is grounded."
Sinaj went on to say that the ambition for Rama's government is "to create a new benchmark for sustainable Mediterranean development."
Some Albanians see advantages to having a Kushner-linked resort
That goal aligns with Kushner's vision for a luxury resort — a five-star ecotourism site, as his wife, Ivanka Trump, laid out in a podcast episode called "Ivanka Trump on Building the Authentic Life."
"For me," said Trump, "this is, it feels more like a challenge than anything else, the culmination of all of my experience in real estate, all of my travel, a lot of reflection on how I want to live."
In the podcast, Trump described both the Zvernec beachfront property as well as Sazan — an uninhabited island across from it — as part of a development project belonging to her and Kushner.
Local tour operator Sherif Durmishaj has made a living taking tourists to Sazan by boat, guiding hikes past foxholes and signs along the trail that warn of active land mines scattered throughout the island's forests. For years, this island was a fortified military outpost.
Durmishaj says he's seen the ongoing protests against the Kushner project, but he takes a different view of it.
"I work in tourism, and I'm from here," he says, "and if you've seen how local developers, along with the mafia, have built this region, it's just a massacre. They've destroyed so much of what is a beautiful coastline, and I support the Kushner project because it's going to be ecologically sustainable and it will set a good benchmark for future projects."
"We are a small country," Durmishaj says, "and Kushner and Trump are very big names."
At least one big name will be in the crosshairs of the incoming Democratic Congress in the U.S.
Regarding Kushner, "This is an individual in the Trump family who has essentially been two-timing on the American people," says Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to chair the House Judiciary Committee and will have the power to investigate and subpoena members of President Trump's family.
He says he'll be focusing on Kushner, who he says has been splitting his time between foreign policy and making business deals on the side.
"American foreign policy has never seen anything like that before," says Raskin. "And in this, of course, he is only imitating his father-in-law, who declared that he got $2.2 billion on the side in his first year in office. Uh, that's more than $1 million an hour."
Raskin says the luxury resort project in Albania is one of many Kushner-backed deals that have prompted investigative inquiries from his committee, and there could be more as the new U.S. Congress is sworn in in January.
Fjori Sinoruka contributed to this report.

The map circulating online is an official document from the United States Department of Agriculture that shows the origin of agricultural products by market value in 2012. Further data suggested that Iowa remains one of the top agricultural states in 2026. It's important to note that the map does not show the expected spread of the lead plume or any other environmental effects resulting from the detonation.
Rumors that the U.S. Army planned to detonate a toxic compound in an area that is notable for its high concentration of agricultural output circulated in November.
The rumor circulated amid reports that the U.S. Army planned to detonate a stockpile of lead azide, a highly explosive compound used to detonate munitions, in late November. The detonations took place on Nov. 25, 2026, several days after the original scheduled date of Nov. 20.
People on social media shared a purported map that depicted blue dots representing the highest areas of food production in the U.S. and suggested that one of its most condensed areas of agricultural production was where the Army planned to explode the compound.
One post read, "The blue is where our food supply is grown. The red is where our government is exploding a large cache of lead azide on Wednesday."
The claim that the map shared online accurately depicted a high concentration of agriculture production in the same area as the lead azide detonation is true, with some important context. 
Snopes previously confirmed reports that the U.S. Army planned the detonations at the Iowa Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, whose location appeared on the agriculture map as an area of high agricultural production.
The map originated from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service, which mapped out the country's leading producers of agriculture in terms of sales value back in 2012.
The department stated that while California was the country's largest producer of crops and livestock based on sales, "Iowa, Texas, Nebraska, and Minnesota round out the top five agricultural-producing States, with those five representing more than a third of U.S. agricultural-output value."
The detonation site in Middletown, Iowa, is located in the southeastern region of the state.
Comparing the agriculture map side-by-side with a Google Maps search for the Iowa Ammunition Plant showed that the site of the lead detonation was located in a highly concentrated area of agriculture production.
Below, we've overlaid the Iowa portion of the Department of Agriculture's map with a transparent Google Maps screenshot depicting the location of the detonation.
(U.S. Department of Agriculture/Google Maps/Snopes Illustration)
Further, a Google Maps search in the area surrounding the Iowa Ammunition Plant revealed numerous farms of varying size and crops surrounding the area. The address listed on the plant's official website matched that listed on Google Maps.
While the map is authentic, it's crucial to note that it does not contain any information about the expected spread of the lead plume or any other environmental effects resulting from the detonation. Rather, it simply shows the detonation site's location in the context of a map showing the concentration of agricultural products' market value in 2012, with each blue dot representing $20 million.
For up-to-date information on the spread of the plume, the U.S. Army is releasing lead azide deposition maps. In addition, the open-source tracking alternative Iowa Lead Tracker, which is independent of the Army, is also tracking the plume.
We've reached out to the U.S. Army and the Department of Agriculture for further comment on the potential impact of the toxic plume resulting from the detonation on local agriculture and the wider national food supply.
(Google Maps)
It's worth noting that, although the map circulating online was from 2012, it is featured as the most current available data on the Department of Agriculture's website, where it appears on a web page last updated in February 2024.
According to the American Farm Bureau Federation, self-described as "the national advocate for farmers, ranchers and rural communities," Iowa remains one of the nation's leading states in agriculture.
The organization reported that in 2026, "net farm income was highest in California ($26 billion), Texas ($15 billion), Iowa ($10 billion), and Nebraska (more than $8 billion), which together accounted for over 30% of the national total."
On Nov. 24, the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship issued a guidance for livestock farmers within 20 miles of Middletown, which suggested, among other recommendations, keeping "livestock at an alternate location or indoors until the U.S. Army gives the 'all clear' and the air plume has passed by your area. It may take several hours for the dust particles to settle, according to the U.S. Army."
According to the Army as reported by The Associated Press, the detonation was successful and there was "no lead in the air around the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown," but officials warned "the wind is expected to carry the plume southwest toward Missouri and away from the nearby city of Burlington and the Mississippi River."

'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
‘Medicare for all’ is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight over "Medicare for All."
The midterm elections resulted in victories for several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act, which despite incendiary politics made incremental reforms, barely squeaked into law in 2010 after similar disputes..
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
"It's cosplay"
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase "Medicare for All" actually means. "It's cosplay," said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. "When you say 'Medicare for All,' people think 'Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.'"
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF's public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
"I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs," she said of survey respondents' support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. "I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program."
Medicare faces headwinds
A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033.
Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump's second term began.
"Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs," Brodie said.
There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.
Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as "a socialist takeover of our healthcare system" — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.
Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It's the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.
A deeper dissatisfaction?
There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous "Harry and Louise" ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially.
KFF's September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That's a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they'd rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have.
Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it's up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page.
HealthBent, a regular feature of KFF Health News, offers insight into and analysis of policies and politics from KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner, who has covered health care for more than 40 years.

Shadowfax has acquired the Indian entity of global same-day intra-city delivery platform Borzo (formerly known as WeFast) for ₹23.3 Cr, the logistics major disclosed today. With the acquisition, Shadowfax is set to enter on-demand intra-city goods transportation category and expand its reach into small and medium business (SME) and C2C deliveries. Shadowfax had earlier launched Shadowfax 360 to open its express parcel network to SMEs and D2C brands, and scaled the service up to over 6,700 transacting sellers within two quarters. The deal now enables the company to extend the same model from parcel shipping to intra-city goods transportation. Founded in 2012 by Mike Alexandrovski, Aleks Shamis, and Dmitry Zubkov, Borzo had raised over $55 Mn from investors like Mubadala, AddVenture, Russian Direct Investment Fund, and Flashpoint. Founded in Russia and based in Amsterdam, it later relocated its headquarters to Mumbai in 2024. It currently operates in over five Indian cities with a fleet of over 32K delivery partners. The company claims it fulfils over 1.2 Cr deliveries annually. In CY25, it earned around ₹200 Cr in adjusted revenue. “Moving goods within cities is one of India’s largest logistics opportunities, and it has barely begun to go digital. Every day, shop owners, distributors and families still rely on phone calls and informal networks to get goods across town. That is set to change at scale, and Shadowfax intends to lead it,” added Shadowfax’s MD and CEO Abhishek Bansal. Founded in 2015 by Bansal and Vaibhav Khandelwal, Shadowfax provides last-mile delivery services to ecommerce platforms and D2C brands. The company listed on the bourses in January after a ₹1,907 Cr IPO. On the financial front, Shadowfax’s consolidated net profit jumped over 5X YoY to ₹68 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue rose 56.6% to ₹1,537.7 Cr.

The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
- Published
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.
Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.
At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.
Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.
India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

A new study has found that DNA methylation, a natural process that acts like a "dimmer switch" to turn genes down or completely off, varies more than expected across different brain regions in genes linked to PTSD.
Stress and trauma can leave molecular marks in the brain that may help explain the development of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a mental health disorder in which one experiences flashbacks or nightmares of a terrifying or life-threatening event.
The study, published in the journal 'Cell Reports', also found that among people affected by PTSD, the molecular variations appeared to be driven by a number of factors, including the sex and race of the person, and whether the trauma exposure occurred in childhood or adulthood.
"The question that our research aims to address is 'What is really different about the PTSD brain?'" corresponding author Frances Champagne of the University of Texas at Austin, US, said.
"The study found greater variation in DNA methylation patterns across brain regions in people with PTSD than in people with major depressive disorder. It also revealed considerable differences among individuals with PTSD," Champagne said.
The findings could open the door to more individualised treatment options for people with PTSD in the future, the researchers said.
A detailed methylation profiling was done of postmortem brains from 302 people -- 101 with PTSD, 100 without psychiatric disorders and 101 with major depressive disorder.
Three different regions of brain were analysed in each sample: the prefrontal cortex, involved in higher level functions, including decision-making, the amygdala or the emotional centre of the brain, and the hippocampus, which manages memory.
The study uncovered specific changes in the brain linked to PTSD, including a relative reduction in oligodendrocytes -- cells that form the protective covering of neurons (myelin sheath) -- in the amygdala of people with PTSD, particularly in those exposed to trauma in adulthood.
PTSD was also associated with more pronounced DNA methylation differences in the prefrontal cortex, while major depressive disorder was associated with methylation differences in the amygdala.
The molecular patterns were associated with differences in the composition of different cell types in the brain, the researchers said.
Because they analysed postmortem brain tissue, the team was not able to confirm whether the methylation differences contributed to PTSD, resulted from PTSD, or were influenced by other factors.
The authors also noted that they lacked detailed information about symptom type and severity for each individual, which would be important for developing more personalised methods of diagnosis.
