A world-class winger - Louis Rees-Zammit 2.0
- Published
Australia wing Harry Potter had Louis Rees-Zammit exactly where he wanted him.
As Wales attacked in Cardiff on Saturday, Potter showed Rees-Zammit the outside – a four-metre channel between him and the touchline.
The touchline is a defender's best friend. An extra defender. The edge of the cliff. It would take something extraordinary to beat Potter without running out of ground.
A shake of the hips and a change of direction later, Potter was diving like a cricketer in the outfield, grasping at thin air. Rees-Zammit was on his way to setting up a wonderful try for Blair Murray.
Rees-Zammit has been turning heads for years. On the pitch with his pace, off it with his pristine teeth and pop star looks.
But it wasn't raw speed that had left Potter on the turf.
This was Rees-Zammit 2.0 - more than just speed.
- Who should Wales pick for autumn finale v Japan? 
  - Published1 day ago
- Did beaten Wales still show they have come a long way? 
  - Published2 days ago
- Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat 
  - Published2 days ago
More wide receiver than running back
Alex Cuthbert knows a thing or two about running. A former national-level 400m runner and British and Irish Lions wing, he spent much of his rugby career working on his technique.
What fascinates him about Rees-Zammit now is not his speed but how he generates it.
"His leg drive and strength from his knee to his hip has got so much stronger," said Cuthbert, who scored 17 tries in 57 Tests for Wales.
The difference is most apparent not over 100 metres but over four or five, changing direction and accelerating before a defender can adjust his feet.
"If you do that shimmy and you stand any sort of player up, you can't recover. Literally can't recover," Cuthbert said.
Cuthbert attributes much of that development to Rees-Zammit's 18 months in American football with the Kansas City Chiefs and Jacksonville Jaguars.
"I thought last season he was a little bit heavy. He looked like a running back last year, whereas this year he is more of a wide receiver," Cuthbert said.
A running back, says Cuthbert, powers through traffic, a wide receiver thrives in open space. He now sees elements of both in Rees-Zammit.
'I'm a world-class winger'
Rees-Zammit's coach at Bristol Bears, Pat Lam, estimates he returned from America eight or nine kilograms heavier.
"What was very clear was his pace was still there, if not quicker, but he was a bigger man and he needed to adjust," said Lam.
Lam is arguably one of rugby's most system-driven coaches. Understanding your role is fundamental at Bristol, where only a select few are afforded the freedom to deviate from the script.
Having established himself as a wing before his American adventure, Rees-Zammit was keen to experiment on his return to rugby.
"He spoke to me about a desire to play full-back and give full-back a go," said Lam.
Lam sees the modern full-back as an auxiliary centre in attack, responsible for creating opportunities for others.
Rees-Zammit's greatest gift is exploiting them.
"But we had to go through that process for him to actually say to me, 'Pat, I'm a world-class winger and I'm a world-class finisher'. And I said, 'I agree'," Lam said.
According to Lam, Rees-Zammit now considers himself a wing who can cover full-back, rather than a full-back who can play on the wing.
The numbers behind the evolution
Another moment from Saturday offered a reminder of Rees-Zammit's extraordinary pace when Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i intercepted a Welsh pass and set off downfield.
The Australian, a formidable athlete in his own right, had a head start of at least five metres.
One commentator confidently declared he would not be caught.
Rees-Zammit caught him.
The speed has always been there. The numbers reveal how much more there is to his game now.
Rees-Zammit scored five tries in 10 Premiership appearances for Bristol last season. This season he has matched that tally in five games, beating 28 defenders and making 12 clean breaks.
Against Japan earlier in November, he beat 13 defenders and made more line breaks in 80 minutes than in the entire Six Nations, when he started all five games at full-back.
But Rees-Zammit is not the only thing that has changed since March, Wales have changed too
Even the quickest wing in the world is of limited use if he receives the ball standing still with two defenders in front of him.
"But as a winger, you do rely on your boys inside you," said Cuthbert.
With Wales generating more momentum up front, Cuthbert highlights Blair Murray's ability to engage defenders before releasing Rees-Zammit.
Wales are also deploying both wings on the same side of the field. Rees-Zammit and Josh Adams combining for full-back Murray's try was a fine example.
Scrum-half Tomos Williams has perfected the art of the sharp, accurate pass that bypasses players and gets the ball into the wider channels early.
It helped create Rees-Zammit's try against New Zealand and, eight minutes into Saturday's game against the Wallabies, looked to have created another.
Having dived for the corner, Rees-Zammit's first instinct on getting to his feet was not to celebrate or appeal to the referee, but to fix his hair.
The try would not survive the television replays. The hair had survived the tackle.
Image matters to Rees-Zammit. He is Welsh rugby's most marketable player, its biggest draw. He puts bums on seats and gets people out of them.
There is a lovely soundtrack to Rees-Zammit receiving the ball in space at the Principality Stadium. A low hum of excitement followed by the rattle of thousands of seats folding up almost simultaneously.
The thrill is in the anticipation, and these days there is rather more to anticipate.

You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time
You can keep track of the time without missing a beat, thanks to a discreet Apple Watch setting that comes in a few versions to suit your schedule.
One of the ironies of smartwatches is that for some people, telling the time is low on the list of priorities. You can always check your iPhone if you need to, and most of us spend hours every day in front of some form of clock, whether it's a PC or an old analog ticker hanging on the wall. It's actually features like fitness tracking and quick notification checks that elevate the best Apple Watches to must-haves.
One way or another, we need to know the time, and Apple Watches come with a variety of ways to communicate it. Something you may not have heard of, though, is the ability to get it via vibration. It's something Apple calls Taptic Time, a reference to the Taptic Engine that produces haptic feedback.
Here we're going to explain how to enable Taptic Time, how it works and, perhaps most importantly, why you'd want to bother. The short answer to the last item is that for some people, a visual check just isn't an option.
How to turn on and use Taptic Time on your Apple Watch
To enable Taptic Time, launch the Settings app on your Apple Watch. Next, select Clock, then Taptic Time. Toggle the feature on. At that point, you'll be presented with three options: Digits, Terse or Morse Code.
That last one should probably be avoided unless you're a 19th-century telegraph operator. Terse may not be much better, though. It uses long taps to indicate that five hours have passed since midnight, short taps for additional hours, then long taps again for quarter-hour increments. It's not hard to learn, but a 15-minute margin of error could mean the difference between catching your rideshare to the airport and having to rebook your flight.
The most precise and intuitive option is Digits. This uses long taps for tens and short taps for ones and applies that to both hours and minutes. For example, 10:09 would be one long tap, a pause, then nine short taps.
When VoiceOver is on, you can also turn on Taptic Time by double-tapping the watch face while the screen is inactive. Apple notes, though, that Taptic Time won't work in any fashion if your Apple Watch is set to always speak the time. To fix that, you can go to Settings > Clock, then turn on Control With Silent Mode under Speak Time.
Who should actually use Taptic Time on an Apple Watch?
The honest answer is that most people shouldn't. Even if it's just every 15 minutes, having your wrist vibrate repeatedly can be annoying, much less trying to interpret a coded pattern. That's particularly true on recent Apple Watches, which have motors strong enough that alerts can be startling, even when you're expecting them.
The main beneficiaries of Taptic Time are going to be the visually impaired. In that scenario, it might initially seem strange to buy one of the best smartwatches. But with the right accessibility options enabled, you don't need to see well to benefit from some of the Apple Watch's selling points, like fitness tracking, or controlling music and some of the best smart home accessories without having your iPhone nearby.
If your eyesight is fine, you might nevertheless want haptic feedback to keep you more mindful of the time, in which case Terse mode will be the least intrusive choice. It's also conceivable that your job or hobbies might put you in situations where checking your wrist is impractical. I like to ride electric unicycles, for example — while that keeps my hands free, sometimes I need to focus on carving the pavement.

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has arrested a Delhi-based lawyer for allegedly receiving more than ₹15 crore from Saurabh Chandrakar, the alleged mastermind of the Mahadev online betting app scam, on the promise of influencing judges, advocates and government officials connected with the case, according to a PTI report. The accused, Himanshu Shekhar, was reportedly remanded to the ED's custody until November 28 by a special Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) court in Raipur late Monday night. The remand came hours after the Bombay High Court set aside a Mumbai court order that had rejected the agency's request for his transit remand. ED counsel Sourabh Kumar Pande told PTI that Chandrakar had named Shekhar during his custodial interrogation and alleged that the lawyer had promised to manage people in the government and judicial system, including judges and advocates. According to the agency cited by PTI, Chandrakar told investigators that he had paid Shekhar ₹15 crore, followed by additional amounts in smaller instalments. The ED subsequently issued a lookout circular (LOC) against the lawyer to prevent him from leaving the country. Shekhar was reportedly detained by immigration officials at Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport around 3 pm on November 20, when he was scheduled to board a flight to Dubai. He was subsequently handed over to the Customs Department, which informed the ED about the lookout circular, Pande said. An ED team from Raipur reached Mumbai and took Shekhar into custody at around 1.10 am on November 21. After questioning him, the agency produced him before a special court in Mumbai at approximately 2.45 pm the same day and sought transit remand to take him to Raipur for further investigation. However, the Mumbai court rejected the application, citing procedural grounds. According to the ED's counsel, the court observed that Shekhar should have been produced during the first session of working hours rather than towards the end of the 24-hour period. The dispute also involved the calculation of the period of detention. The ED maintained that the clock began ticking at 1.10 am on November 21, when its officials formally took Shekhar into custody. The Mumbai court, however, considered his detention to have started at 3.03 pm on November 20, when immigration officials first detained him under the LOC. The court subsequently directed Shekhar to appear before the ED's Raipur office on November 23. The ED challenged the Mumbai special court's decision before the Bombay High Court, which quashed the order on Monday, clearing the way for the agency to proceed with the arrest in Raipur. Shekhar's lawyer, Faizal Rizvi, disputed the ED's account of the subsequent events. Rizvi claimed that the agency had told the Bombay High Court that his client failed to appear before its Raipur office, whereas Shekhar had actually reached the office at 4.25 pm on Monday. He further said that Shekhar was arrested after reaching the office. The defence has also approached the special court in Raipur seeking directions to preserve CCTV footage and entry registers of the ED office. According to Rizvi, these records could be produced before the Supreme Court in any future legal proceedings. The alleged payment to Shekhar is linked to the wider investigation into the Mahadev online betting app network. Chandrakar, who was extradited from Oman earlier this month following an operation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), is currently lodged in Raipur Central Jail in judicial custody. The ED has alleged that illegal betting operations through the Mahadev app and associated money-laundering activities continued, with the total proceeds of crime estimated to have exceeded ₹92,000 crore. Investigative agencies have alleged that Chandrakar and Ravi Uppal, both natives of Bhilai in Chhattisgarh's Durg district, promoted the Mahadev Book App and ran an online betting network through a system of panel and branch operators. The alleged network involved payments described as protection money to police personnel, administrative officials and influential political figures to facilitate its operations. According to investigative agencies, Chandrakar and other promoters operated from Dubai, which they allegedly treated as the network's headquarters. The promoters are accused of recruiting several youths from Chhattisgarh to work as managers, supervisors and other staff members to run the betting operations. The alleged network functioned through multiple panels and branches, allowing betting activities to be conducted across locations. The ED's investigation has reportedly focused on the alleged generation and laundering of proceeds from these operations, as well as the suspected involvement of officials and influential individuals who may have helped the network function. The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
71
Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
- Published
The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that the country had carried out genocide against the Rohingya minority – marking the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.
The UK is joined by several other countries, external in acknowledging the ICJ ruling, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action."
- How do you define genocide? 
  - Published4 April 2022
The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.
Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.
He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."
Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".
The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.
He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention, external.
In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.
Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, was deposed by the military in 2021.
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

Bisleri International has maintained that its packaged drinking water is safe for consumption, disputing the findings of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), which has sanctioned prosecution against the company after a water sample was declared unsafe following laboratory tests.
In a statement issued on Monday (November 23, 2026), the company said the matter related to a batch manufactured in September 2025 at its Goa facility, one of 143 plants in its network, and dated back about 14 months.
Bisleri said the FSSAI collected six samples from the facility on September 30, 2025, of which five met all applicable standards. The sixth sample recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
Following an appeal by the company on November 22, 2025, the FSSAI referred the sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. Bisleri said the referral laboratory found the bromate level to be within the prescribed limit, but separately flagged the presence of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).
The findings came after the initial laboratory examination had found the sample non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits, and declared it unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The referral laboratory also declared the sample unsafe, citing the detection of PAHs. Based on the laboratory findings, the FSSAI subsequently sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri.
Questioning the differing test results, Bisleri said the difference between the two sets of findings raised questions that it believed warranted clarification. The company said it arranged for the same sample to be tested independently at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, where the bromate level was also found to be within the prescribed limit.
Bisleri said it submitted the independent test results to the FSSAI’s Western Regional Office along with a formal letter dated February 2, 2026.
“We received no further communication from FSSAI after that submission and understood the matter to be closed. To date, Bisleri has received no notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI’s website,” a company spokesperson said.
The company’s management is deciding on the next steps, the spokesperson said. The company said it maintained stringent quality controls, including more than 90 tests across its 10-step manufacturing process. It added that it would continue to cooperate with the FSSAI and address the matter through the appropriate regulatory process.

Egg prices have plunged 10%-20% across India over the past 8-10 days as a bird flu outbreak in Tamil Nadu disrupted exports, pushing surplus supplies into the domestic market amid weakening seasonal demand, as per a report.
In Namakkal, Tamil Nadu, India's poultry hub, egg prices climbed to ₹6.70 apiece on November 11 but fell to ₹5.60 following the confirmation of bird flu in Cuddalore on November 13, marking a decline of nearly 19%, The Times of India reported.
Prices have dropped by more than 15% across most southern states, while Delhi, West Bengal, Gujarat and Maharashtra have recorded relatively smaller declines of 6%-10%, according to TOI.
Namakkal accounts for over 90% of India's egg exports, and the disruption in shipments has worsened the domestic supply. The region's daily egg exports, which stood at around one crore during the corresponding period last year, had dwindled, the news outlet said.
The price slump has hit poultry farmers as feed costs remain elevated. Maize prices have risen nearly 50% over the past year, while soybean meal has become around 30% more expensive, further squeezing farmers' margins, TOI reported, citing industry sources.
Poultry farmers struggling to recover costs amid higher feed prices and reduced demand.
The crisis has also hit chicken producers, with production costs exceeding ₹120 per kg, while farmers are receiving around ₹80 per kg.
Feed manufacturers are also facing mounting losses amid the downturn, with industry representatives warning that the combination of high input costs and depressed poultry prices is threatening the sector's viability.
Around one lakh chickens have died or been culled following an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) in Tamil Nadu's Cuddalore district, prompting authorities to intensify containment measures and surveillance to prevent the virus from spreading to humans.
The outbreak was confirmed on November 13 after samples from a poultry farm in Kattiyankuppam, Kurinjipadi taluk, tested positive for H5N1 at the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal. Bird deaths were first reported on October 30 in Thamanampatti village, with more than 35,600 birds subsequently dying across 15 farms before confirmation.
A central government team visited the district on Saturday to inspect containment measures, while doctors from the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) are monitoring medical camps and assessing surveillance for suspected human infections.
Authorities have undertaken culling within a 1-km radius of infected premises, along with deep burial of carcasses, sanitisation and restrictions on poultry movement. A three-month ban on poultry farming and restocking has also been imposed in affected areas.
The outbreak has affected villages around Kullanchavadi, including Kattiyankuppam, Nadukattu and Thyagavalli. Tamil Nadu's Director of Public Health Dr Somasundaram said no human infections had been detected so far, while urging people to avoid handling sick or dead birds.
The state has also stepped up surveillance across poultry hubs, including Namakkal, following other localised H5N1 detections in Chennai's Vandalur Zoo and Tiruvallur district.
The poultry industry is facing one of its worst crises in 50 years amid soaring maize and soybean prices, prompting the All India Poultry Breeders Association (AIPBA) to urge the government to intervene to prevent further losses to farmers and a potential spike in chicken and egg prices.
The association has sought stock limits on maize and soyabean and urged the government to release around 3 million tonnes of maize from state stocks to poultry producers at concessional rates, similar to the support extended to ethanol manufacturers.
Poultry feed prices have risen by around ₹15,000 per tonne, making production increasingly unviable and forcing farmers to cut output or shut operations, AIPBA president Bahadur Ali said. He alleged that hoarding and artificial scarcity were driving up prices despite adequate crop production.
According to industry estimates cited by the association, feed plant production and demand have fallen 15%-20%, while 20%-25% of poultry farms have shut down or are facing closure. Farmers are reportedly losing ₹40-50 per kg on chicken sales as rising feed costs outpace selling prices.
The association warned that chicken prices could rise by ₹40-50 per kg and egg prices by ₹3-4 apiece if the crisis persists. It also said profits earned by integrated poultry companies between April and October had been wiped out by November.
While some relief in maize and soybean prices is expected by January, the near-term outlook remains uncertain, Ali said, warning that prolonged disruptions could threaten the livelihoods of millions of rural families dependent on poultry and dairy.

In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.
Modern governance, however, forgot what Ashoka and Virchow knew. It allotted people to one ministry, livestock to another and forests to a third, and pathogens, which recognise no such allocation of business, have exploited the gaps ever since. One Health, which the world marks on November 3, is the effort to recover that lost unity with the tools of the 21st century by bringing human, animal and environmental health into a common framework for research, surveillance and prevention. The Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, which regards the world as one family, resonates with this understanding of interconnected life.
This year the case makes itself. Lumpy skin disease (LSD) has returned to India. The September forecast from ICAR-National Institute of Veterinary Epidemiology and Disease Informatics’ early-warning system placed 219 districts across 28 states and Union Territories at risk, and Rajasthan had recorded more than 10,400 cases in 10 eastern districts by mid-September. In Siberia, a young technician at Irkutsk’s anti-plague institute died in early October, of what Russian authorities called pneumonia of unknown cause, amid reports of pneumonic plague. Nearly 200 people were placed under observation. Whatever the final diagnosis, Yersinia pestis, the organism of the Black Death, has never left us. It persists in rodents and their fleas, from the marmots of the Central Asian steppe to the prairie dogs of New Mexico and the rats of Madagascar.
Neither story respects a departmental boundary. LSD does not infect people, but it drains milk cans, household incomes and children’s nutrition. Plague is at once a problem of wildlife ecology, laboratory biosafety, clinical medicine and public trust.

Even as judges have blocked visa restrictions and other limits on foreign scholars and scientists, the Trump administration is winning outside court. New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.
That paradox was on full display last week. On Nov. 16, a federal judge issued a final ruling blocking a proposed four-year cap on how long international students and postdoctoral researchers can remain in the country. The next day, a judge in a separate case issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from narrowing eligibility for a work authorization program widely used by foreign students.
To student advocates like Fanta Aw, CEO of the nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the rulings represented two wins in two days. “I’ve always believed that our judicial systems are strong and are very much still in play, and I felt relieved,” said Aw, whose organization is a plaintiff in both cases. “Our members, and in particular our students, I felt, were vindicated.”
But data released the same day as the ruling in the visa time limit case paint a less celebratory picture. A survey of more than 800 U.S. institutions conducted by the Institute of International Education found that foreign student enrollment for the current academic year has decreased 9% overall compared with 2025, with a 15% drop among newly enrolled students and graduate students. While IIE won’t have complete data until next year, the preliminary numbers suggest this will be the third consecutive year graduate enrollment has dropped — with the largest year-to-year decrease in at least 20 years, according to historical data from the nonprofit.
That trend extends to biomedicine, where foreign students make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates, according to new survey data from the Association of American Medical Colleges. A poll of 37 AAMC member institutions showed that the number of international students starting biomedical Ph.D. programs has decreased by about 30% since 2024, more than twice the 14% overall decline in matriculation in these programs.
The growing body of data as well as STAT’s interviews with students and immigration experts suggest that, despite the legal losses, the Trump administration’s policies on immigration have had a chilling effect on students considering coming to the U.S., and on those who are already here. Meanwhile, enrollment of foreign students is rising at some Asian universities, and experts warn that these opposing trends could jeopardize the nation’s biomedical preeminence and that it could take years to repair the loss of trust from students who no longer see the U.S. as a welcoming destination.
“People are looking at us from overseas, going, ‘We don’t really recognize this country,’” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. Even if Democrats’ new majority in Congress prevents further restrictions, she added, “I think we have a lot of ground to make up.”
When contacted for comment, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in an email that the agency’s records don’t support the decline reported by IIE, though it didn’t say whether its own data show lower enrollment by foreign students, and that President Trump should be credited for cracking down on rampant visa fraud.
“Institute of International Education’s ‘reporting’ is completely misleading and not backed up by any real evidence,” the DHS spokesperson said. “So far, [the Student and Exchange Visitor Program] has not experienced a 9% drop of foreign student enrollment.”
A recent independent analysis by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration of the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, a DHS database that has for more than 20 years monitored foreign students, found that international student enrollment declined by 6.3% between October 2025 and October 2026.
Concerns that the Trump administration would make it difficult for foreign scientists to enter or stay in the U.S. preceded the president’s inauguration. Since then, the administration has enacted travel bans affecting dozens of countries; instituted “extreme vetting” for visa applicants, including the review of social media profiles; and revoked more than 8,000 student visas. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also stepped up enforcement of alleged visa violations, including the recent detention of a Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student who had been traveling home after presenting at a scientific meeting.
But many of the administration’s efforts to more tightly regulate international scholars have not come to fruition. That includes the attempt to end “duration of status,” a policy that for nearly half a century allowed students and postdoctoral researchers to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training. DHS’s proposed four-year cap would likely have forced the vast majority of new foreign life science students to apply for extensions to stay in the country given that, on average, it takes five to six years to earn a biomedical doctorate. But a federal judge found that the proposal violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a law that governs how agencies implement new regulations.
The Trump administration has also proposed a $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience; academic institutions would be expected to pay the fee. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are often used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as biotech.
Even though these restrictions have not been enacted, they’ve left many foreign students with a clear sense that they aren’t wanted here.
“All these rules, it just made me feel like my immigration was a crime. That’s the biggest recurring feeling that I’ve had these past few years,” said a biomedical Ph.D. student at the University of Washington, who requested anonymity to speak freely. “You know what? I’m just here to study. I’m just learning, and I’m focused on my science. But it has felt very disruptive.”
There are growing signs that fear is impacting student decisions. A poll this summer from the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications fell 21%.
A more recent survey of 437 universities, including more than 200 in the U.S., found that nearly 60% of U.S. institutions reported lower graduate enrollment between August and October compared with the same period last year. Ninety percent of U.S. respondents cited restrictive government policies as a significant obstacle.
That trend isn’t unique to the U.S. The Global Enrollment Benchmark Survey found that nearly 80% of institutions in the United Kingdom, which has also instituted tougher immigration controls, reported reduced foreign graduate student enrollment. By contrast, nearly 60% of Asian universities that responded, including five Chinese institutions, said graduate enrollment had increased. It’s a shift that Aw says could have major implications for the global economy and the future of innovation.
“There is truly a global competition for talent,” she said. “China has made no secret that one of its most pressing priorities is international education and to bring as many talented students to its shores as they can from around the world. That used to be the United States.”

'Best midfielder in the world' - where does Bellingham rank?
- Published
Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?
Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.
"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world."
Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.
While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.
"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10."
While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?
BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.
Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid)
Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.
He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.
He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.
He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.
When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.
He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.
Vitinha (Paris St-Germain)
While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.
But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.
The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".
He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.
Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.
"It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level."
Declan Rice (Arsenal)
Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.
He briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.
Rice created 17 big chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.
The 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.
He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.
Rodri (Barcelona)
The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.
It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.
The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.
His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.
The former Manchester City player has slotted in seamlessly since joining Barcelona in August, and averages 106 successful passes per 90 minutes in La Liga - the second-highest figure, behind Vitinha, of any player in the top five European leagues.

  - Published3 October
Pedri (Barcelona)
Pedri may be six years younger than Rodri, his midfield partner at the Camp Nou, but he boasts extraordinary experience for a 24-year-old, having made more than 250 appearances for Barcelona, not to mention playing at two European Championships and two World Cups.
The Tenerife-born midfielder combines tigerish work-rate with quality in possession.
He has created 26 chances from open play in La Liga this season, the sixth-highest total across Europe's top five leagues, and wins possession an average of 7.6 times per 90 minutes, the 10th-highest figure.
However, such is Spain's wealth of midfield options that he is not even guaranteed a starting place for his country, with Fabian Ruiz preferred for their final three matches at the 2026 World Cup.
Paris St-Germain midfielder Ruiz, who finished 10th in this year's Ballon d'Or rankings, also deserves to be in any debate about the world's best midfielders.
Fermin Lopez (Barcelona)
He might not yet have the profile of Barcelona team-mates Rodri or Pedri, but on current form alone, versatile youngster Lopez is one of Europe's best box-to-box goalscorers.
The 23-year-old already has nine goals and seven assists this season. Counting only goals scored in Europe's top five leagues and the Champions League, no central midfielder has more.
While Lopez can also operate on the wing, the presence of Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon means he has mainly featured as a number eight or a number 10 this term.
The Barcelona academy graduate played only a bit-part role as Spain won Euro 2024 and was unfortunate to miss the World Cup after breaking a bone in his foot in May.
However, a summer off enabled him to hit the ground running this season, and he has not looked back.

British drugmaker GSK’s subsidiary GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals (GSK India), as part of a strategy to sharpen focus on cancer therapies, on Tuesday announced the launch of monoclonal antibody-drug conjugate BLENREP (belantamab mafodotin) as a combination therapy for those with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma.
The launch marks introduction of GSK’s third precision oncology therapy in India. “Last year, we began our oncology journey in the country with Jemperli and Zejula in solid tumours. With the launch of BLENREP, we are expanding into haemato-oncology...” GSK India managing director Bhushan Akshikar said in a release.
BLENREP has been approved by CDSCO as a combination therapy for adult patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma who have received at least one prior line of therapy, the company said.
Beyond haematological and gynaecological cancers, GSK said it is focusing on lung and gastrointestinal cancers, and other solid tumours. It is currently conducting 15 oncology clinical trials, including studies evaluating dostarlimab in head and neck cancer and colon cancer, the company said.

For the first time in more than a year, the Food and Drug Administration has sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information.
The agency sends such notices when a trial sponsor fails to comply with a federal law that requires studies to be registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, a federal government database, within 21 days after the first human subject is enrolled. Summary results must also be posted to the database within 12 months after the trial’s primary completion date.
The FDA, however, has rarely sent noncompliance letters, despite years of criticism over lax enforcement. In recent years, calls for greater transparency have sparked a raft of studies showing a failure by drug companies, universities, and academic medical centers to comply with disclosure requirements. Bangladesh raises minimum wage for garment workers after weeks of protests
A government-formed wage board in Bangladesh has raised the minimum monthly wage for entry-level garment workers by 36% to 17,000 takas, or $136, from 12,500 takas after weeks of violent protests
DHAKA, Bangladesh -- DHAKA, Bangladesh (AP) — Bangladesh raised the minimum monthly wage for entry-level garment workers Wednesday by 36% to 17,000 takas ($136) from 12,500 takas after weeks of violent protests that closed factories and disrupted production as workers demanded the minimum wage be doubled.
The workers took to the streets, fought with police and attacked factories for weeks as they demanded better wages and said higher inflation had made their lives difficult.
The garment industry is Bangladesh’s main sector to earn foreign currency through exports, mostly to the United States and Europe. It represents about 80% of the country’s total exports and directly employs about 4 million workers, mostly women from rural areas.
A government-appointed wage board approved the new wage structure early Wednesday after nearly 12 hours of meetings between workers’ and employers’ representatives.
The six-member board, including two representatives each for workers and employers, approved the new wage structure in a 4-2 vote supporting 17,000 takas as the minimum wage. The other two board members sided with workers’ revised demand for 18,000 takas per month.
The wage board also revised monthly wages for other workers.
It was not immediately clear if the workers would accept the new wage structure.

Following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), the Special Summary Revision (SSR) is now underway in Uttar Pradesh, with the stated objective of preparing an error-free electoral roll. An analysis of Form 6 applications by Alt News, however, reveals a sharp and unprecedented surge in applications for inclusion in the electoral roll, with daily submissions rising from a few thousand in early November to over four lakh by November 22.
The SSR process began with the publication of the draft electoral rolls on November 17. About two weeks earlier, on October 30, Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath had said at a BJP state working committee meeting in Lucknow that the names of around 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing from the electoral rolls. He urged party workers to launch a systematic campaign to ensure their inclusion.
Again, on November 22, The Indian Express reported that Uttar Pradesh BJP had instructed its workers to focus on Form 6 additions in the SSR is to ensure inclusion of names of individuals eligible to be voters but left out during the SIR for some reason.
Tracking Form 6 application data from the SSR process, Alt News found that between November 1 and 16, an average of around 10,000 applications were submitted daily across the state. The numbers began rising sharply from November 17, the day the draft rolls were published, and accelerated dramatically over the following five days. On November 22 alone, around 4.16 lakh applications were submitted.
What Alt News Found
An analysis of Form 6 application data from Uttar Pradesh shows that around 2,000 applications were filed across the state on November 1. The numbers began rising the following day, with around 10,000 applications submitted on November 2. A similar number were filed on November 3 and 4, followed by 9,000 on November 5.
The state recorded around 12,000 applications each on November 6 and 7, before the figure dropped to 4,000 on November 8. Around 9,000 applications were submitted on November 9.
On November 10, 11 and 12, the daily figures stood at 15,000, 16,000 and 15,000, respectively. Applications declined to around 11,000 each on November 13 and 14, and further to 9,000 on both November 15 and 16.
The pace of submissions changed significantly on November 17, when the SSR process began and the draft electoral roll was published. Around 31,000 Form-6 applications were filed across Uttar Pradesh that day. The numbers climbed further over the next two days, with 46,000 applications on November 18 and 68,000 on November 19. On November 20, the figure stood at around 60,851.
The surge became even more pronounced from November 21, when around 2.31 lakh Form-6 applications were submitted. The following day, November 22, the figure more than doubled to approximately 4.16 lakh.
Who Are Filing these Applications?
Alt News’s analysis found that some of the new applicants had been deleted from the electoral rolls during the SIR.
To identify such applicants, the Alt News team matched new Form 6 applicants against the 2.89 crore names deleted during the SIR under the categories of absent, shifted, dead or duplicate.
Of the approximately 10.4 lakh applications examined between October 29 and November 22, Alt News found around 45,000 applicants whose names had been deleted during the SIR and who were now applying for inclusion in the electoral roll of the same assembly constituency. These applicants accounted for around 4.3% of all the applications examined.
Put another way, the 45,000 applicants represent approximately 1.6 in every 1,000 people whose names were deleted during the SIR (45,000 out of 2.89 crore). Most of these applicants had previously been marked as absent or shifted before their names were deleted.
A Closer Look at Form 6 Applications
A closer examination of the Form 6 applications reveals several serious anomalies, like instances of multiple applications carrying identical applicant details.
In Siwalkhas assembly constituency in Meerut district, for instance, 44 applications were submitted from the same address: “Gotka, Gotka, Gotka, Gotka, 250344, Sardhana.” All 44 applications were filed on November 5 and 6.
Alt News also identified 6,969 repeat Form-6 applications submitted between November 20 and 22.
These repeat applications were found within the same assembly constituency and carried identical applicant names and father’s or husband’s names.
For instance, in Bindki constituency in Fatehpur district, an applicant named Himanshu submitted five Form 6 applications. Four were filed on November 21 and another on November 22. All five applications carry the same applicant name, his father’s name, Baburam, and the same address.
The application serial numbers also show that three of these applications were submitted consecutively.
In another instance, Alt News identified an applicant named Aadhya Seth who submitted six Form 6 applications over three days, between November 20 and 22. In all six applications, the applicant’s name, father’s name and address are identical.
To identify similar instances, we matched applicants by name and their father’s or husband’s name within each constituency for the period October 29 to November 22. The exercise identified 10,773 individuals whose names appeared more than once, accounting for 11,684 additional applications.
According to Alt News’s analysis, approximately one in every 90 Form 6 applications was a repeat submission. The analysis also identified 427 individuals who had submitted applications in two different assembly constituencies.
The data shows that most repeat applications were filed on the same day, often in immediate succession.
A closer analysis also reveals that repeat applications increased alongside the overall surge in Form 6 submissions. On November 17, 18 and 19, the number of repeat applications stood at 340, 458 and 699, respectively. Before this, the daily figure had rarely crossed 400, reaching around that mark only on November 10 and 15.
On November 22 alone, however, 4,325 repeat applications were submitted. This means approximately one in every 100 Form 6 applications filed that day was a repeat submission.
Making Sense of the Surge
The overall volume of applications saw a sharp increase ever since the SSR draft role had been published. Between October 29 and November 22, a total of 10,56,778 Form 6 applications were submitted across Uttar Pradesh. Of these, 1,65,289 were filed between November 1 and 16, while 4,37,235 were submitted in just five days, between November 17 and 21.
On November 22 alone, the number stood at 4,16,380. According to data compiled by the Alt News team, more Form-6 applications were submitted on November 22 than during the first 20 days of November combined.
According to the figures available from November 20 to November 22, Kheri district (33,836) saw the most number of Form 6 applications. Other districts such as Ghaziabad (25,438), Agra (24,715), Barabanki (21,652), Prayagraj (21,433), Azamgarh (20,642), Bareily (20,625), Lucknow (20,369), Unnao (16,376) and Bulandshahr (16,217) also saw significant number of applications.
Interestingly, Ghaziabad and Bulandshahr showed zero entry on November 20. So all the applications for these two districts are from November 21 and November 22.
Ghaziabad district recorded the highest number of Form 6 applications so far on November 22, with 39,828 submissions. Other districts with substantial numbers of applications include Agra (39,091), Lucknow (32,324), Kheri (27,904), Prayagraj (19,764) , Azamgarh (19,135) , Fatehpur (18,253), Bulandshahr (18,120), Barabanki (15,782), Bareily (15,096) and Gorakhpur (12,474).
A similar trend was observed in constituencies such as Loni, Ghaziabad, Lakhimpur, Etmadpur, Zaidpur, Bangermau, Dadri, Chakia and Barabanki.
Across the state, an assembly constituency typically recorded an average of around 17 Form 6 applications between November 1 and 16. However, the average rose sharply to 496 applications on November 21 and further to 966 on November 22.
Amid this surge, however, some pockets of western Uttar Pradesh recorded no substantial number of Form 6 applications. For instance, in Bijnor district, eight constituencies recorded no Form 6 applications, according to the compiled Form 9 lists on November 20 and 21. In Muzaffarnagar, six constituencies recorded a similar trend on November 20 and 21, while 22 constituencies did so on November 22.
Similar patterns were observed in pockets of Saharanpur, Moradabad, Meerut, Rampur, Bulandshahr and Shamli, among other districts.
The Back Story
On April 10, the final SIR roll for Uttar Pradesh was published. The total voters in the state plummeted from 15.44 crores to 13.39 crores in the process.
In December 2025, Yogi Adityanath warned that nearly 4 crore eligible voters could be missing during the SIR, claiming that 85-90% of them could be BJP supporters. Following the publication of the draft electoral roll on January 6, which reportedly recorded around 2.89 crore deletions, the BJP expressed concern, particularly over urban constituencies, and mobilised workers to help voters re-enroll.
In January 2026, a Newslaundry report said that the BJP was worried that large-scale deletions in urban constituencies could affect its electoral prospects. In 50 constituencies, more than one lakh voters had reportedly been deleted, 47 of which the BJP had won in 2022. The final roll, published on April 10, 2026, contained approximately 13.39 crore electors, down from around 15.44 crore before the SIR, with several BJP minister held constituencies reportedly recording substantial deletions.
On October 30, Adityanath claimed that 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing, citing discrepancies involving panchayat electoral rolls, welfare beneficiaries and young voters. He mentioned 66 lakh names allegedly present on panchayat rolls but absent from Assembly rolls, 55 lakh welfare beneficiaries and approximately 4.5 lakh young voters.
On November 14, the BJP reportedly set targets of restoring 10,000–25,000 voters per assembly constituency, with party leaders estimating that 40–80 lakh voters could be re-enrolled. Following the publication of the SSR draft roll on November 17, the party planned to launch a booth-level voter addition campaign from November 20.

Migration to Spain's Canary Islands breaks day record with nearly 2,000 arrivals
Spanish authorities report nearly 2,000 migrants arrived at the Canary Islands on Tuesday, setting a record for a single day
BARCELONA, Spain -- Spanish authorities said nearly 2,000 migrants arrived at Spain’s Canary Islands on Tuesday, a record high for migrants reaching the archipelago on a single day.
The islands located off the coast of West Africa saw a surge in arrivals just before Spain holds a national election later this week, when migration will be a major concern for many voters.
Spain’s maritime rescue service said that 1,990 people arrived on 15 different boats as search and rescue vessels accompanied one dinghy after another to the small island of El Hierro.
“Sadly, this is a historic day,” the Canary Islands' regional leader Fernando Clavijo said in an interview with Spanish radio Cadena Ser.
There were around 100 minors among Tuesday’s arrivals, including a four-day-old baby that had been born during the journey, Clavijo said.
The Canary Islands, a tourist hotspot for many Europeans drawn to its year-round mild weather, have for years been a key entry point for migrants desperate to reach Europe. The route is also extremely dangerous with thousands dying in the attempted crossing.
Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. The journeys can last days or weeks, with many boats missing their target and drifting into the open Atlantic.
Over 26,000 people have reached the Canary Islands this year, with half that total coming in November. The previous single-day record was hit just two weeks before, when 1,400 people arrived at Gran Canaria on Nov. 7.
In June, Pope Leo XIV warned people smugglers that they will face God’s wrath for exploiting the desperation of migrants when the pontiff visited the islands.
Departures from West Africa are seasonal, and November often sees spikes in numbers as many leave before the ocean becomes rough during winter. The seas have been calm recently, which has contributed to the high number of departures.
Most of the boats that arrived on Tuesday were from Senegal and Gambia, Clavijo said. Despite the European Union’s efforts in West Africa to reduce the number of migrants, many believe that leaving is their only option to find work and build a better life.
“The sailing conditions were favorable and there was a full moon, so these people looking for a better future ended up on our shores,” Clavijo said.
Clavijo said that El Hierro, the western-most member of the archipelago, with a population of 12,000, could not handle such a large influx of people, many of whom arrived exhausted and in poor condition.
He said that overall he was satisfied with the transfer of adult migrants to mainland Spain, but added that he asked for help from other regions to take in unaccompanied minors who need to be taken care of by authorities.
Spain’s conservative Popular Party is aiming to unseat the ruling Socialist-led central government in Sunday’s elections. To do so, it would likely have to form a government with the far-right Vox party, which is campaigning heavily on expelling migrants and social policies that favor Spaniards over foreigners who have recently arrived.
Without mentioning Vox, Clavijo, who belongs to the regional Canary Coalition party, denounced any attempts to demonize the migrants, calling it “a xenophobic discourse of bad people.”
The Canary Island leader also slammed the recent deal by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands to send migrants to Rwanda, calling it “ridiculous.”
“Europe is on the wrong path,” Clavijo said.

While Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi’s Ramayana: Part 1 continues to dominate headlines for its record-breaking box office run—crossing ₹1,735.15 crore worldwide and closing in on the ₹1,000-crore mark in India—a former crew member has painted a starkly different picture of life behind the scenes.
A visual effects artist, Rahul Dhanwe, who worked on Ramayana, criticised Namit Malhotra-owned DNEG in a LinkedIn post, alleging that he was laid off after 4.6 years with the company without receiving a single salary increment for over four years.
Dhanwe, who claimed that he spent the last two years working on the mythological film, questioned the treatment of artists in the visual effects industry and urged fellow professionals to treat DNEG as their “last option”.
In his post, Dhanwe said that senior management repeatedly asked employees to stand by the studio during a difficult period, and that he did so in the hope that conditions would improve.
“Well played, Namit Malhotra and The Ramayana World. Really well played! I spent 4.6 years at DNEG, including the last two years working on Ramayana. Senior management repeatedly asked us to support the company during difficult times. We did,” he wrote. “For over four years, I worked without a single rupee of salary increment, hoping things would eventually improve. But what did we get in return? A layoff!”
He added, “I never expected a special reward for supporting the company. But after investing 4.6 years of my career, this is certainly not the treatment I expected. We gave two years of hard work, skills, and dedication to Ramayana.”
He said, “In a way, our personal sacrifices became part of our contribution to the film. We won't share in its future success or profits. It honestly feels like we worked for charity.”
Dhanwe said his biggest regret was spending 4.6 years at the studio, adding that he believed he could have grown further professionally, financially and creatively elsewhere.
“I understand companies are businesses, but does that mean artists should be treated as disposable resources?” he asked.
"My biggest regret is that I wasted 4.6 important years of my career at DNEG. Had I spent those years elsewhere, I genuinely believe I could have grown much further professionally, financially, and creatively. I am also concerned about the artists currently working on Ramayana Part 2. I sincerely hope they don't face a similar situation," he wrote.
Calling his stint at the company the worst studio experience of his career, Dhanwe advised other VFX artists to weigh their options carefully.
"Honestly, DNEG has been the worst studio experience of my professional life. Such a big name, yet such a disappointing experience when it comes to treating artists," he wrote.
He also flagged concerns for the artists currently working on Ramayana: Part 2.
“To fellow artists: Think carefully before joining DNEG. If you have another good offer, consider it first. Keep DNEG as your last option. I wasted 4.6 years. Please don't waste yours. Artists are not disposable resources. They deserve respect, stability, and fair treatment,” he said.
Neither Malhotra nor DNEG had issued an official response to the allegations at the time of publication.
In a follow-up comment on the same post, he shared an update on his settlement, writing, “I have received a gratuity now. Thank you, guys.”
