Quick Answer
The Dreame X60 Ultra Complete offers powerful suction, heated-water mopping, a slimmer design, and smarter obstacle handling. At ₹1,34,999, it delivers an impressive cleaning experience with greater convenience, though the value of its premium features depends on your home’s needs.
When I reviewed the X40 Ultra, it was the first robot where I didn’t have to plan a backup round of cleaning. Months later, the L40 Ultra AE beat it on suction and mopping for Rs 20,000 less. The X60 Ultra Complete has to answer a question both reviews left open: what does a Dreame flagship do that the cheaper model does not?
On paper, quite a lot. It also costs more than twice what the L40 Ultra AE did, so the real question is whether the additions change daily cleaning in an Indian home or mostly change the spec sheet.
Table of Contents
Design and Build: Slimmer Robot, Smarter Moves
At first glance, the X60 Pro Complete looks like any other premium Dreame device. You get the familiar circular body, a large docking station, and a design that is more functional than flashy. But there’s one important difference. At just 7.95 cm tall, the X60 is noticeably slimmer than the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE. And that’s thanks to the retractable navigation sensor that pops up when needed and slides back into the body when the robot needs to squeeze under low furniture.
This might sound gimmicky at first (remember OnePlus 7T Pro?), but it has a practical value. In 2026, most robot vacuums already do a decent job of cleaning open floors. The real challenge is getting under sofas, beds, and cabinets without getting stuck. The X60 needs just over 8 cm of clearance to enter these spaces with its sensor retracted.
The price of that slim body is a 235 ml onboard bin, which is significantly smaller than what we saw on the L40 Ultra (395 ml) and X40 Ultra (350 ml). That means the robot keeps returning to the dock to empty the bin more often than expected in heavy sessions, especially if you have a pet at home. Not a big deal, but the trips do add time.
The slimmer body isn’t the only trick up the X60’s sleeve. Dreame has also upgraded its obstacle-climbing system, allowing the robot to lift itself over raised thresholds and door tracks that might stop a regular robot vacuum. This is particularly useful in Indian homes, where bathrooms, balconies, and even some rooms have raised entrances.
Genuinely, this is a big step-up (pun intended) in the evolution of robot vacuums. But you should ask yourself this question: are the obstacles in your home tall enough to trouble a decent mid-range robot vacuum and require a top-of-the-line robot? So while the X60’s climbing ability is impressive on paper (single thresholds up to 4.5 cm and double-layer steps up to 8.8 cm), how much value it adds depends on the layout of your home. If your existing robot already moves between rooms without getting stuck, this upgrade alone won’t justify spending significantly more. In fact, your home’s layout, flooring, and the presence of pets matter far more than the specifications alone. We’ve covered these and other factors in our robot vacuum cleaner buying guide.
The dock is significantly shorter and wider than the L40 Ultra I tested last, and its gold-accented finish looks more at home in a living room than the matte black L40. The trade-off is the capacity: 4.2 liters of clean water and 3 liters of dirty water, down from 4.5 and 4 liters on the L40. The 3.2-liter dust bag is unchanged.
As I pointed out in my earlier Dreame reviews, the company continues to ship its robot vacuums with a bulky 16A plug, and the X60 Ultra Complete is no exception. Most Indian homes don’t have a 16A socket conveniently located where you’d want to place the docking station, making an adapter or a dedicated socket an unnecessary hassle for such an expensive product.
Cleaning Performance: Does the Extra Power Make a Difference?
Dreame has made a big deal of the X60 Ultra Complete’s suction power of 35,000 Pa, and understandably so. But having reviewed the X40 Ultra (12,000 Pa) and L40 Ultra AE (19,000 Pa), I’ve reached a point where raw suction figures don’t excite me as much as they once did. Both those robots were already capable of keeping my floors clean without much intervention. So with the X60, I was less interested in how much more powerful it was and more curious about whether that extra power translated into noticeably cleaner floors.
On tile and stone floors, the X60 Ultra Complete does an excellent job of picking up everyday dust, crumbs, and pet hair. The extending side brush also does a great job of cleaning along walls and around furniture legs, areas where robot vacuums often leave some dirt behind. Hair handling is noticeably better than on the X40 Ultra, which struggled with long human hair and clumps of dog fur.
Obstacle avoidance is something Dreame has mastered, and it’s no different on the X60. In my month-long testing, it easily avoided the usual suspects like cables, socks, and small toys. But that was the case with the cheaper L40 and X40 vacuums, too. While it handled thick carpets well, light fabric rugs were pulled towards its inlet a couple of times.
Two newer touches stand out on the X60 Ultra. The robot maps the house during its first clean, so there is no separate mapping run. Also, its proactive-light dirt detection spots hair and light liquids and adjusts cleaning. Image processing happens on the device, per Dreame, and the app shows when the camera is active.
Mopping Performance: Where the X60 Makes a Stronger Case
When I interviewed Manu Sharma, the head of Dreame India, he made an interesting observation: for Indians, a house isn’t truly clean until the mopping is done. And that’s where the X60 Ultra Complete brings some meaningful upgrades. Unlike the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE, which used hot water only to wash the mop pads at the dock, the X60 actually mops the floor with water heated to 40°C. The pads spin at up to 230 RPM, apply 15 N of downward pressure, and extend towards walls and furniture legs to clean areas that regular circular mops often miss.
For everyday mopping, the results are quite impressive. Footprints, light spills, and the grime that builds up on floors throughout the day are handled well. Even some dried stains can be removed, although older, stubborn stains may need a second pass or a targeted zone clean. This is one area where the X60 makes a stronger case for its premium pricing, especially if you mop your floors daily rather than occasionally.
There is one catch, though. The X60 tends to leave floors noticeably damp after mopping. Not enough to make them dangerously slippery, but enough for water marks to show up on wooden-finish tiles. Thankfully, you can adjust the water level in the Dreame app, and I’d recommend starting with a lower setting before increasing it if needed. For homes with carpets, the mop pads can lift up to 21.5 mm to avoid wetting them. You can also have the robot leave the pads at the dock when vacuuming carpets, which is the safer option for thicker rugs.
Multifunction Dock: Almost Hands-Free, But Not Quite
A big part of what you’re paying for with the X60 Ultra Complete is its multifunction docking station. Once the robot finishes cleaning, the dock takes over. It empties the dustbin, refills the robot’s water tank, washes the mop pads, and dries them with hot air. This also makes the smaller onboard dustbin less of a concern, as the robot can return to the dock and empty itself whenever needed. It’s the sort of convenience that makes you forget how much work goes into keeping a robot vacuum clean.
But don’t mistake this for a completely hands-free system. During my testing, I had to refill the clean-water tank and empty the dirty-water tank roughly every other day. Your experience will vary depending on the size of your home, how often you mop, and the water settings you use. You’ll also need to replace the dust bag occasionally and clean the dock’s washboard and other parts. Then there are the recurring costs of dust bags, filters, brushes, and cleaning solution. Dreame includes a decent number of spare accessories in the Complete package, which is nice, but you’ll eventually need to buy replacements. For my usage of roughly 800 sqft home, that’s like replenishing every 6 months or so.
The dock itself is fairly large and needs a permanent spot in your home. Make sure there’s enough room to remove the water tanks comfortably, and preferably place it somewhere you won’t have to carry a tank full of dirty water across the house. These might sound like nitpicking, but when you’re spending this much on a robot vacuum, even small inconveniences are worth pointing out.
App and Battery Life: Plenty of Features, Room for Improvement
I’ve said this in my earlier Dreame reviews, and I’ll say it again. The Dreamehome app can do almost anything you want, but finding the right setting can sometimes be a task in itself. The X60 Ultra Complete is no different. You can clean individual rooms, set up no-mop zones, save up to four maps, and control the robot using Alexa, Siri, Google Home, or Dreame’s own “OK Dreame” voice commands. There’s plenty to play around with, but the app could really do with a simpler interface. Stain Recognition is still in beta, while Matter support is something Dreame has promised through a future software update.
There are some new pet-specific features, too. The X60 can recognize pet bowls, give extra attention to areas where pets spend time, and even locate your pet using its camera. You can also use the camera for live video and two-way communication. There’s an Apple Watch app for starting cleaning sessions and checking their status, along with phone widgets for quick access to cleaning routines.
As for battery life, the X60 packs a 6,400 mAh battery, the same capacity as the X40 Ultra and larger than the L40 Ultra AE’s 5,200 mAh unit. However, a bigger battery doesn’t necessarily translate into longer cleaning sessions, especially with all the extra features running. The good news is that charging is much faster than on the L40 Ultra AE. In my testing, charging times ranged from around 90 minutes to just over two hours, compared to roughly three and a half hours for the L40. Battery life itself isn’t particularly impressive for a flagship, especially in larger homes, but the robot can return to its dock, recharge, and resume cleaning from where it stopped. So, unless you’re in a hurry to get the entire house cleaned in one go, this shouldn’t be much of a concern.
Dreame X60 Ultra Complete Verdict: Worth the Price?
At Rs 1,34,999, the Dreame X60 Ultra Complete is not an easy robot vacuum to recommend, especially when the L40 Ultra AE costs less than half as much and already does an excellent job of keeping floors clean. But after spending time with the X60, I can see where the extra money goes. The slimmer design helps it reach places other robots struggle with, the improved obstacle-climbing system is useful for homes with raised thresholds, and the heated-water mopping is a meaningful upgrade over the X40 and L40. Add reliable vacuuming, better hair handling, excellent edge cleaning, and a multifunction dock that takes care of most of the dirty work, and you have a very capable cleaning system.
That doesn’t mean it’s without flaws. Despite the improvements, I still noticed some hair around the rollers. Mopping can leave floors wetter than I’d like, and stubborn stains may need another pass. The smaller 235 ml dustbin means more trips to the dock during heavy cleaning sessions, while battery life is good enough rather than exceptional. The Dreamehome app remains powerful but unnecessarily complicated, and the dock still needs regular attention. And yes, Dreame continues to ship a 16A plug, something I’ve complained about in my previous reviews. These aren’t deal-breakers individually, but they are harder to ignore at this price.
The X60 also faces some serious competition. In India, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X11 OmniCyclone, and Narwal Flow 2 offer their own take on premium robot cleaning. In the US, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone, and eufy Omni S2 are worth considering against the X60 Max Ultra Complete. I haven’t personally tested these competing models, so I can’t tell you whether they clean better or worse than the Dreame. But based on their features, they’re certainly worth comparing before spending this kind of money.
And that brings me back to the question I raised at the beginning of this review. Does the X60 Ultra Complete do enough to justify its substantial premium over the L40 Ultra AE? For most homes, probably not. The L40 already handles everyday vacuuming and mopping well enough that the X60’s extra suction and smarter features won’t necessarily translate into noticeably cleaner floors. But if you have low furniture, tricky thresholds, pets that shed a lot, and want the most advanced cleaning system Dreame currently offers, the X60 makes a stronger case. You’re paying less for a dramatic improvement in cleaning and more for the ability to clean difficult areas with less intervention.
If you’re unsure which of these premium features you actually need, try our interactive robot vacuum buying checklist. It lets you choose features based on your home and cleaning needs, so you can decide where it’s worth spending more and where you can save.
The X60 Ultra Complete is an excellent robot vacuum, but it’s also a reminder that the best robot vacuum isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. It’s the one that cleans your home well enough that you stop thinking about cleaning. And Dreame had already come remarkably close to achieving that with its cheaper models.
- Excellent suction and everyday cleaning performance
- Slim design gets under low furniture
- Impressive obstacle climbing and avoidance
- Heated-water mopping with excellent edge coverage
- Improved handling of pet hair and long hair
- Multifunction dock reduces manual cleaning effort
- Super premium pricing
- Small onboard dustbin means more dock visits
- Mopping can leave floors noticeably damp
- Dreamehome app remains overly complicated
- Bulky 16A plug remains an inconvenience

A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years
The Ariston Cafe along Route 66 in Litchfield, Ill., has been a favorite for more than 90 years. Just past the front door, underneath the vintage neon signs that read "Ariston" and "Budweiser," is a diner staple: a glass case, full of sweet temptations. It took one of the Ariston's owners, Will Law, nearly a full minute to reel off all 12 of the day's choices.
"There's a peach crisp bread pudding with the vanilla bourbon sauce," he said. "Then, of course, a traditional cheesecake with or without cherries, and we have a chocolate delight, a lemon delight, a coconut delight."
They were all delightful to look at and the kind of classic American comfort desserts that you might crave while you're road-tripping on America's most famous highway. All of them — like everything else served at the Ariston — are still made in-house.
Litchfield isn't the most natural stop on Route 66; it's a sleepy town about an hour outside St. Louis. But the Ariston Cafe, which sits just across the road from the charming Litchfield Museum & Route 66 Welcome Center, has become an institution in its own right with its wooden chairs and cozy decor.
Travelers still flock to the Ariston, thanks to the internet and social media. The waitstaff says many visitors come in already knowing exactly what they intend to order based on what they've read and seen online.
Right by the front door there's a guest book for diners next to a basket of reading glasses to make reading and signing easier. Within just a few days, the Ariston has welcomed patrons from Australia, South Korea, Nicaragua and Germany, among other nations. And they come from all over the U.S. too.
Bob Dickson celebrated his 75th birthday with his wife, Ann, by traveling Route 66.
"I said to her, 'I would love to go out west to Los Angeles and bring Highway 66 all the way back to where we live,'" he said. "So we did that. We took 31 days, stopped every place you can imagine on and off the highway. We had a great time, an absolutely great time talking to people and just seeing the sights."
On this day's visit, they are just a couple of hours away from their home in Quincy, Ill., and they've stopped for a last celebratory lunch on their big trip. The menu offers so many choices, from patty melts to turkey clubs to pork chops and stuffed shrimp. They said this restaurant, with its throwback vibes and sprawling menu, encapsulates the spirit of their whole road trip.
"It was really adventurous and old fashioned and very joyful," Ann Dickson said.
Opinions run hot about what exactly is the oldest eatery along Route 66, but the Ariston Cafe claims to be the oldest continually operating restaurant on the highway.
Nick Adam is one of the Ariston's former owners. His father, Pete, founded it as a candy shop in 1924. Adam says his father was very young when he arrived in this country.
"He left when he was 10 to come to the United States," Adam explained. "He went back to Greece when he was 12, and then he came back to this country."
Pete Adam seems to have had big ambitions even back then: The shop's name, Ariston, means "the best" in Greek. In 1935, he moved it to its present location on Route 66. Then Nick and his wife, Demi, ran the restaurant for decades.
From first dates to engagements, Demi Adam said the Ariston Cafe has been a fundamental part of this community for decades.
"To be honest," she said, "there's nothing else like this around."
Eight years ago, when the Adams were ready to retire, they sold the restaurant to Will Law and his partners. Law said the Ariston's position as a place locals and visitors alike choose for the big moments in their lives remains unchanged.
"I can't tell you how many wedding proposals have happened in those booths," he said. "We have a couple from Iowa that will come back every year for their anniversary just to have dinner. I see a 50th anniversary at least once a week, if not 60, 65. How cool is that? And they want to share that with you."
In 2006, the Ariston Cafe was put on the National Register of Historic Places. It's another lasting reminder of what this restaurant that steps back in time can mean to visitors in the present.

Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers
- Published
Tolu Arokodare was the hero as Nigeria boosted their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with a 3-1 home win over tournament co-hosts Tanzania.
With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, the Super Eagles are battling for the one qualification spot available in Group L and have little margin for error after losing 3-0 in Guinea-Bissau in September.
Alhassan Yusuf kept his composure to slot Nigeria into a second-minute lead in Uyo from Ademola Lookman's pass, but the visitors equalised through Alphonce Msanga just after the half-hour mark.
Arokodare climbed off the bench at half-time and cleverly flicked home Wilfred Ndidi's low ball to restore the lead for the West Africans in the 52nd minute.
And the Ajax striker, who is on a season-long loan from Wolves, gave the Super Eagles breathing space eight minutes later when he controlled Moses Usor's cross from the left and smashed in from 12 yards out.
With three games played in the group, Eric Chelle's side are now one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.

Elsewhere, Mohamed Salah scored twice late on against Malawi as Egypt cruised to a 5-0 victory in Ali Maher's first match in charge.
Achraf Hakimi netted two stunning goals and Yassine Bounou saved a penalty to help Morocco continue their unbeaten start with a 5-1 win over Niger.
Meanwhile, Tunisia are in danger of missing out on the finals for the first time since 1992 after suffering a 2-0 defeat at home against Libya, and Kenya scored a last-minute equaliser to end South Africa's perfect start.
The third round of qualifying culminates with three games on Saturday, while the fourth round of fixtures are split across Monday and Tuesday.
Salah and Hakimi shine
Egypt reached the semi-finals of Afcon 2025 and the last 16 of this year's Fifa World Cup under Hossam Hassan but parted company with the 60-year-old earlier this month.
The Pharaohs had taken four points from their opening two games in Group B, with Salah substituted after an hour in their 0-0 draw with Angola before missing the win in South Sudan.
The former Liverpool forward returned as captain against Malawi, and Egypt cruised into a 3-0 lead at the break through goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany.
Salah got on the scoresheet when he stooped to head in a cross from the left and rounded off proceedings by dinking in a penalty after Hamza Abdelkarim was tripped in the box.
Victory in Maher's first game at the helm puts Egypt three points clear of Angola, who take on South Sudan on Saturday.
In Group A, Morocco had also looked like they would ease to three points against Niger in Casablanca after Yassir Zabiri's early effort and a brilliant long-range strike from right-back Hakimi put them 2-0 up after 27 minutes.
But Mohamed Abdourahmane headed in to halve the deficit and Niger had a chance to level from the spot on the stroke of half-time after a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.
However, Atlas Lions goalkeeper Bounou moved to his left to keep out Youssouf Oumarou's penalty, and Hakimi made it 3-1 in first-half stoppage time with a dipping free-kick from distance.
Youssef En-Nesyri steered in the fourth in the 77th minute from a Hakimi pass and Ayoub Oufkir completed the scoring from close range in the final minute.
Earlier in Group A on Friday Gabon beat Lesotho to move on to six points thanks to two second-half goals from Denis Bouanga.
The LA FC forward smashed the right-hand upright with a penalty but broke the deadlock with a header a minute later and then scored from 12 yards when the Panthers were awarded a second spot kick.
Tunisia downed as McCarthy frustrates Bafana
Tunisia have appeared at a record 17 consecutive Afcons but are winless and bottom of Group H - another section with just one qualifying place on offer - after defeat by their North African neighbours Libya.
The Carthage Eagles could complain about refereeing decisions going against them in Sfax, with Ali Maaloul penalised for a shirt pull on Muad Eisay just before half-time and Ali Youssef converting the resulting spot-kick.
Tunisia had a goal ruled out following a marginal offside call in the second half and three minutes later a low shot from Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 to the Mediterranean Knights.
Libya, who last played at an Afcon in 2012, climb to second in the table and go level on points with Uganda.
South Africa are a point clear of Guinea at the top of Group D after a 2-2 draw against Benni McCarthy's Kenya in Johannesburg.
Amos Wanjala's own goal gifted the hosts an early lead before Michael Olunga levelled from the penalty spot just before half-time.
Relebohile Mofokeng restored Bafana Bafana's advantage with 13 minutes remaining, but Kenya claimed a point when Ryan Ogam's low shot from 20 yards crept inside the left-hand upright in the 90th minute.
Elsewhere, Burkina Faso joined Benin on seven points at the top of Group F thanks to Elohim Kabore's 94th-minute winner against Mauritania in Ouagadougou.
Ethiopia upset Mozambique
Mali extended their winning start to go top of Group K after Mamadou Camara completed a 3-2 comeback win at home against Rwanda, who had led twice in Bamako.
Rwanda had won their first two fixtures and are three points ahead of Cape Verde, who registered their first points with a 4-2 victory over Liberia in Praia.
Ethiopia registered their first win to upset Mozambique in Maputo, with Kenean Markneh scoring the only goal in the 87th minute after Mambas keeper Ernan spilled a low shot from Carlos Damtew.
The East Africans move on to three points but remain bottom of Group J, behind Sudan on head-to-head record, while Mozambique are on four points and three behind leaders Senegal.
Zambia moved level on four points with Group I leaders Algeria after a 1-1 draw at home to Burundi. The North Africans have the chance to open up a three-point gap when they host Togo on Saturday.
In Group G, Comoros were held to a goalless draw by Congo-Brazzaville in Moroni. Cameroon lead the section on seven points, with Comoros on four, Namibia on three and the Congolese bottom on two points.

సౌదీ అరేబియాలో చర్చి కట్టడానికి అనుమతి ఇచ్చేంతవరకూ యూరప్‌లో మసీదు నిర్మాణానికి ఒప్పుకోమంటూ పోలండ్ ప్రభుత్వం నిర్ణయించిందంటూ ఒక పోస్టు సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సౌదీ అరేబియాలో చర్చి నిర్మించడానికి అనుమతి ఇచ్చేంత వరకు యూరప్‌లో కొత్త మసీదుల నిర్మాణానికి ఒప్పుకోబోమని పోలండ్ ప్రభుత్వం అధికారికంగా నిర్ణయించింది.
ఫాక్ట్: పోలండ్ ప్రభుత్వం మసీదుల నిర్మాణంపై ఎటువంటి అధికారిక నిషేధం విధించలేదు. పోలండ్ రాజకీయ నాయకుడు, యూరోపియన్ పార్లమెంట్ సభ్యుడు డొమినిక్ టార్చిన్స్కీ చేసిన వ్యక్తిగత వ్యాఖ్యలను, ఫిబ్రవరి 2026లో 38 మంది ఎంపీలు చేసిన చట్టబద్ధత లేని ప్రతిపాదనను పోలండ్ ప్రభుత్వ నిర్ణయంగా తప్పుగా ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, పోలండ్ ప్రభుత్వం ఇటువంటి నిర్ణయాన్ని అధికారికంగా ఎక్కడైనా ప్రకటించిందా అని పరిశీలించగా, ఎటువంటి ఆధారాలు లభించలేదు. ఇక, వైరల్ పోస్టులో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి గురించి వెతకగా, ఆయన పోలండ్ రాజకీయ నాయకుడు డొమినిక్ టార్చిన్స్కీ అని తెలిసింది.
డొమినిక్ 2015 నుంచి 2020 వరకు పోలండ్ పార్లమెంట్ సభ్యుడిగా పని చేశారు. అలాగే, 2020 నుంచి యూరోపియన్ పార్లమెంట్ సభ్యుడిగా కొనసాగుతున్నారు. జనవరి 2018లో, పోలండ్‌లోని బియాలిస్టోక్ నగరంలో ఒక పెద్ద ఇస్లామిక్ కేంద్రం, మసీదుకు సౌదీ అరేబియా నిధులు సమకూర్చాలని యోచిస్తున్నట్లు కథనాలు వెలువడ్డాయి. అయితే, డొమినిక్ దీనిని వ్యతిరేకిస్తూ (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఒకవేళ సౌదీ అరేబియా పోలండ్‌లో ఒక మసీదుకు నిధులు ఇవ్వాలనుకుంటే, సౌదీ అరేబియాలో ఒక కాథలిక్ కేథడ్రల్‌కు (చర్చి) నిధులు ఇచ్చేందుకు పోలండ్‌ను అనుమతించాలని 2018లో వ్యాఖ్యానించారు.
అలాగే, 2026లో కూడా పలు సందర్భాల్లో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఆయన ఇదే తరహా వ్యాఖ్యలను చేశారు. ఫిబ్రవరి 2026లో డొమినిక్ టార్చిన్స్కీతో సహా 38 మంది యూరోపియన్ పార్లమెంట్ సభ్యులు విదేశీ నిధులతో యూరప్‌లో కొత్త మసీదుల నిర్మాణాన్ని తాత్కాలికంగా నిలిపివేయాలని (మారటోరియం) ప్రతిపాదించారు. అయితే, ఈ ప్రతిపాదనకు ఎటువంటి చట్టపరమైన విలువ లేదు. పోలండ్ లేదా యూరప్‌లో మసీదుల నిర్మాణంపై ఎలాంటి నిషేధం విధించబడలేదు.
ఇక, స్థానిక వ్యతిరేకత కారణంగా బియాలిస్టోక్ నగరంలో సౌదీ అరేబియా నిధులతో నిర్మించాలనుకున్న ఇస్లామిక్ కేంద్రం ప్రాజెక్ట్ రద్దయింది. దానికి బదులుగా, యునైటెడ్ అరబ్ ఎమిరేట్స్ (UAE) ఆర్థిక సహాయంతో అక్కడి ముస్లిం రిలీజియస్ యూనియన్ పాత ప్రార్థనా మందిరాన్ని పునరుద్ధరించి, ఫిబ్రవరి 2021లో మసీదును ప్రారంభించారు.
చివరిగా, సౌదీ అరేబియాలో చర్చి నిర్మాణానికి అనుమతి ఇచ్చే వరకు యూరప్‌లో మసీదుల నిర్మాణాన్ని అడ్డుకుంటామని పోలండ్ ప్రభుత్వం ఎటువంటి అధికారిక నిర్ణయం తీసుకోలేదు.

Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.
Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.
The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.
Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."
Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.
"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."
Morocco raises concerns over CAS process
Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.
In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.
The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.
Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."
CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.
Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.
Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."
Trouble on the field and in the stands
Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.
The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).
Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.
Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.
The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point.
Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.
Soccer's laws versus regulations
Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.
The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.
In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."
The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.
The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.
Soccer fans in Senegal celebrate a win
"Senegal won on the pitch, and the court simply confirmed what we all already knew: We are the real champions of Africa," said Mariama Sidibé, 35, an accountant in the capital, Dakar.
Sidibé said the dispute between Morocco and Senegal should now be left in the past.
"With all of this behind us, we should focus on what unites us now, and who knows, maybe Morocco can have its revenge on the field during the next AFCON this summer," she said.
"At the end of the day Morocco and Senegal are brothers," Sidibé added, referring to the countries' long shared close ties built on religion, trade and culture.
Sidi Sylla, a philosophy student at Dakar's main university, said the court's ruling was "not just a win for Senegal but for football in general."
Historic decision
CAS rulings have stripped many athletes of Olympic medals for doping, but it's rare to overturn the result of a major soccer competition.
CAS refused to change the results of the 2019 Asian Cup, dismissing an appeal that the star striker on winning team Qatar shouldn't have been eligible for the tournament.
A lengthy legal battle over the same year's African Champions League final also ended with the original winner, Esperance of Tunisia, taking the title after its opponent Wydad from Morocco refused to play on.
One notable CAS ruling on a team sport title came at the Winter Olympics in 2022. A doping case involving then-15-year-old Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva ended up with her disqualification, and the Russian team being dropped from gold to bronze in the team event.

US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
- Published
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.
The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.
Losing its voice
The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.
One of the rover’s two UHF radios was unresponsive when it powered up on October 30, triggering an automatic switch to the backup radio and placing the rover in safe mode. Ground teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California later discovered the backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output, NASA said in a statement last week.
“The team has stopped using both radios until they can evaluate potential causes of the issues and one or both are deemed safe to resume operating,” NASA said.
Perseverance is now transmitting signals directly to Earth in X-band, but the connection provides a “significantly lower data rate” than relaying signals through orbiters using the UHF radios. Mission managers paused the rover’s science operations “out of an abundance of caution” as they investigate the radio problem. Their initial focus is on getting the backup UHF radio running before turning their attention on recovering the primary radio, NASA said.

Bengaluru-based VC firm Aeravti Ventures has launched its second fund, Aeravti Ventures II, with a target corpus of ₹300 Cr, securing commitments exceeding ₹150 Cr at its first close. The Category II AIF has attracted capital from LPs of its maiden fund, corporates, family offices, high-net-worth individuals (HNIs), and ultra HNIs. The firm expects to complete the final close within six months and said the capital would be deployed over the next 10 years. Fund II will back 9-10 early-stage startups across three broad themes: food security, health infrastructure, and physical infrastructure. Its focus will span agriculture and allied sectors, biosciences, life sciences, advanced manufacturing, waste management, and energy. The launch expands Aeravti’s investment strategy into physical infrastructure-led businesses, alongside its existing focus on food and healthcare. The new fund will invest from pre-seed to pre-Series A, with a preference for leading pre-seed and seed rounds. Backing Startups Beyond Seed Stage Aeravti plans to write initial cheques of ₹6 Cr to ₹10 Cr per startup, retaining capacity to invest another 2-3 times the initial amount in subsequent rounds. Follow-on investments would typically be considered 12-18 months after the initial investment, with cheque sizes of ₹10–25 Cr. The fund has already backed three startups but the firm did not disclose their names. Aeravti Ventures managing partner Rishabh Singh told Inc42 that founder resilience is the firm’s most important consideration when evaluating early-stage businesses. The strategy builds on its maiden fund, which achieved a final close of ₹76 Cr and is fully deployed across seven startups. Aeravti led the seed rounds in all seven companies. The firm had announced the first close of its maiden fund in May 2023, when it was targeting a ₹100 Cr corpus to back emerging technology startups across deeptech, biosciences, agritech, climate, and enterprise tech. Discussing the fundraising environment, Singh said raising capital has become difficult for venture funds in India and globally, reinforcing the need for investment firms to sharpen their focus. He cautioned against pursuing emerging sectors simply because they are attracting attention elsewhere, arguing that India needs to develop its own VC and startup ecosystem rather than following the US playbook.

3 killed as car rams trolley on Delhi-Jaipur highway: Police
The deceased were identified as Harish Kumar, Devendra Prajapat and Hemant Prajapat, all residents of Mundanwada village.
Three men were killed and two seriously injured after the vehicle they were travelling in rammed a trolley on the Delhi-Jaipur National Highway (NH-48) late on Tuesday, police said.
The incident took place near Dahmi flyover in Behror area. The deceased were identified as Harish Kumar, Devendra Prajapat and Hemant Prajapat, all residents of Mundanwada village.
According to the police, the five youngsters were returning to their village from Bhagwadi in Behror when their vehicle lost control and crashed into a trolley around 1am. The collision badly mangled the front of the car, trapping all five occupants inside.
“We received information about the accident near the Dahmi flyover around 1am. On reaching the spot, we found a car had collided with a trolley from behind. Three people died on the spot and the other two sustained injuries. The injured were immediately rushed to a hospital, where they are undergoing treatment,” Behror station house officer Ravindra said.
The bodies of the deceased were shifted to the mortuary of Behror hospital for post-mortem.
Police said an investigation was underway to ascertain the exact cause of the accident.

Four years after huge asteroid crash, a spacecraft has now returned to assess the damage
- Published
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.
It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.
The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.
The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.
"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.
The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.
The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.
"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.
"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."
The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.
The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.
A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.
The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.
"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.
"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."
She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.
"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.
"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."
Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.
A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.
There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.
Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.
But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.
This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.
Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
- Published
Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.
She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC.
So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor."
Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago.
Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution.
Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year.
North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty.
"The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself, he adds.
First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps.
Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011.
Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees.
Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death.
Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths.
This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions.
Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East."
Rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds.
The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant says she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity".
North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects.
All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt says.
And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot.
Kim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians.
Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang.
One of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian.
When a devastating famine began in the late 1990s, North Hamgyong was one of the first regions to starve because it was cut off from the state's food supply which prioritised Pyongyang. Millions were killed in what the regime described euphemistically as the "Arduous March". It was a time when many North Koreans crossed into China seeking food and work.
Kim was one of them. Aged 22 in 2003, she took what she believed was a job opportunity in China offered by a friend's aunt. But once she crossed the border, she was forced into marriage with a Chinese man and became pregnant.
While picking up a free pram for her newborn daughter at a building adorned with a cross, she encountered a missionary for the first time. Kim would join a growing group of people who discovered Christianity in China - a group that Pyongyang saw as a threat when they were returned to the North, according to Prof Kang.
Kim was arrested in China in 2007 and deported. During interrogation, she says North Korean secret police asked her if she'd ever worn a cross on her neck. She pretended not to understand. She told the police she only recognised the symbol from hospital buildings.
Kim Bo-bin says it was God's blessing the interrogator seemed more interested in whether she intended to flee to South Korea, a grave offence. She says she was beaten for 23 days and sentenced to three years of hard labour at a prison. Her story tallies with multiple accounts in Korea Future's report of extreme police violence causing broken bones and severe bleeding.
Lee Young-joo, who Kim Bo-bin met in prison also after being deported from China, tells the BBC she was interrogated about whether she'd met any missionaries, been to a church or seen a Bible. "Of course you must deny all of it. I said no, I haven't seen it," she told them.
In her prison cell, Lee says she'd keep her eyes open, begging God to save her life. Whenever anyone shut their eyes, guards would swear and shout: "Are you praying?"
Lee is glad she wasn't found to be a Christian, because she says she "would have been sent to a political prisoners' camp. I would be tortured and never allowed to leave and be buried there." This is a widely-held fear among defectors, although Korea Future's report did not hear any first-hand testimonies of Christians being held in such camps.
Lee, who previously shared with the BBC the abuse she suffered inside prison, says she was sentenced to three-and-half years. Outside of hard labour, she would spend time praying, sometimes with other Christian inmates. They would hold hands and whisper Bible verses from memory.
She and Kim Bo-bin eventually returned home after serving their sentences, where they continued to practise their religion in secret, they tell the BBC.
Kim says she managed to convert her younger sister and other relatives: "My aunt's walls are thick. The neighbours can't hear us so I quietly taught them hymns and about the all-knowing and all-powerful God."
Lee tells the BBC her mother was horrified when she learned of her Christian faith. Undeterred, she told her that she would escape again to join her daughter, who had been left in China as Lee was arrested and deported. When her mother protested, she responded saying they could all live together later.
Her incredulous mother asked: where? "In heaven," she replied.
Today, Lee attends a small church of North Korean escapees in Seoul. She prays daily, to thank God for the chicken soup and the stroll along the river. She prays for her daughter, who escaped with her in 2010, to find a nice Christian man to marry. Her mother died in North Korea some years after her escape, she was told.
Kim managed to flee to South Korea eventually, in 2012, at the age of 30, along with her daughter. She prays throughout the day - and not silently. At church on Sundays, she is the loudest singer.

Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.
That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where modest brick houses and tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.
But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.
It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex. The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.
South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.
The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.
Now, not only are the children getting to practice their reading, some of them have tried their hand at writing their own stories.
The newly published authors sit up front, ready to sign the pile of freshly-printed books for sale and answer questions about their process.
Thirteen-year-old Fiona Mogane, the bespectacled author of "Lindani's Modelling Journey," is one of them.
"It's about a girl who discovered a lot of challenges throughout her journey," Fiona explains. One of those challenges is that the main character Lindani's mother is an alcoholic, spending what little money the family has on drink — including government grant money meant for her daughter's welfare. She also shouts at her daughter a lot, and sometimes Lindani worries she will follow in her mother's footsteps.
Fiona writes: "Sometimes a thought intrudes on Lindani's mind, telling her that if she took some alcohol, it would make her feel better and stand up for herself …. However Lindani always pulls herself out of that thought: she knows she is stronger than that."
Phelelisa Somana, one of the coordinators of the book project, says she was impressed with the maturity of Fiona's story.
"When I read her story it had a very deep theme that I didn't expect a child to delve into in a way that she did," says Somana.
It "definitely just reminded me just how much kids are a lot smarter than they think they are," she adds. "They notice a lot more than they think they do."
Learning "Ubuntu"
Fortunately, Fiona's tale has a happy ending. Dreaming of becoming the next Miss South Africa, her character Lindani decides to try and raise the money she needs to enter a modelling contest by baking scones and selling them to her neighbors.
"She believes deep down inside that each one of her homemade scones has something special that makes them really delicious," Fiona writes.
In the end, Lindani makes enough cash to enter the contest. She comes in second place and is crowned "princess."
"She is happy because she has proved to herself that she can make a way when it initially seemed there was none," Fiona writes.
In real life, Fiona — also keen on modeling — is being raised in Alex by a single mom. Alex has high crime rates and poor government services like water and electricity. The young teenager is all too familiar with the problems, but she says there are good things about township life too..
"Alex is a crowded place, but when you're in Alex, you can learn a lot of things," she explains. "You can learn how to have Ubuntu."
Ubuntu is an African philosophy centering on community well-being and shared responsibility. As Fiona puts it: "Ubuntu is to help other people when they are in need."
Fiona, whose favorite subject at school is English, says she'd like to go to university, maybe to study medicine. And there's another dream too.
"One day, if I grow up, I want to build a big house that will be having a room with its own books," she says.
Homes without books
Fiona didn't grow up with books at home. Two-thirds of South African children don't have books at home, according to one study by UNICEF.
They won't necessarily find them at school either.
Only about 15% of public schools in South Africa have a functioning library, according to government data.
The dire state of child literacy has its roots in the home. Many children have weak early learning foundations, according to the UNICEF study, and they have no exposure to books before starting primary school.
"When I became the minister of basic education in 2024 I was confronted by the statistic of 80% of 10-year-olds who cannot read for meaning in any language," Basic Education Minister Siviwe Gwarube told NPR.
The minister says the government is trying to tackle this problem by getting more kids into early learning programs.
"We're investing ten billion rand [$58 million] over the next three years on a massive haul out of early childhood development centers," Gwarube says.
Tebogo Selekane, an English teacher at Kwa-bhekilanga secondary school, says the weekend program at Read Alex has helped some of her students a lot. Two of her students have stories in the book.
"They are doing very well in reading," says Selekane. "There's a lot of change in them... they will respond back with confidence."
A country of storytellers
At the book launch, Wandile Mathe, a 21-year-old South African writer and joint coordinator of the project, says despite South Africa's poor literacy rates, the children he coaches come from a nation of storytellers.
"I think South Africans are natural storytellers," he says. "There's always gossip going around anyway."
"In the taxi, at the line, in a shop, wherever you go, there's always someone willing to tell you a story, whether about their personal life or the things that they're seeing around," he laughs. "We're huge social commentators. Nothing will pass by and we will not comment."
The kids who contributed to the book are true to this storytelling tradition, borrowing from their lives and what they see daily in the township. As well as Fiona's story about poverty and alcoholism, there are tales about peer pressure, dangerous men on the street, losing parents and inability to pay school fees.
But it's not all doom and gloom. The heroes and heroines all find ways to overcome the obstacles, learning important lessons and making friends along the way.
For example, one of the young authors, 13-year-old Anita Maloka, wrote a story about a rural girl who moves to Johannesburg to attend school and dreams of becoming a scientist. But the school is not what she hoped.
"Sometimes two students had to squeeze together on one chair. Textbooks were scarce," she writes. The family doesn't have the money to send her anywhere better though, so the character works toward earning a scholarship at a school that "has a real science lab and an entire room just for learning to program computers and building robots."
Like her character, Anita, who dreams of becoming a marine biologist, is also working toward getting a scholarship that will take her out of the township.
But she stresses that life in Alex is "not just about struggle."
"It's about children who want to travel, to explore and dream and make their dreams come true," she says.

Being a tech reviewer, my entire phone gallery is filled with hundreds of random screenshots. It also holds important photos of family moments, my pet, and a few other travel memories.
Because of this, my phone usually runs out of storage quickly. It also has a habit of running out at the worst possible time, showing storage-full notifications when I am about to capture something important.
I usually back up my photos to Google Drive using the Google Photos app. However, the free Cloud storage is already full.
With every Gmail account, Google offers 15 GB of free storage, which is now shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos. That storage. I wouldn’t prefer paying for more cloud storage, so I needed something that I could use to back up without paying for the cloud, and that is easy to sync between devices without manually transferring
While searching for options and thinking of building it myself, I found Syncthing, a free, open-source app that automatically transfers photos taken on your phone to your Windows PC or Mac. This is especially useful because, with a recent MacBook upgrade, I had gigabytes of unused storage.
It’s so seamless that once you take a photo on your phone, it automatically appears on your Windows PC or Mac without connecting a cable. It requires no monthly subscription and removes the friction of manually backing up files. It is also a free, open-source tool and works over Wi-Fi.
The best part is that it comes with flexible options. You can choose where photos are stored, back them up to an external hard drive, and configure it to keep copies even when you delete photos from your phone.
However, setting up Syncthing might be complex for beginners. So I created this detailed, comprehensive guide to help you set up Syncthing to automatically back up photos taken on your Android phone to either Windows or Mac.
Table of Contents
Before you begin, here are the minimum requirements for these steps to work
- You need an Android phone (I used a OnePlus 13R with Android 16)
- Ensure both are on the same Wi-Fi network for the initial setup.
- You need a Windows 10 or 11 PC, or a Mac
- Make sure your Mac or Windows PC has enough free space to back up your phone photos.
Install Syncthing-Fork on your phone
Step 1: Open the Google Play Store, search for the Syncthing-Fork app, and tap Install.
Step 2: Once the app is installed, tap Open
Step 3: The app welcomes you with an onboarding screen. Click Continue
Step 4: Next, you need to grant storage permission to the app. Tap the Grant Storage Permission button
Step 5: You will be taken to the file access settings of the Syncthing-Fork app on your phone. From there, enable the toggle that says Allow Access to Manage All Files.
Step 6: Next, you need to grant permission for battery optimization for the Syncthing-Fork app
Step 7: Next, tap Allow
Step 8: On the next screen, the app asks for location permission; you can skip it. Tap on the Continue option.
Step 9: On the next screen, the app asks for Notifications. The app uses notifications to alert you about device connections for the sharing required in the form of notifications. So you need to allow the app to send notifications. It also keeps the app running in the background.
Step 10: Tap Grant permission, then tap Allow to allow app notifications.
Step 11: That’s it; your app onboarding and setup are complete. Next, you need to download Syncthing on Windows.
Install Syncthing on Windows
Step 12: On your Windows PC, open any browser and go to the Syncthing downloads page. Scroll down and tap on the Syncthing Windows Setup option.
Step 13: Next, under the Assets section, download the installer
Step 14: Once the download is complete, click Open file
Step 15: Similar to mobile, you need to go through multiple screens to set up on Windows. There isn’t much to do; just click Next on the first five pages.
Step 16: Now, enable or disable additional tasks based on your needs. I recommend enabling automatic syncing when logging on and starting syncing after installation. Also, create a desktop shortcut to the Syncthing configuration page so that it will be easy to access in the future
Step 17: Once selected, click Next
Step 18: Finally, click Install to install it on your Windows.
Step 19: If the Windows Firewall block prompt appears, click Yes to the firewall rule
Step 20: Next, click Allow to continue installation.
Step 21: Once installed, click Finish. Make sure you enable the Syncthing configuration page.
Step 22: The configuration page opens in your default browser. The default browser security blocks access to the page. No need to worry; to bypass it, click Advanced on the warning page.
Step 23: Next, click Continue to 127.0.0.1
Step 24: Next, choose whether to send usage reports. I would suggest No.
Step 25: Next, click OK on the password notice
Install Syncthing on a Mac
If you are using a Mac, you can also set up Syncthing on your Mac to sync photos between your Android phone and your Mac. Follow the process below.
Step 26: On a Mac, open the Syncthing downloads page. Here is the link. On the downloads page, under the downloads section, click on the Syncthing-Mac OS link.
Step 27: Next, scroll down and download the .dmg file
Step 28: Click Allow to download
Step 29: Once downloaded, drag Syncthing to the Applications folder.
Step 30: Next, Open Syncthing on your Mac and allow local network access
Step 31: It opens in the default browser. Select No when the Allow Anonymous Usage reporting prompt appears. That’s it.
Connect your phone and computer
Next, connect your phone to Windows or Mac to start sharing photos. The process is similar on both macOS and Windows. For this demonstration, I am using Windows.
Step 32: Next, open the Syncthing page on your computer and click Actions at the top right.
Step 33: Click Show ID
Step 34: Syncthing shows the computer’s device ID as text and as a QR code. Scan the QR code with your phone to copy the device ID.
Step 35: Open the Syncthing-Fork app on your Phone and tap the Devices tab
Step 36: Tap the Add Device button
Step 37: Tap the QR code button, then scan the QR code shown on the desktop using your phone camera. If Android asks for camera access, tap Allow.
Note: If the QR code isn’t working, you can type the ID instead, or click Copy on the computer, send the ID to yourself in a chat or email, then paste it here.
Step 38: Next, check the device ID. Remember that it should match the ID on your computer screen.
Step 39: Give the computer a name. Tap Name and type a name you will recognize, such as Windows PC or My Mac or something that you can recognize.
Step 40: Once done, tap the check mark
Step 41: Within a minute, a yellow New Device box appears on the Syncthing page on your computer, asking you to connect your phone. It also displays a name; cross-check that the name is your phone’s model (mine is CPH2691). Then, click Add Device.
Note: If nothing appears after a few minutes, ensure both devices are on the same Wi-Fi, then reload the page. On a Mac, check that you have allowed local network access.
Step 42: Next, enter the phone name and click Save. You can enter any name that is easy to recognize, similar to how you name your desktop on your Android phone.
Step 43: Next, open the Syncthing-Fork app on your phone and check that the phone says Up to Date.
Share the Camera folder from your phone
Step 44: Next, choose the folder you want to back up. On the phone, tap the Folders tab, then tap the Add Folder button at the top right (the folder with a plus sign).
Step 45: Type the folder name. In this case, I am naming it a camera.
Step 46: Next, tap Directory to choose the folder on your phone.
Step 47: Android’s folder picker opens. If you want to back up photos from the camera, tap DCIM; this is the folder where phone cameras save photos.
Step 48: Next, tap the Camera folder.
Step 49: Finally, tap the Use this folder option

Step 51: Next, under Devices, turn on the switch next to your computer’s name. This shares the folder with it.
Step 52: Next, choose the Folder Type. By default, it says Send & Receive. It means it also copies the images from your desktop to your phone. Keep it if you want to sync photos between both devices, or select Send Only in the next steps. Tap Send & Receive to open the list.

Step 57: Now, on the computer, a yellow New Folder box appears once again. Click Add.
Step 58: Choose where to save the photos. In Folder Path, type where the backup should go. I used my Pictures folder. For instance, you can type the path: C:\Users\YourName\Pictures\Phone Backup. You can also save the photos on an external drive. You can enter the external drive path here.

Step 62: Next, under Clean out after option, set Keep Clean Out to 0. Zero means forever, so deleted photos are never removed from the computer.

Check that it works
Step 67: Next, your phone will start transferring photos to your computer. You will see an up-to-date status as a green dot next to the folder under Remote Devices. My 224 photos and videos (3.5 GB) took about two minutes over Wi-Fi. Keep both devices awake and on the same Wi-Fi until it finishes.
Step 68: You can also see the status on mobile too. On the phone, the Camera folder also says Up to Date and shows how many files it has sent.
Step 69: You can also test it by taking a photo with your camera app, then open Syncthing-Fork again. Within a few seconds, the folder shows the new photo’s name as the last file sent.
Step 70: To open the backup photos on Windows, open File Explorer and click Pictures in the left sidebar. On a Mac, open Finder and go to your Pictures folder.
Step 71: You can see a Phone Backup folder. Open it.
Step 72: You can find all backup images here.
Back up only on Wi-Fi
If you have limited data, make sure the phone backs up on Wi-Fi only, so it never uses your mobile data. Follow the steps to back up images only using the Wifi.
Step 73: In Syncthing-Fork, tap the menu button at the top left.
Step 74: Tap Settings
Step 75: Tap Run Conditions

Step 77: Also, make sure Run on mobile data is off
Step 78: This is Optional: You can also enable backup only while charging, so it won’t affect your battery life; these services need to run in the background.
Automatically Back Up Your Photos Without the Cloud
This is how you can back up your photos from your phone to a Mac or Windows PC. This is especially useful if you have limited storage on your phone and don’t want to pay for cloud storage.
If you have free space on your Mac or Windows device, photos will be backed up automatically. The best part is that Syncthing also lets you back up photos to an external device connected to your computer, so all your photos are backed up without affecting your computer storage.
However, there are a few things to note. For the backup to work, make sure your phone and computer are on the same Wi-Fi, and that the Syncthing-Fork app shows a green dot at the top.
If you are using a Mac, allow local network access in System Settings (Privacy & Security > Local Network). If the backup stops after a while, the most likely reason is that Android has paused the app. To run the app again, open Settings, go to App Settings, and select the Syncthing-Fork app. In the battery settings, choose Unrestricted.
I have also noticed that sometimes the folder is out of sync on my computer. This is most likely because of the limited storage space on my Mac. To fix this, free up space and choose a folder on another drive on a Mac or Windows. If you are facing any other issues, comment below, and I will be happy to help you.
