Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”
He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.
This is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Big Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.
For the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”
Mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a new toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.)
As it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production company that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.
What started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”
The videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”
Meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he says. “So I got a kick out of it.”
Meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their shows.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.
To Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Big Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”)
Though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.
Though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
“This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he says. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”
Others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek says the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.)
What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”
Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.
So what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of new, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.
Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he says. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”

Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
- Published
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which also included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
The BBC contacted the US Department of Justice for comment.
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.
"The RICO count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

Facebook users are sharing posts listing seven rules that U.S. President Donald Trump allegedly proposed to limit privileges for lawmakers in Congress.
These alleged rules included proposals like removing pensions for Congress members and requiring lawmakers to participate in the same government-run social services many Americans use, like Medicare for health care insurance and Social Security for retirement paychecks. Here's how the claim usually went, per these posts:
I'm in agreement with Fox News. I wonder how loud it'll get if Trump could pull this off. It will be interesting.
President Trump is asking everyone to share this, in three days, most people in the United States will have seen the message. This is an idea that should be passed around, regardless of political party.
The TRUMP Rules:
1. Tenure / No Pension. A Congressman/woman collects a salary while in office and receives no pay when they're out of office. And no more perks go with them.
2. Congress (past, present, & future) participates in Social Security. All funds in the Congressional retirement fund move to the Social Security system immediately. All future funds flow into the Social Security system, and Congress participates with the American people. It may not be used for any other purpose.
3. Congress must purchase their own retirement plan, just as ALL Americans do.
4. Congress will no longer vote themselves a pay raise. Congressional pay will rise at the ok same rate as the COLA for monthly Social Security recipients minus 1% if having a budget balance deficit.
5. Congress loses their current care system and participates in the same health care system (Medicare) as the American people.
6. Congress must equally abide by all laws they impose on the American people (i.e. NO MORE INSIDER TRADING!!!).
7. All contracts with past and present Congressmen/women are void. The American people did not make this contract with Congressmen/women. Congress made all these contracts by and for themselves.
Serving in Congress is an honor and privilege, NOT a career.
The Founding Fathers envisioned citizen legislators should serve their term(s), then go home and go back to work … not get all kinds of freebies. Term limits of 2 terms and treat them like a regular citizen!
You will need to copy and paste.
I AGREE SO IM SHARING!
Note:
This should be done immediately!!!
Thank you! Copy/Paste and shared
Meanwhile, Snopes readers asked about similar posts and searched the website for verification.
The above text is a copypasta — a copy-and-pasted internet hoax common on Facebook. As Snopes previously reported, variants of this particular copypasta have spread online since at least 2009, when a version of the rules listed above were labeled "The 28th Amendment" and attributed to business magnate Warren Buffett.
Internet users circulated it as the "Congressional Reform Act of 2017" during Trump's first term and the "Congressional Reform Act of 2025" in 2025, during his second term.
Fox News, which the copypasta cited as its source, has never reported on "The TRUMP Rules" as of this writing, per a search of the news outlet's website (archived). Trump has also not mentioned or posted about this particular copypasta online, according to two databases that track his social media output (archived, archived). The White House webpage for news releases didn't reference these supposed rules. Finally, a search for "The TRUMP Rules" on Google returned no credible and relevant results treating the list as a legitimate proposal (archived).
Thus, we have rated this claim false.
The so-called reforms listed in the act also include a mixture of rules that already exist and proposals that would actually change existing policy. Here's a breakdown of what these supposed reforms would and would not change:
Do Congress members receive pensions?
Congress members, like most federal employees, are eligible for a pension. Here are the pension eligibility requirements, according to the Congressional Research Service:
Members of Congress are eligible for a pension at the age of 62 if they have completed at least 5 years of service. Members are eligible for a pension at age 50 if they have completed 20 years of service, or at any age after completing 25 years of service. The amount of the pension depends on length of service (as measured in months) and the average of the highest three years of salary. By law, the starting amount of a Member's retirement annuity may not exceed 80% of his or her final salary.
Do Congress members pay into Social Security?
Per our previous reporting, Congress members have paid into Social Security since 1984, when they first became eligible for Social Security benefits.
Congress members first elected in 1984 or later are covered automatically under the Federal Employees' Retirement System, which other government workers use, and can decline coverage.
Aside from Social Security, lawmakers elected before 1984 can be covered under the Civil Service Retirement System; a separate pension plan, CSRS Offset, which is a mix of CSRS and Social Security; or Social Security alone. Lawmakers also pay into these plans — how much they pay and which plans they pay into differs based on when they were elected.
Can Congress members give themselves a raise?
Congress members can vote for a pay raise as dictated by the Constitution, but the raise doesn't take effect until the next election due to the 27th Amendment.
Technically, a law passed in 1989 grants Congress an automatic cost-of-living pay raise, but lawmakers have blocked those pay increases from taking effect for years. Rank-and-file members of Congress, who receive $174,000 annually as of this writing, have not increased their pay since 2009.
Do Congress members have own health care system?
Under the Affordable Care Act of 2010, commonly known as Obamacare, lawmakers must give up the insurance coverage previously provided to them via the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and buy health insurance through a plan or exchange created under the act. The Office of Personnel Management has also dictated that members of Congress must purchase through DC Health Link, a program offered under the ACA.
Members of Congress also pay into Medicare and are eligible for it, just like any American.
Are Congress members allowed to participate in insider trading?
Congress members are allowed to trade stocks, but legally, they're not supposed to conduct insider trading. The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012 — known as the STOCK Act — prohibits members of Congress from using "any nonpublic information derived from the individual's position … or gained from performance of the individual's duties, for personal benefit."
Critics argue the STOCK Act failed to stop insider trading, however, and no member of Congress has been prosecuted for insider trading under the STOCK Act as of this writing — although policy experts have said there's been "persistent credible allegations" of insider trading since the act passed.

Can you play GTA 6 from an external hard drive on PS5 or Xbox Series X/S?
Rockstar’s behemoth takes up a lot of storage space.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game of the year by some distance, having racked up $3.79 billion in pre-orders and day-one sales. On PlayStation 5 alone, more than 39 million unique players took control of dual protagonists Jason and Lucia on opening weekend, making it the biggest game debut in the 32-year history of PlayStation.
There will be many other folks who want to play the game and haven't had a chance to jump in yet. One thing they should note is that, with a hefty install size, GTA 6 will take up a significant chunk of their PS5 or Xbox Series X/S storage space.
You might be wondering whether you can install GTA 6 on an external hard drive to avoid having to delete other games and data from your console. You can move GTA 6 to your external storage when you're not playing it. However, to run the game locally, you'll need to have it installed on your system's built-in storage, an SDD you've installed in your PS5 or a compatible NVMe expansion card that's plugged into your Xbox.
As with many other recent games, GTA 6 needs to take advantage of the fast-loading capabilities of the PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. The consoles are unable to load data for these titles quickly enough from an external hard drive over a USB connection. For the same reason, disc-based PS5 and Xbox Series X games are installed onto system storage before you can play them. The PS5 can run PS4 games from external storage, though. Likewise, an Xbox Series X/S can run older Xbox One and Xbox 360 titles directly from an external hard drive.
That said, there is a way to play GTA 6 without first having to free up a whole lot of console storage space. It's possible to stream the game from the cloud on Xbox Series X/S. There are two things to note if you'd like to go with that option, including that Xbox just brought in new cloud gaming time limits. Game Pass subscribers get up to 15 hours of cloud gaming included each month. You can pay extra for more access. Also, GTA 6 is limited to Xbox Series S graphics settings on Xbox Cloud Gaming.
On the PlayStation side, cloud streaming works on PS5 and PlayStation Portal if you're a PlayStation Plus Premium subscriber. There are no cloud gaming time limits on PS Plus. You'll also need to purchase GTA 6 for PS5 or Xbox Series X/S to stream the game from the cloud, as it's not included in the PS Plus or Game Pass libraries — and it probably won't be for quite some time.

India rejects US excess capacity claims, says no structural overcapacity in any sector
“The Notice is currently under examination,” the ministry said, adding that India had engaged constructively throughout the investigation.
The government of India on Wednesday said it was examining a notice issued by the United States Trade Representative (USTR) in a probe into manufacturing capacity across 14 economies, including India, and reiterated that the country does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.
In a statement issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the government said it had taken note of the notice of determination and request for comments issued by the USTR under Section 301 of the US Trade Act.
“The Notice is currently under examination,” the ministry said, adding that India had engaged constructively throughout the investigation.
Deep Dive
The Department of Commerce had stated, in its response to the notice of initiation and subsequent proceedings, that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector, the statement said.
India also reiterated that trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of the ongoing negotiations for the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA).
“The Government of India remains committed to working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement,” the ministry said, referring to the framework announced on February 2 and the joint statement issued on February 7.
US report targets India's manufacturing policies
The USTR's 189-page report, released on Wednesday, has built its case around India's flagship manufacturing programmes, including Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme.
The report describes India's manufacturing policies as an effort to expand production beyond what market demand would support. It concludes that India's “acts, policies, and practices” concerning manufacturing capacity are unreasonable and burden US commerce.
The USTR estimates that raising manufacturing's share of India's GDP to 25%, as envisaged under Make in India, would require about $500 billion in additional output at 2025 levels.
India has rejected the allegations throughout the eight-month investigation, arguing that it is building manufacturing capacity to meet domestic demand and reduce dependence on certain countries for critical inputs.
In its submissions, India said production rises and falls according to orders and market conditions, rather than being directed by the government. It also argued that Make in India and PLI should not be viewed as schemes to create manufacturing capacity unrelated to demand.
India participated in confidential consultations with the USTR during the investigation. Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal had also rejected the charge at the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee in October, saying India “does not have structural excess capacity” in the sectors identified.
Tariff proposal and trade deal talks
The USTR has proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods under the Section 301 investigation. The rate could fall to 17% if India signs a trade agreement with Washington.
The report focuses on sectors such as steel, solar, health and information and communications technology (ICT), and also flags India's labour laws, market access barriers and growing imports of inputs from China.
The proposed tariffs exempt generic medicines in dosage form, hundreds of drug ingredients when used in pharmaceuticals, and patented drugs.
Written comments on the proposed tariffs are due by January 5, 2027, while hearings are scheduled to begin on January 25.
India and the US have been negotiating a bilateral trade agreement since February 2025. The two countries announced a framework for an interim deal in February, with Washington outlining an 18% reciprocal tariff on a range of Indian goods.

Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
MONGUÍ, Colombia — Moisés Moreno greets visitors at his greenhouse 10,000 feet high in the Andes Mountains. Underneath the plastic roof, he nurtures tiny seedlings that can grow to be 30-feet tall.
"Do you know anything about frailejons?" Moreno asks his visitors, who are mostly clueless.
Related to the sunflower, frailejons are the iconic flora of Colombia's high mountain wetlands, which are known as páramos, and are vital for the country's water supply.
The wooly fuzz on their leaves protect frailejons from the cold and absorb water from the cloud cover. This helps maintain moisture in the páramos, which are the source of major rivers, and much of Colombia's water.
But frailejons and the páramos where they grow face a growing array of threats, including farmers, cattle ranchers and coal miners who are gradually pushing higher into the Andes. In addition, climate change is warming the mountains, allowing invasive species to survive at higher altitudes and disrupt their fragile ecosystems.
Of the nearly 150 species of frailejons, two-thirds are at risk and 17 are endangered, says Mauricio Diazgranados, a Colombian expert on the plant who is chief science officer at the New York Botanical Garden.
"They are a keystone species for maintaining the páramos and play a key role in water production," he says. "But most frailejons are in trouble,"
When explorers first spotted the shrubs mysteriously protruding from the mountain fog centuries ago, they reminded them of hooded monks. Hence the name frailejon, which is Spanish for "big friar."
The long, thin leaves of some species bend toward the sky and resemble palm fronds. Many are stout in the middle because, rather than falling to the ground, their dying leaves slump down to form a brownish outer shell to their trunks.
The Muisca Indians, who once populated the area, considered frailejons to be sacred guardians of the water. When he first came across the plants as a teenager in Colombia, Diazgranados says: "I became completely captivated."
By contrast, Moreno, 53, who runs the frailejon greenhouse, used to be one of the plant's predators. Growing up on a mountainside farm near the central Colombian town of Monguí, Moreno and neighboring farmers knew little about them and chopped them down to make way for potato fields and cow pastures.
"We viewed them as a nuisance," Moreno says.
Later, while employed by a coal mine, he was injured during a cave-in and vowed to work above ground in the fresh mountain air.
On his own he began studying páramo ecosystem that he'd grown up in, started his greenhouse and began leading tourists and volunteers on expeditions to replace the frailejons that had been wiped out.
"I felt inspired to do something to protect the páramos," he says.
Elsewhere, Colombia's National Parks agency and even its armed forces have gotten involved in reforestation campaigns after wildfires scorched thousands of acres of frailejons.
Yet many average Colombians have learned about the plant's importance through an enormously popular cartoon character called Ernesto Pérez. Shaped like a frailejon, he exhorts people to conserve the flora and fauna of the Andes, similar to the way Smokey Bear promotes forest fire prevention in the U.S.
In fact, several of the volunteers Moreno is guiding up the mountain say the cartoon and its earworm theme song introduced them to the frailejon.
"The song is very contagious," says Nicolás Coronado, 25, who works for a Bogotá-based plastics company, and is carrying a 6-inch frailejon that he will plant in the páramo.
The hike takes the group up to an altitude of 11,000 feet, past streams, waterfalls and lagoons. Underfoot, the ground is damp and spongy. The area is a state park and frailejons dot the landscape. But there are also barbed-wire fences erected by farmers and a half dozen cows grazing on the mountainside.
Moreno and his assistants show the volunteers how to dig shallow holes, then add a bit of shredded tobacco as fertilizer, before nestling the tiny frailejons into the soil.
Their survival is no sure thing. Many die in the cold, harsh climate and those that take hold grow just a few inches per year.
To help them along, the volunteers hold an impromptu ceremony, with one member reciting a prayer to connect with the mountain spirits and another blowing on a conch shell.
By now, some volunteers have grown attached to the frailejons that they've carried up the mountain and have bestowed names on them. Among them is biologist Julieta Barba has baptized hers "Gerry," in honor of her mother.
After patting some dirt around the plant's roots, she says: "I'm very excited for her future here in the páramo."

Quick Answer
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia is about more than personal misconduct. It raises serious questions about conflicts of interest, abuse of power, and Silicon Valley’s habit of excusing tech leaders. His departure sends a vital message: no amount of genius, wealth, or market success should place anyone above accountability.
So Jensen Huang will not be returning to Nvidia, in spite of a groundswell of support. And though it might shock some tech bros, I think it is the best thing that could have happened to tech.
The tech world witnessed one of its most dramatic unravelings this month, perhaps the most significant one in years, if not decades. All was going smoothly; AI was still the sun the tech world was revolving around, and one of the biggest planets revolving around it was Nvidia. The company was not just in on living, breathing, and thriving on AI development but at the center of bettering AI for others, as it manufactured AI chips.
When current affairs become… well, current affairs
It all came crashing down when a report was published in The New York Times, revealing news of an affair. This was not the run-of-the-mill gossip that’s seen in the scandal section in tabloids, but news that changed the trajectory of Nvidia and possibly AI.
Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, was found to be having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (unrelated, although having the same surname), a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company. Alice was suspected of being a Chinese spy by US intelligence. Megaspeed was one of the major buyers of Nvidia’s AI chips, and, as per reports, it diverted chips worth USD 2 billion to China against regulations, although both Megaspeed and Nvidia deny any wrongdoing.
Following the news, A LOT went down. Huang seemed to swing into damage control and issued an apology for the affair, promising cooperation with an investigation into it. The tech world thought the worst was over. After all, what could make this worse? Then the New York Times, on 11 November, released a report citing another extramarital affair. This time it was reported that he was in a relationship with Nvidia’s Vice President of Health Care, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to Huang. After trying to save face and his 41-year-long marriage (Jensen Huang is married to Lori Huang), Huang had to resign and leave his post as CEO at Nvidia on 12 November.
But this is not the story of a person’s personal slip-ups, or the extra-marital affair story that much of the media is making it to be. It is actually much bigger than that.
It’s not about infidelity, but about power and misconduct
While Huang has received a fair deal of criticism for his conduct, he has received a lot of support too, especially from Silicon Valley, where it seems that when there is a tech billionaire in question, the rules that apply to the rest of the world cease to apply to them. If you build an important enough product, accumulate billions of Dollars, and build some political connections, what would otherwise be a big no-no suddenly becomes negotiable, and the boundaries around right and wrong start to get hazy.
Affairs and flings are nothing new to the world of tech in particular, or the world of celebrities in general, but this case is more than just a personal lapse of judgment. Had Huang’s affair(s) been something that had happened outside of the workplace or if he had fallen for someone who had nothing to do with tech (an actress, an influencer, a trapeze artiste, et al.), this would have been an entirely different conversation. But his intimate relations with his employee and a customer – and the fact that we are being asked to overlook them – shine a light on what might be wrong with the inherent culture at not just Nvidia but in Silicon Valley.
While most concerns have revolved around Alice Huang being a Chinese spy and sensitive AI technology crossing borders, allegations which have not yet been proved, what is clear beyond doubt is that Huang misused his position as the CEO of one of the biggest companies in the world, on both the client and employee side.
In both of his affairs, Huang was the person of power, with Alice Huang and Kimberly Powell. The client in question bought billions of dollars’ worth of AI chips from Nvidia, and given her intimate relationship revelation with Huang, it would be difficult to rule out that the business deals made between the two were in no way influenced by the relationship. We are not even getting to the part of Alice Huang being a Chinese spy, and whether she managed to get sensitive information and AI chips from Jensen Huang for China, which would give China the AI leverage it needs to get ahead of the US in the AI race. Even if she was “just another client,” does it not still remain a bother that a person who has been hailed as a tech demi-god could not control his urges long enough to get through business? Similarly, his second affair with a senior employee working at Nvidia who directly reported to him, and, as per reports, was promptly promoted during her time at Nvidia, does bring up some very serious questions about preferential treatment, conflict of interest, and company power dynamics.
This is not about Huang’s infidelity, but his ability to make sound decisions. A lot of the evidence suggests that in a situation where he could misuse his position of power, he did. It was not just his moral compass that was compromised, but his professional one too. The fact that this happened, and that the former Nvidia CEO has still received a lot of support, not only raises concerns about the culture at Nvidia, but also about the overall priorities of Silicon Valley.
When the stock market decides where to draw the line
Since Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, a number of executives, tech CEOs, and even the US President himself have come out in support of him. Media channels have had extensive discussions on the matter, and many have marked the (so far) two affairs as a “personal lapse of judgment” and think Huang’s potential as a tech genius outweighs his failings. Elon Musk has compared his exit as “it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak”, while other leaders like Sam Altman, Steven Chen, Tim Sweeney and many more have pushed for his comeback. President Donald Trump has said he would “not mind” seeing Huang reinstated as CEO, and Musk has even offered to hire him.
Now, there is no doubt that Jensen Huang is a genius who has built one of the most important businesses in the world of tech. Many fear that without him, Nvidia would tank, and this would have a devastating impact on AI. However, since the reports of his affairs have come out and his resignation, Nvidia’s stock has taken a nosedive, and so have many other AI stocks. In fact, many are predicting that Huang’s exit might burst the AI bubble, which, for obvious reasons, is way worse for the tech world in general than any lapse in professional and moral code of conduct. Accountability seems to count for little as long as the stock market is doing well.
Time to take the Tech God pedestal away?
Given this groundswell of support, the easy decision for Nvidia would perhaps have been to let Jensen Huang walk back in as if nothing happened and sit back and see the share prices spike. It actually seemed likely, and Huang himself had posted on X (where he was given a free blue tick by Elon Musk), offering to make a comeback if the board considered it would be in the best interest of the company. However, on 18 November, Nvidia ruled out the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. And while this led to groans of disappointment from many of the tech bros, we actually think it was the right call to take.
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…
— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026
While a company has responsibilities towards its shareholders, it also has to keep its employees and clients in mind. Share prices cannot be used as an automatic defense against misconduct, especially at the highest level. Unfortunately, over the past few decades, tech brilliance has been placed on a pedestal, giving a handful of people immunity from general human misconduct. Bouts of bad temper, abusive behavior, and so much more are often turned a blind eye to because a person is perceived as a “Tech God,” a person who is part of the genius crowd that is building a better, brighter future for us all. But recent times have revealed that many of these tech gods whom we have trusted, and largely exempted from strict governance or interference, cannot even follow simple, basic rules that govern mere mortals. And these handful of people, who cannot even follow the basics, are sitting in boardrooms and are now deciding the future of billions of people, even those who have not opted for an AI-laden future or are not even aware of what AI is.
Jensen Huang’s conduct – and the support he has received – now raises the question of whether the people we were told are tech geniuses are as reliable and trustworthy as the narrative around them has painted them out to be. Or are they just a bunch of power-hungry, wealth-accumulating techies who have way too much autonomy for comfort?
The Huang affair (pun intended) marks an important phase in modern tech. While we still do not know how it will all end – there are endless conspiracy theories doing the rounds – we do hope it will teach many in the tech world not to turn a blind eye to “personal and professional misconduct,” just because a person is seen as a genius and is perceived to be good for the world in general and the stock market in particular.

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

A young couple was assaulted by a group of minors at Pramod Mahajan Garden in Kurla West, Mumbai, near Phoenix Marketcity Mall, on 20 November 2026. A viral video showed the group surrounding the couple, verbally abusing and assaulting them with sticks, kicks, punches, a belt, and stones before chasing them away. Police registered a case against eight minors after a video of the attack went viral. They were sent to a juvenile correctional home until 4 December 2026 (here, here). 
Against this backdrop, a video showing several men being paraded by the police is being shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows the Mumbai Police parading those involved in the assault on the couple. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows Mumbai Police parading the accused who assaulted a young couple in Kurla West, Mumbai.
Fact: The viral video shows the accused arrested in connection with the murder of 18-year-old Santosh More in Surat, Gujarat, and not those involved in the assault on a couple in Mumbai. The Surat Police had paraded the accused in connection with the murder case. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a video uploaded by an Instagram account called Gujarat Live on 14 November 2026, predating the Kurla, Mumbai incident. The text accompanying the video claimed that it showed the accused arrested in the murder of Santosh More, a youth from Surat.
A keyword search based on this led us to several media reports (here, here, here) featuring visuals from the viral video. According to these reports, 18-year-old Santosh More was allegedly stabbed to death in Surat’s Rasulabad area on 8 November 2026, following a dispute reportedly linked to a love affair and previous rivalry. The accused were identified as Javed alias Nawab Sheikh, Hansraj Kushwaha, Shakib Maniyar, Shahid Sheikh, and Piyush Sahu.
We also found similar visuals in a video uploaded by the Surat Police on X on 12 November 2026. The video showed the same accused being paraded. The caption stated, “Khatodara Police arrested the accused and taught them a lesson in the law in the case of the murder of a youth in Azad Nagar, Khatodara police station area.”
To sum up, the video of Surat Police parading the murder accused is falsely linked to the Mumbai couple assault case.

Pope Leo laments lack of climate commitments after UN talks end without agreement
Pope Leo XIV has expressed concern over the failure of United Nations climate talks to reach an agreement
VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday expressed concern over the failure of United Nations climate talks to reach an agreement, saying that “extreme environmental events linked to the climate crisis are becoming increasingly frequent.”
The pope has embraced defense of the environment in his papacy, taking up one of the core teachings of his predecessor, Pope Francis, whose landmark encyclical Laudato Si (Praised Be) cast care for the planet as an urgent, existential moral concern.
Leo issued an appeal during his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square to “never forget the human face of the climate crisis, which affects the lives of millions of people, strikes entire communities and undermines the prospects of future generations.”
He called for “fundamental changes in behavior, socioeconomic systems and the governance of our societies,” directing his appeal to “the international community and to each individual.”
During his recent trip to Peru, Leo demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, Leo’s No. 2, in a statement to COP31 recalled Leo’s earlier appeal to “bear in mind the human face of the climate crisis,” as a reminder that the talks were not “merely technical … but concern people’s lives.”
The talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Sunday without reaching an overarching agreement because of disputes over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming.

Dottin out to 'free ball' after historic WBBL decision
- Published
A bizarre dismissal in the Women's Big Bash saw Brisbane Heat's Sarah Glenn bowling to an empty set of stumps, external after Melbourne Renegades new batter Deandra Dottin was ruled to have taken too long to face the delivery.
Experienced West Indies all-rounder Dottin walked out to bat, following the dismissal of Georgia Wareham, with her equipment in disarray and proceeded to adjust her helmet and begin putting on her gloves after arriving in the middle.
Rules introduced before the 2021 WBBL season to speed up play state that an incoming batter must be ready to face - or the non-striker to receive - the next delivery within 75 seconds of a dismissal or retirement.
The umpires adjudged Dottin to have exceeded this time limit and instructed her to stand aside from stumps, while awarding Glenn a free ball.
Glenn hit the middle and leg stumps to remove Dottin for a golden duck. The bowler was initially uncertain how to celebrate - she laughed and covered her face with her hands - before being mobbed by her team-mates.
However, despite the wicket reducing the Renegades to 97-5 with 41 runs needed from 34 balls, they completed their chase of 138 off the final delivery of the match to win by three wickets.

Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving cola giants a tough fight in India
- Published
It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.
Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.
Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.
There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.
According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.
"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."
Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.
But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.
Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.
"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.
Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.
But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.
"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.
"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed
You don't have to leave your TV's refresh rate at 60fps.
If you were to travel back in time thirty years and show someone a smart TV from today, their head would likely explode. In addition to the seemingly limitless amount of content one can find and interact with on a modern television, your Roku TV also may have the ability to let you watch movies in a far more compelling way.
Buried deep in your Roku TV's settings is a way to alter the refresh rate, and there's a very specific reason that you might want to do that. Most Roku TVs default to a refresh rate of 60fps. While that's going to be perfectly fine for some situations, it doesn't make for the most theatrical viewing experience — for the most part, movies are filmed and projected at 24fps. It's the standard, and it has defined the way movies look and feel for decades. When you go to the movie theater, you're watching a 24fps output.
Roku allows you to alter your TV's refresh rate to match that, offering something a bit closer to the original intent of those films.
How to change your TV's refresh rate to 24fps to achieve a film look
There are a lot of ways to change the overall look and display of your Roku TV, but most of that discourse seems centered around colors and contrast. Those things are important, but if you really want to achieve a "movie look," then you'll want to change the refresh rate.
In your Roku TV, to match this unique look, you'll need to first go to the main menu. From here, select Settings, and then go into System. In this menu, you'll find something called Advanced System Settings, which will allow you to access Advanced Display Settings. You want to turn Auto-adjust display refresh rate on.
It's a one-click and done solution, as it will self-adjust itself to match the native refresh rate of any movie or TV show you put on. Because films have a native refresh rate of 24fps, your TV will now run them as such. The same goes for TV shows, which may be filmed at 30 or 60fps. It's a tiny adjustment, but it's one that will make your viewing experience even better.

In early and mid-November, people shared numerous videos online appearing to show jellyfish- or octopus-shaped objects hovering high in the sky. Users referred to the alleged phenomenon as "jellyfish UFOs," with some alleging the objects were the secret reason for the U.S. air travel ground stop and other service outages.
However, Snopes' investigation of the clips failed to uncover any definitive proof of aliens. Rather, of the many videos people shared, those with identifiable locations appeared to line up with parks or beaches, suggesting the clips simply captured people flying jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites (or balloons). Some of the clips also appeared to have been created with artificial intelligence; for example, one video clearly displaying an AI-generated content label.
Snopes has not added a fact-check rating to this article, as our standards require comprehensive details and conclusive proof to establish a rating. This matter involves numerous videos, including some quite clearly showing kites, as well as others exhibiting signs of AI or lacking definitive information about their date and location.
We contacted a handful of users appearing to originally post some of the videos and have included the responses below.
Clips' spread started with Anchorage video
People have discussed supposed "jellyfish UFO" sightings for years. For example, a video from 2024 showed an object appearing to hover above a U.S. military base in Iraq.
Going back decades, The Associated Press, citing the Russian news agency TASS, reported (archived) about an event in Petrozavodsk, Russia, on Sept. 20, 1977, involving "a huge mass of light" that "hovered over the city in the form of a jellyfish sending down a multitude of fine beams." People now refer to that story as the Petrozavodsk phenomenon.
The wave of "jellyfish UFO" videos circulating in November appeared to begin with reposts of a video recorded in Anchorage, Alaska, in June, followed by some news media outlets reporting on the matter.
For example, a Nov. 3 Reddit post (archived) of the video displayed the title, "Video taken in Alaska of a strange jellyfish object. (Kite?)."
Video taken in Alaska of a strange jellyfish object. (Kite?)
by u/FrankMurphys in InterdimensionalNHI
The Reddit user linked to Facebook user Sara Jane Osborn's original post (archived) from June 15.
We identified Osborn's location in Google Street View after seeing the words "Alaska Geologic" on a building near the end of her video — matching the west side of the Alaska Geologic Materials Center. Osborn shared with us an image of the exact location where she recorded her video while her husband, Peter Osborn, sat in the driver's seat, confirming they faced directly east.
The object hovering in Osborn's video appeared clearer than the distant mountain haze, suggesting its closer proximity to the camera.
Using Google Earth, we moved directly toward where the object hovered, traveling over or very near at least three different parks or fields — nice spots for flying kites — first the large Russian Jack Park (about 1 mile east of the Osborns' location), then Creekside Park (about 2.4 miles east) and the Muldoon Elementary School athletic field (3.3 miles east).
Interviewing Sara Osborn
In an interview via Messenger, Sara Osborn said she and her husband were driving in Anchorage and stopped to take photos of a rainbow just after 10 p.m. (Sunset in Alaska occurs around 11:30 p.m. in June.)
She sent to us multiple photos, the video and metadata proof to help confirm she didn't use AI or other editing tools to create or manipulate her content. One photo, shown below, features the object hovering at 10:13 p.m.
(Sara Jane Osborn via Facebook, Snopes illustration)
Sara Osborn said she and her husband checked some nearby parks and kept searching but didn't locate the object again. She said she didn't believe it was a kite or balloon: "It was after 10PM… People were at home, getting ready for bed to go to work the next day." She added, "Only God & the government know what it is."
In 2010, Joint Base Elmendorf–Richardson, a military base located farther north and not in the same area of the hovering object's location, reported about launching weather balloons on an Alaskan island. Those weather balloons appeared white and round, and not in the shape of a jellyfish.
A spokesperson for the military base told us via email, "We are aware of a video circulating on social media regarding a reported aerial sighting near Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson from June 15, 2026, but have no additional information to provide at this time."
Local kite group member says 'definitely' octopus kite
To learn more about the Anchorage video, we reached out by phone to Debbie Wik, who represents the Alaskiters kite flying group and lives just southwest in Kenai.
Wik, who said she's been flying kites since about 1990 and has attended kite festivals for years, told us she believed the object in Osborn's video was "definitely" and "100%" an inflatable octopus kite, "probably at least a 50-meter inflatable black and white octopus." She also said she has no knowledge of anyone in her group flying that night.
She pointed us to recent photos and videos of her flying kites over Kenai in the daytime and LED-lit kites at night. Regarding the night flying Wik said, "I thought we were gonna cause an accident because everybody was pulling over and it was really cool."
The group created an interactive map in Google Maps identifying both Russian Jack Park and Creekside Park, as well as an area just south of Creekside Park, as prime flying locations.
Other 'jellyfish UFO' videos
Several social media accounts posted collections of various "jellyfish UFO" sightings. One of those collections began with an object resembling the two distinctly striped arms of an octopus foil kite that Amazon (archived) sells with 328 feet of string.
Another collection began with a video that the Pangram AI-detection website determined contained at least some inauthentic elements. That clip possibly originated from a Facebook post. We contacted that account to ask if the user created the clip. (Snopes does not entirely rely on AI detection tools to make conclusive determinations.)
The second clip in the collection, also a slideshow, featured two women looking at two jellyfish- or octopus-shaped kites, imaking fun of people who might believe the objects are aliens. The @swanvr Threads account recently claimed ownership of that clip, saying it dated back to 2024 and that "they're kites." The remaining four clips all appeared to show kites, as well.
A third collection displayed six still images of purported "jellyfish UFO" sightings, beginning with one from Osborn's Anchorage video. As one example, a search for the text caption's words, specifically "In the skies over Nashville," located a Facebook video appearing to show the man recording the clip of a "mysterious squid," including saying, "Nah, I think it's a kite."
Another example video (archived) out of Buffalo, New York, appeared to show the view out of a hospital window toward Ralph Wilson Park, also suggesting a kite.
One of the AI-generated videos
Another video showing a dark, octopus-shaped object flying in the sky displayed the words, "Clearest video to date thanks to my Canon EF-S 55-250mm Nov. 13th Arlington, Texas."
TikTok user @silversagag told us in a private message that he used AI to generate that video using images from two sources. The clip displayed an AI-generated content label, as well.
According to an AI prompt screenshot that the user shared with us, those two sources included Facebook user Deon Morris' post (archived), in which Morris claimed he found one of the supposed "alien babies" in his backyard, as well as a December Reddit post (archived) found on an Augusta, Georgia, subreddit mentioning Columbia County and "Evans Park."
In other words, the AI-generated video appeared to originate from some authentic content — meaning photos and videos genuinely recorded in reality — though the purported Augusta-area video still showed an object resembling a kite.
(Deon Morris via Facebook)
One close-up video (archived) that Morris recorded showed fibers, with commenters believing it was an old, dirty dog toy — potentially a rope dog toy that had unraveled or a no-sew octopus dog toy. We sent a private message to Morris to ask about his post and will update this story if we receive further information.
For further reading about similar untrue, fantastical matters, we recently investigated whether a video showed a pterodactyl flying in Mexico.

Seeing a rise in caesarean deliveries in India -- from 8.5% in 2005 to 21.5% in 2021 -- which is well above WHO-recommended levels, researchers are calling for policy measures, including more regulation in private healthcare, in an analysis published in The Lancet Regional Health Southeast Asia journal.
Study highlights
Delivering a baby via a caesarean section (C-section) involves making a surgical cut in the mother's abdomen and uterus.
The researchers, including those from the Institute of Public Health Bengaluru and Christian Medical College in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, said that while a medically indicated C-section is vital to preventing maternal and newborn mortality, rates of caesarean deliveries exceeding 10 per cent in the population are not linked with reduced mortality -- as noted by the World Health Organization.
An unjustified caesarean delivery is related to longer hospital stays and higher healthcare costs, with babies born through the procedure known to be at an increased risk of asthma, obesity, type 1 diabetes and allergies, among other health problems. The team reviewed 75 previously published studies -- mostly from India, followed by Bangladesh and Pakistan -- and examined factors in the countries' health systems contributing to caesarean procedures in the population.
Financial concerns
The authors said that an avoidable caesarean delivery can be financially stressful for families across South Asia, where a substantial fraction of deliveries occur in the private sector.
For example, out-of-pocket expenditures for a C-section in India will cost around Rs 43,000 in private hospitals, and around Rs 8,500 in public ones, suggesting that avoidable caesarean deliveries unnecessarily burden the healthcare system and families, they said.
Limited regulation and insurance coverage were among other factors associated with increased C-section rates. Decision-making at the healthcare provider's level was influenced by financial incentives, medico-legal concerns and scheduling convenience, the researchers said.
Driving factors
Mother's education, socioeconomic status and age, and family preferences were found to be individual and community-level factors driving an upward trend in caesarean deliveries.
Caesarean deliveries in Bangladesh are estimated to have increased from 18 per cent in 2011 to 45 per cent in 2022, while those in Pakistan rose to 20 per cent in 2018 from about three per cent in 1990. Data from national surveys were analysed for arriving at the figures.
The authors said that caesarean deliveries are being resorted to at nearly double the rates since 2000, with one in every five births involving the surgical procedure.
Coordinated policies needed
C-section rates in Asia rose from 4.4 per cent in 1990 to 19.5 per cent in 2014, with south Asia reflecting similar upward trends seen across the continent, they said.
"The review highlights the need for coordinated policy responses across levels, including payment reforms, regulatory oversight, and improved antenatal counselling, to ensure (C-section) use aligns with clinical need rather than socio-economic or institutional pressures," the authors wrote.

Sonia Gandhi, in her recently published memoir, recalls being advised surgery for suspected breast cancer in 2010. Since she is a prominent public figure, she wonders, in her book, whether she was entitled to even a modicum of privacy with regard to her health. Her account assumes renewed significance following a recent petition before the Madras High Court that inquired about the health of Kolathur MLA V.S. Babu (now deceased). These episodes expose a fundamental legal tension between the privacy politicians may want about their health, and the accountability they owe their constituents in a democracy. Does the public’s right to information justify waiving or limiting an office-holder’s medical confidentiality? How should a democracy reconcile these competing interests?
Medical information is among the most sensitive forms of personal information. A diagnosis may reveal not merely someone’s present condition but also their reproductive history, genetic predispositions, psychiatric illness or future health risks. Disclosure can invite discrimination, political exploitation and public speculation. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court recognised privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. Holding public office does not automatically extinguish this protection. A politician receiving treatment need not publish laboratory reports. Nor does a disability establish an inability to govern. State intrusion needs lawful justification, not curiosity.
The Constitution does not prescribe a general medical-fitness requirement for occupying high public office. Article 58 sets eligibility conditions for the President but requires no medical-fitness certificate. Article 65(2) allows the Vice-President to perform presidential functions when the President cannot do so through absence, illness or another cause. The Constitution recognises presidential illness but does not specify a detailed procedure or medical authority to determine contested incapacity. This distinction between eligibility to assume office and capacity to continue functioning deserves closer scrutiny.
For legislators, Articles 102 and 191 prescribe disqualification when a person is of ‘unsound mind’ and stands so declared by a competent court (not by a medical board). Section 16(1)(b) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, similarly provides for disqualification from electoral registration (by court not medical board). For Supreme Court judges, Article 124(4) permits removal on proof of incapacity, while the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, provides a procedure that may involve a Medical Board. Article 317(3)(c), governing Public Service Commission members, permits removal for unfitness arising from ‘infirmity of mind or body’.

The Highlanders started on the front foot, forcing two corner kicks within the first two minutes of the match, but it was SC Delhi that struck the first blow. Mohammed Aimen scored a sensational opening goal, receiving the ball down the left flank, cutting inside into the penalty box and unleashing a beautifully curled effort into the top corner past Gurmeet.
NorthEast United hit back close to the half-hour mark as Moyano displayed exquisite ball control, trapping dead a deft lobbed pass from Nikhil Barla. Escaping the Delhi backline, the Spaniard cut back inside to fire a low shot past Nora Fernandes at the near post.
With the scores level at half-time, there was drama in the 55th minute as Lalrinliana Hnamte’s goal was ruled out.
Rodriguinho’s mazy run ended with him hitting the deck after being blocked by Eneko Satrustegui, but Hnamte was alert to the loose ball and slotted home. However, the decision went against Delhi as Hnamte was deemed to be offside.
In the 77th minute, Alaaeddine Ajaraie thought he had scored a screamer from distance to put NorthEast in front, only for the officials to rule it out for a foul in the build-up involving Macarton Louis Nickson.
The home crowd was in full voice towards the end as NorthEast piled on the pressure, with Ajaraie involved in creating more chances, but SC Delhi managed to hold fort at the back. The result keeps NorthEast third with 12 points from seven matches, while SC Delhi stayed fourth with three points fewer.
NorthEast United will host Punjab FC next on November 30, while SC Delhi will travel to Kochi to face Kerala Blasters on December 10.

(Bloomberg) -- Record flooding from king tides is inundating the California coast Wednesday, compounded by a Pacific storm that’s contributing to flight delays in San Francisco.
Tuesday’s high tide of 8.23 feet (2.51 meters) was the largest ever recorded in the city during the month of November. Wednesday’s high tide may surpass it, said Sebastian Westerink, a US National Weather Service meteorologist in Monterey.
“Today and tomorrow around noon are going to be the worst,” Westerink said. “Then it is going to start lowering from there.”
About 145 flights through San Francisco International Airport were delayed Wednesday, according to FlightAware, a tracking site.
Flood warnings remain across San Francisco, much of the Bay Area and the Pacific coastline. Gauges on Wednesday in Santa Barbara and San Diego recorded their highest tides ever, the weather service said, breaking records set about a month ago.
Rough seas and dangerous swells have been spotted along California’s shores. Authorities in Marin County north of San Francisco issued a “shelter-in-place” order to residents in the Calles area of Stinson Beach as waves push past the beach. There’s also an evacuation warning in Stinson Beach — a community of 541 people — as large waves are expected through 2 p.m. local time.
Evacuation warnings are in effect more than 300 miles (483 km) south in Ventura County. The alerts encompass waterfront neighborhoods recently fortified with protective berms.
California’s king tides, the highest predicted tides of the year, recur when the sun, moon and Earth align and the moon is closest to Earth. This year, they’re arriving after El Niño helped raise sea levels and powerful waves battered the state’s coastline, damaging roads and destroying homes.
Travel has become dangerous at times: King tides have forced road closures and shut down portions of the Pacific Coast Highway in Orange County, south of Los Angeles.
