But nobody knows for sure because nobody has time to read all the papers. “It’s like this endless buffet. Even if it’s the most amazing food, how much of it can you digest?” is how Scott Aaronson put it to me. Aaronson is a theoretical computer scientist who has helped draw important connections between computer science and physics over the last 15 years.
Eventually, and perhaps soon, the endless buffet will require some new ways of organizing how physics as a field operates. Syracuse University physicist Aron Wall thinks it will increase the necessity of personal references and relationships. “My source for papers on the arXiv usually is somebody tells me about them, and if they don’t, then I don’t need to know,” he said cheekily. (Wall consults for Anthropic.)
Maldacena, for his part, isn’t sure what the solution might be, but he thinks it’s not an insurmountable problem. “It’s hard to process. But I think it’s great, and we’ll learn how to do that,” he said.
An uncertain future for young physicists
The flood of papers may be the kind of manageable change science has always had to deal with. But AI could have more profound impacts on the career prospects of young physicists.
Established physicists like Maldacena probably don’t have much to worry about. They’ll likely be able to keep their tenured academic jobs in any event. But physicists in training may not be so lucky.
Until recently, performing calculations was a rite of passage. It allowed young people to build both a reputation as a physicist and an intuition for how to approach the deepest problems.
“It’s how we judge students, how we decide students have talent,” Raju said. “I went into physics because I participated in the International Physics Olympiad, and that was considered to be a sign of having talent.”
“If you do enough of this mechanical grinding through problems, at some point, you pick up the concepts behind it,” Karch said.
But Karch said that trajectory may now be changing: “It’s not clear how you jump over that step” if AI is performing all the routine calculations.
“A lot of them feel like that is being taken away from them,” Aaronson said.
Karch also mentioned a burgeoning fear of getting scooped. “If you tell somebody, they’re going to run and ask the agent to solve it,” he said. “You have to be much more guarded if you think you have some big idea.”
Raju told me he’s not taking new PhD students until he gets a better sense of what their futures might look like.
All this is compounded by funding cuts the Trump administration is making to science, which were already threatening the field’s inherently tenuous career path. And while many physics skills translate to AI—Anthropic and OpenAI have both had physicists in high positions—the frontier companies aren’t hiring great numbers of them these days, especially outside top departments like Stanford or Berkeley.
Some students are taking on gigs writing training problems for data companies like Mercor or Scale AI for $80 to $100 an hour. “This is good money on the side, but it’s not a career,” Karch said. “No health insurance comes with this.”
Physics might be just months behind mathematics
As far as anyone can tell, the flood of physics papers doesn’t contain any major AI-aided physics discoveries. The closest thing so far has been OpenAI’s October announcement that one of its models had proved that the math behind the gluons that carry the strong nuclear force holds together in four dimensions. (Brian Greene has a helpful explanation here.)
A panel of physicists and mathematicians examined a Lean version of the 1,147-page proof and concluded it is correct. This is half of a Millennium Prize solution and a triumph of mathematical physics that has eluded humans for decades. The theory, called pure Yang-Mills, was first proposed in the middle of the 20th century. But the consensus among physicists seems to be that, technical impressiveness granted, at heart this solution firms up something everybody already knew.
“Existence of Yang Mills? It’s just tying up a [loose] end for the hyper mathematically minded. I don’t think any physicist gives af,” Karch tweeted.
At the same time, nobody I spoke to was confident enough to rule out major discoveries from AI happening soon. They’ve all seen what just happened with math.
Indeed, we’re starting to see AI discoveries in mathematics that could have significant implications for theoretical physics. One of them relates to a major problem involving black holes. In 2012, a few physicists made an alarming discovery: quantum mechanics seemed to demand that a literal wall of fire sit at the event horizon of a black hole—an absurdity that would violate general relativity.
Harlow and a colleague figured out a way of saving the situation, coming up with an elegant loophole of a sort physicists are partial to. They didn’t directly disprove the “firewall paradox”; they simply pointed out that based on our understanding of how information works, testing the paradox would take so long that the black hole would evaporate first, so the question was moot.
But as Aaronson pointed out to me, one of the 722 mathematics papers OpenAI released on October 6 looks like it shows that if one of computer science’s biggest unproven conjectures, a cousin of P versus NP, turned out to be false, testing the paradox would become more feasible. This leaves Harlow and his colleague’s defense of spacetime as we know it on somewhat weaker—though in all likelihood still safe—terrain.
Aaronson told me some of the physicists he knows tend to guess physics is about six to 12 months behind math.
“The reason why this has come for math and for programming earlier than for other things is just that we have very, very self-contained ways to verify whether an answer is right or not,” he said. “And that is what AI needs to help to power its training process.”
Or as Harlow put it, “nobody can just give you a Lean certificate that says, ‘Here’s the theory of quantum gravity.’ So in some sense, that’s the hardest kind of thing for one of these things to try to do because it’s so vague and poorly defined. The rules of the game are completely unclear.”
But Schwartz expects this situation to be temporary. “It’s certain by next summer, the AI will be able to do most of those creative steps on its own and really do papers end to end. And then the summer after that, we won’t even understand what it’s doing,” he said.
AI industry insiders seem to think the same. Last month, the prominent OpenAI researcher known as roon tweeted, “unified field theory / quantum gravity within the next 12 months?”
“The problem isn’t the ideas, it’s the experiments”
When Harlow and roon mentioned quantum gravity, they were referring to the deepest open problem in all of physics.
The first half of the 20th century delivered the two pillars of contemporary physics: general relativity, which essentially describes the force of gravity, and quantum mechanics, which essentially describes the three other fundamental forces (electromagnetism and the weak and strong nuclear forces).
The lion’s share of the work in the second half of the century was devoted to fleshing out the second theory. This resulted in what’s called the Standard Model of particle physics, which lays out the properties of all known fundamental particles that make up the universe. The Standard Model was essentially completed in 2012, when the final major particle it predicted, the Higgs boson, was discovered at the Large Hadron Collider.
But those two central theories of general relativity and quantum mechanics not only don’t match up everywhere, they conflict in places. There is no confirmed theory of the physical world that encompasses everything physicists know. This is where quantum gravity comes in. It’s a placeholder term—the name of a theory that doesn’t really exist yet.
The closest candidate is string theory. It does contain both quantum mechanics and gravity, which is why it attracted a lot of excitement when it was developed a few decades ago. It also, among other issues, allows for so many possible universes, 10,500 by one common estimate, that nobody knows if our particular universe is among them.
One reason we don’t know is that we can’t test string theory.
The accretion disk of a black hole as visualized by Jeremy Schnittman for NASA.
The Large Hadron Collider is the most powerful particle accelerator physicists have constructed to date, but it would take a machine roughly a quadrillion times more powerful to make gravity’s quantum effects strong enough to directly observe; a collider as powerful as the LHC would need a radius measured in the hundreds of light-years. Indirect, non-collider tests have been proposed, but so far, nothing significant has panned out.
As Karch put it, “the problem isn’t the ideas, it’s the experiments.”
This means theoretical physicists interested in quantum gravity have faced a difficult choice. Some have moved on to other problems. Others have made significant—if publicly underappreciated—advances using little more than mathematical consistency and human intuition as their guides.
As I wrote last year in The Wall Street Journal, this project has been controversial in some quarters—unfortunately so, since I and many others consider it to be an enormous feat of human intellectual effort and creativity. Several of the physicists I quoted in this story have worked on what’s called the black hole information paradox—a central front in the clash between quantum mechanics and general relativity.
There is an ironic possibility looming. Suppose AI improves in physics as it has in math, going from talented student to somewhat incomprehensible master very quickly. Maybe in a year or two, an AI agent will generate a brilliant solution to quantum gravity that is consistent with what we know about our universe. But unless technology changes, testing such a solution will remain impossible.
The end of “shut up and calculate”
Some of the most impressive physics theorists were never known for their calculating prowess. Take Einstein in the past, or the likes of Leonard Susskind today.
In the most human-friendly case for the near future, the job of theoretical physicist returns to something like Einstein’s famous method, Gedankenexperiment, or thought experiment, the act of pressing on contradictions until they break.
Quantum gravity, for instance, is a question requiring extraordinary conceptual imagination as well as intensive mathematical ability. There are few conceptual guides and, compared to many areas of physics, relatively few clearly defined questions to calculate. One of Maldacena’s central innovations, expressed in one of the most cited theory papers ever, hints at the idea that everything in our three-dimensional world might be described or encoded on a two-dimensional boundary far away.
Wall said this way of working requires a certain amount of something other than raw intelligence. “Science doesn’t just progress through smartness, it also progresses through stupidity in a crucial way,” he said. “Stupid means you’re getting the question wrong, and you have to go back and figure out why you’re getting it wrong.”
Many of the physicists I spoke to feel that moving toward an emphasis on concept-work like this and away from human calculation might not be such a loss. “I feel like that style of doing physics and math is probably done, or will be soon,” Harlow said. “But I don’t really mourn that too much, to be honest.”
“For a long time we’ve been told to ‘shut up and calculate.’ [Maybe AI] frees us up to stop and think, and it lets us think about ambitious problems that we couldn’t think of earlier,” Raju said in a recent talk. “Shut up and calculate” is the cliché expression of a widespread mid-century attitude toward quantum mechanics: Nobody understands what the theory really means about the world, but the equations work impeccably, so do the math and don’t worry about the rest.
Raju thinks this relatively cheery paradigm will hold for the next few months at least. Past that, he doesn’t know.
If it doesn’t hold, one possibility is that theoretical physics, long a relatively individual field, will start to look more like experimental physics, which is much more collective. If progress on important questions depends on burning huge amounts of compute, physicists will pool resources together, apply jointly for grants from the government and large institutions, and collectively judge the most important questions to ask the AI. Just a few weeks ago, 51 physicists authored a proposal to this effect.
To Schwartz, whatever structure it takes, the promise of AI and physics is thrilling. “I am excited for the science. I think fundamentally most scientists are interested in answers,” he said.
Maldacena concurred. “I’m more excited than concerned,” he said. “That means that we have lots of possibilities and promise for the future.”
Raju was more circumspect but said it will be hard to complain about AI-driven discoveries: “If somebody tells us the nature of dark matter, then I suppose we have to welcome it. We can’t say, ‘Oh, we didn’t want to know it so fast.’”
The trade
If AI meant the end of human physics as we know it but we got a solution to quantum gravity or other discoveries of similar size, would that be a worthwhile trade? “Making a deal with the devil—sell your soul for the answer?” Schwartz asked jokingly. “Yeah, I would. I think you just have to be a little bit more humble.”
Maldacena, who has done as much as anyone alive to probe the boundaries of human knowledge of the universe, said, “I think it doesn’t matter who generates the knowledge,” as long as we can still understand it.
Harlow, by contrast, wouldn’t take that trade. “No. And I probably wouldn’t even read the result,” he said. “I’d just be off playing piano in a bar somewhere or something.”
In this scenario, theoretical physics might start to look something like a humanities field. Handed-down truths? Unprovable or unintelligible knowledge-objects? That sounds like biblical studies or art criticism.
There would still be physicists in this world. On paper, at least, one of the chief jobs of a physicist is to teach physics to other humans. But they would not be discovering knowledge so much as interpreting it. Indeed, it can be argued that math is already entering this state.
This sort of interpretation has been part of physics for a long time, though perhaps not as much as it should have been. Take quantum mechanics. The predictive power of the equations of quantum mechanics is beyond dispute. At the same time, any real understanding of what quantum mechanics means about the world is wildly disagreed upon and even sorely understudied, as the physicist Sean Carroll frequently argues.
Wall was relatively sanguine about this direction.
“People have this idea of physics and mathematics as something where it’s all about just answering the question, making discoveries,” he told me. “But it’s the most common thing in the world for the paper that discovers a thing to be completely incomprehensible to other people because it’s expressed in that person’s language, and maybe the person who translates it into language other physicists can understand gets as much credit sometimes. And that’s actually fair, because that’s an equally important job.” (This is something of a reversal of the science-like ways humanities fields have tried to position themselves in the last few decades, and not to enormous success. As the political theorist Samuel Goldman pointed out recently, “The conflation of scholarship with ‘creating new knowledge’ has been a disaster for the humanities and social sciences.”)

A crude bomb was allegedly hurled by ABVP activists at a bookstall set up by the Students’ Federation of India (SFI) in College Street, Kolkata’s principal hub of bookshops and publishing houses, late on November 18.
Titled Sangrami Boipotro (Literature of Struggle), the stall was set up by the Calcutta University unit of the SFI to commemorate the November Revolution. ABVP activists allegedly attempted to vandalise the stall, accusing the Left student outfit of selling ‘anti-national’ books, resulting in day-long tension in the ‘boi para’.
The confrontation began around 11 am on Wednesday and continued late into the evening. Tensions escalated when ABVP activists allegedly hurled a firecracker, locally known as a ‘chocolate bomb’, into the SFI stall as activists, including women, were packing up the books before closing for the day. Video footage shows the firecracker exploding in a small burst of flames and smoke filling up the area.
The incident took place in the presence of a large contingent of Kolkata Police personnel. SFI activists alleged that the police attempted to shield the ABVP activists. The Right-wing student organisation, on the other hand, claimed SFI activists had assaulted its members and vandalised its bookstall.
Reacting to the allegations and counter allegations of violence, BJP state president Samik Bhattacharya said, “These are matters related to student politics. They are young. Political movements were never entirely peaceful here. These things happen.” He also said ABVP was not related to the BJP.
The SFI’s Version of Events
According to SFI activists and videos circulated on social media, the confrontation began around 11 am. The bookstall was scheduled to open at that time, with senior Left leader Biman Bose slated to inaugurate it.
However, as SFI activists were setting up the stall, a group of ABVP activists gathered outside the main gate of Calcutta University, which opens onto College Street, and attempted to prevent them.
To contain the situation, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel formed a human barricade between the two groups. Videos show ABVP activists repeatedly raising slogans and displaying aggression. However, the police did not remove them from the spot.
Around 1 pm, tensions appeared to ease somewhat, with ABVP workers setting up a makeshift bookstall a few metres away from the SFI stall. The two stalls were positioned on either side of the university’s main gate, with the ABVP stall to its left and the SFI stall to its right. Police personnel placed metal barricades in front of the SFI stall to prevent a direct confrontation between the groups.
Around 2 pm, Left leaders Biman Bose and Sujan Chakraborty visited the stall.
However, as Bose was leaving, ABVP workers were heard raising slogans such as “Biman Bose Go Back” and “Slap Biman Bose across the face with shoes”.
The ABVP protest blocked a section of College Street. Its activists allegedly charged towards the SFI stall several times in the presence of police personnel. They also threw water and eggs at the stall, staining a National Flag at the venue and several books, the Left outfit alleged.
Around 7 pm, the situation escalated with the ABVP gathering allegedly hurling bricks, wooden sticks and water bottles towards the SFI enclosure, while police personnel continued to maintain a barricade between the two groups.
Videos also show plastic chairs being hurled form either side.
Around this time, SFI activists were packing up the stall for the day when a ‘chocolate bomb’ was seen flying towards it from the direction of the ABVP gathering.
The firecracker exploded inside the SFI enclosure, producing a flash and filling the area with smoke. The explosion further escalated tensions, with SFI activists seen rushing towards the ABVP gathering. Police personnel struggled to pull them back and prevent a direct confrontation.
Following the incident, the SFI decided to lodge an FIR at the nearby Jorasanko police station. Activists also organised a protest march from College Street to the police station.
According to SFI activists, police initially resisted registering a written complaint but eventually agreed following their sustained pressure.
SFI activists further alleged that after they had left for the police station, ABVP workers vandalised the stall site, damaging tables, benches and chairs.
The SFI is scheduled to reopen the bookstall at the same location on Thursday. It will remain open until November 20.
Trouble Erupted on November 17 as well
According to SFI sources, the organisation has been setting up the bookstall at the same location for the past four years. This year, too, its members informed the Joint Commissioner of Kolkata Police about the stall and its schedule through an email. They also paid the requisite fee to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) for setting up the stall. However, on Monday, the police informed them that they would not be allowed to erect any permanent structure at the site.
On Tuesday morning, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel arrived in front of Calcutta University and attempted to prevent SFI activists from setting up the bookstall.
Around 12:30 pm, SFI activists blockaded College Street and began selling books while sitting on the road.
This led to a scuffle with the police, following which 41 SFI activists, including the organisation’s West Bengal state secretary, Debanjan Dey, were detained and taken to Lalbazar, the headquarters of Kolkata Police.
In response, the SFI organised a mobilisation outside Lalbazar, demanding the release of those detained. Around 6 pm, all 41 activists were released.
According to SFI activists, the joint commissioner of police held lengthy discussions with them, following which it was agreed that they could set up the stall without erecting any permanent structure. They were also asked to ensure that the stall did not obstruct traffic on College Street.
The SFI activists attempted to set up the stall on Wednesday in accordance with these conditions. However, their efforts were disrupted by ABVP activists, who objected to the organisation’s programme.
The ABVP’s Response
ABVP further alleged that SFI activists had destroyed books on Swami Vivekananda, claiming that its own bookstall had been set up to encourage reading among students. It accused the SFI of sabotaging an initiative intended to promote education.
The Facebook page of ABVP Paschimbanga also shared a clipping from Bengali news channel TV9 Bangla, which purportedly showed Arunava Dutta, an ABVP national executive council member, being assaulted by SFI activists.
In a separate post, ABVP shared a video showing a stone being hurled from near the Left book stall.
In a separate Facebook post, ABVP Paschimbanga condemned what it described as attacks on its activists at Calcutta University, Calcutta Medical College and Presidency University. “The throwing of bombs inside university campuses and the targeted attacks on ABVP activists by SFI and Left organisations are deeply alarming and condemnable,” the organisation said.
In the video, ABVP national secretary Shravan B Raj said, “The SFI and Left extremist groups are unleashing violence on ABVP karyakartas.”
Vandalism at Calcutta Medical College
In another incident on the same day, intern doctors at Calcutta Medical College, located adjacent to Calcutta University and barely a 100-metre from the site of the book-stall clash, alleged that ABVP-backed miscreants entered the college campus and assaulted them.
The incident came amid a protest by students and junior doctors against show-cause notices issued to eight interns who had spoken out against alleged mismanagement at government hospitals following the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal which claimed 19 lives.
According to a Facebook post by the West Bengal Junior Doctors’ Front, the college principal and other senior officials had initially agreed to withdraw the notices after acknowledging a shortage of medicines. However, following a phone call from a “higher authority”, the principal reportedly refused to issue a written order confirming their withdrawal. This prompted students to stage a sit-in protest.
The post alleged that around 70–80 outsiders subsequently entered the campus, vandalised property and assaulted interns and medical students, leaving several injured. It further alleged that the principal left the campus under heavy police protection while the attackers continued their rampage in the presence of police personnel.

Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday.
It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.
Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick said. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”
Utah drops criminal charges
Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi, as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.
In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown said. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those plans, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”

The Union Health Ministry has proposed an amendment to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, to include ‘antimicrobials’ in the definition of ‘New Drug’ under Rule 2(1)(w)(v).
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health concern and the proposed amendment has been initiated in view of concerns regarding the grant of manufacturing licences for antimicrobial products without adequate regulatory scrutiny, including the requirement for studies such as bioavailability and bioequivalence and stability studies.
The proposed amendment seeks to bring antimicrobials within the regulatory framework applicable to new drugs under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019. Accordingly, manufacturers would be required to obtain permission from the Central Licensing Authority before applying for a manufacturing licence from the concerned State Licensing Authority. This is expected to strengthen central regulatory oversight and help ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products.
Meanwhile, the Ministry has also proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to introduce a separate application form (Form 19-BC) and licence form (Form 20-BC) for the sale of bulk drugs (active or inactive bulk substances), distinct from the existing licensing provisions for formulations.
At present, a common licence covers the wholesale sale of both formulations and bulk drugs. The proposed amendment seeks to establish a dedicated licensing framework for bulk drugs, enabling more focused regulatory oversight of their wholesale sale and greater accountability in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
The proposal was agreed upon by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) in its 67th meeting held on November 17, 2025, and by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) in its 93rd meeting held on February 16, 2026.
Under the proposed framework, the licence will capture the categories of bulk drugs handled by wholesalers, including drugs covered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985. The sale of bulk drugs will be carried out under the personal supervision of a competent person, thereby strengthening accountability in their distribution and handling.
“Upon implementation, the proposed amendment will: give better control over the sale of bulk drugs by way of wholesale, strengthen enforcement control in relation to antimicrobial resistance and the movement of NDPS drugs and require wholesalers of bulk drugs to obtain a separate license for sale.” Stakeholders and members of the public are invited to submit their objections and suggestions.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Meta restricted 5.44 million items from view in India on local-law grounds between January and June 2026, a significant increase from 41,357 in July to December 2025 and 28,030 in January to June 2025, according to its Content Restrictions Based on Local Law report. These restrictions were based on legal requests and proactive enforcement of local laws, and do not include content removed under Meta’s Community Standards, which is reported separately.
Identical copies
The India figure was approximately 131.5 times higher than the previous half’s count. Meta states it began large-scale content restrictions using automated detection of “100% identical copies” under the amended IT Rules in select countries. This increase results from changes in restriction methods and underlying demands. It does not represent the number of legal requests.
Facebook and Instagram
Meta’s India product data shows:
- Facebook: 2.82M restrictions, up from 27,353 in July- December 2025; 2.80M were posts.
- Instagram: 2.62M restrictions, up from 14,004 in July-December 2025; 2.60M were media items.
Facebook and Instagram counts combine Meta’s product categories, as Meta does not publish platform totals. Meta also reports restricting “over 20,000” items on Threads, which is not included in its country or product totals.
India and the world
Meta’s eight Facebook and Instagram product categories recorded a global count of 27.11M in January–June 2026, a 2.7% decrease from 27.86M in July–December 2025. India represented 20.1% of the total. Indonesia reported 20.59M, a 24.4% decline from 27.25M in the previous period.
India had the second-highest number of content restrictions worldwide, following Indonesia. South Korea ranked third with about 410,000 restrictions. India and Indonesia together represented approximately 96% of Meta’s global content restrictions.
What Meta does not say
Meta’s India account does not specify a legal basis for most of the January-June 2026 restrictions, other than citing proactive measures under local law. For July-December 2025, it reported restricting ‘over 9,000’ items at the direction of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, and over 22,000 items following court orders relayed by local law enforcement. These figures represent minimum counts, not precise totals.
India is among seven regions where Meta does not disclose to users which authority requested a restriction.

Easy daily use. Lots of LEDs and medical-grade lasers. Simple to wear. FDA-cleared tech. Results started to appear within a month.
TIRED
Must be used consistently. Portable battery is an extra $99.
The Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.
I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.
However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand said science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.
The Scientific Crown
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.
Red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.)
The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.
If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.
Growth Spurt
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't plan to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.
During the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a big no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
Within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while new growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.
The effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.
Rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.
A Hairy Situation
In addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.
The supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.)
Ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," says Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.
Photograph: Julia Forbes
As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite showed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

At least 30 killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the vehicle had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.
The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.
Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.
Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.
Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.
A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the companies said Tuesday, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs.
The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its massive blockbuster Dupixent, an inflammation-targeting drug approved in nine indications. The company, where Belén Garijo took over as CEO earlier this year, had been vocal that it was looking for takeover targets with late-stage or even commercial assets that fit with its existing focus in immunology and rare diseases.
Sanofi is paying $175 per share for New Jersey-based Insmed, through a combination of debt financing and cash. Insmed’s share price was roughly $120 before Bloomberg reported last week that the deal was in the works, which sent the stock up.

And why isn’t Magnus Carlsen playing? We (mostly) have the answers Play through 22 famous world championship games Jump to When and where is the World Chess Championship? Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Where do they rank internationally? Who is the current world No 1 in chess? How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Who are their seconds? What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? What is the schedule and how does the match work? How can I watch the World Chess Championship? What else should I know? India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is making his first defense of the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek star Javokhir Sindarov over the next three weeks in the affluent Geneva suburb of Cologny. Both players are 20 years old, making it the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. But is that all you need to know? What about the format, how much they’re getting paid and why the world’s No 1-ranked player is watching from the sidelines? Read on for all the answers … When and where is the World Chess Championship? The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the picturesque enclave overlooking Lake Geneva. The opening ceremony is scheduled for 22 November, with games played once daily from 24 November except for designated rest days on 27 November and 1, 5 and 9 December. It’s the first time a world title match has been held in Switzerland since 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik retained his title by drawing 7-7 with Peter Leko in Brissago, two years before the sport’s rival championships were reunified. Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Gukesh Dommaraju, commonly known as Gukesh D, was only 18 when he became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed world chess champion by defeating China’s Ding Liren in 2024. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai native rose to international prominence when he became the second-youngest grandmaster in history at the time, aged 12 years and seven months. Five years later he stunned the chess establishment by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament at 17 to secure a world title shot. He went on to win and shatter the age record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 rematch in Moscow. His victory made him a national hero in India, where he was mobbed by supporters on his return and feted by prime minister Narendra Modi. But the 20-year-old has struggled badly for form since then, plummeting to No 26 in the world from a career-high ranking of No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances. Gukesh Dommaraju receives a hero’s welcome at Chennai airport after becoming the youngest undisputed world chess champion in December 2024. “Clearly so far I’ve not been able to handle it in the best possible way,” Gukesh admitted in a recent interview. “There have been major setbacks ... Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure that I’m dealing with and I’ve not found the right way to maybe handle it.” From Bobby Fischer to Magnus Carlsen: 22 of the most famous world chess championship games Read more Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Javokhir Sindarov is an Uzbek prodigy, roughly six months older than Gukesh. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster earned his crack at the world championship with an imperious performance at this year’s Candidates in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws to turn back a stacked field that included longtime stars Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. The first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the title, Sindarov has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup last November in Goa. He enters the biggest match of his life on a tailwind of confidence, having won a four-player rapid tournament in St Louis three weeks ago over Nakamura, Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, capped by a brilliancy against the world No 2 that showcased his tactical brio. His ascent has added fuel to a remarkable chess boom in Uzbekistan, where he belongs to a golden generation of grandmasters, along with Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Nodirbek Yakubboev, who have transformed the central Asian nation into a global powerhouse with two golds and a bronze at the past three Chess Olympiads. Javokhir Sindarov explains his brilliant victory over Hikaru Nakamura to grandmaster Maurice Ashley after their game in St Louis. “This tournament will be the hardest tournament in my life,” Sindarov said in August of his showdown with Gukesh. “I don’t know if I will get a second chance [at the world championship]. It’s hard to play 14 games against the same person in three weeks.” Tale of the tape Where do they rank internationally? Sindarov, ranked 25th in the world a year ago, has climbed to a career-best No 4 with a Fide classical rating of 2782, while Gukesh has slipped to No 26 with a rating of 2710. That makes Gukesh the lowest-ranked reigning world champion of the Elo era, which dates back to 1971, eclipsing the previous low of No 23 set by Ding in 2024. The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Who is the current world No 1 in chess? Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old Norwegian has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted, though that extraordinary reign is suddenly under threat after a disastrous 10-game winless streak last week in Budapest reduced his once-comfortable lead over his nearest rivals to single figures. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash. If you can name only one chess player active today, chances are it’s him. The youngest undisputed men’s classical world chess champions Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila. Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi in a thrilling, sometimes messy scrap for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, taking the decisive 14th game on a catastrophic blunder to claim a 7½–6½ victory and become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize. Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his eye-watering 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation. (He’s also gotten married, become a father and is by all accounts pretty good at fantasy football, too.) How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Despite being contemporaries, they have played only three times in classical games. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad. Many of the world’s top players have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.” Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.” Who are their seconds? Neither Gukesh nor Sindarov has publicly disclosed his full team of seconds, the trusted cadre of advisers who help prepare openings and analyze the opponent. That’s not unusual: players tend to keep the identities of their seconds closely guarded before and during a match to avoid revealing clues about the direction of their preparations. But we do know a little bit. Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who led a formidable backroom team during his 2024 title-winning campaign that included five other GMs and analysts from Poland, India and Germany, with additional support from Anand (acting as more of a mentor than a practical second). According to reporting from ChessBase, Sindarov is expected to be working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, while the 22-year-old Abdusattorov, the former world rapid champion and current world No 5, revealed on a podcast that he will be in Geneva to help his compatriot prepare. Another Uzbek grandmaster, Mukhiddin Madaminov, has also been mentioned as a member of Sindarov’s team. Photograph: Europe Echecs What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games. Gukesh’s world ranking Each player received a $200,000 advance on their winnings one month before the first game, deducted from the prize fund. The remaining balance will be remitted to the players within 30 working days after the completion of the match. The stakes are particularly high in a sport where even the biggest stars rarely earn seven figures in annual prize money. According to a new ranking published by World Chess, no player has crossed the $1m mark in tournament winnings in 2026, with India’s Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu leading the way on $666,229. Sindarov ranks third with $589,061, while Gukesh sits 48th with just $41,500. The world championship alone will assure its winner at least $1.25m, enough to vault either player to the top of the annual earnings list. What is the schedule and how does the match work? Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played). The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter. If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023. The complete official regulations can be found here. Cambodia hosts Chinese military for largest Golden Dragon joint exercise yet
Cambodia and China have started joint military exercises aimed at strengthening cooperation between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- China and Cambodia launched their eighth joint military exercise on Wednesday, seeking to strengthen ties between Beijing and its closest political partner in Southeast Asia. Cambodian military spokesperson Thong Solimo said the drills are the largest since the exercise began in 2016.
The 15-day Golden Dragon-2026 exercise will end on Dec. 9. Its stated focus is counterterrorism, humanitarian assistance, anti-piracy operations and disaster relief.
The drills are part of Beijing’s broader push to expand its regional influence. Cambodia consistently backs Chinese foreign policy, while Beijing is its most important ally and benefactor. Chinese aid and investment have helped fuel Cambodia’s rapid economic growth in recent decades.
The United States, China’s main rival for influence in the region, has expressed concern over the military ties between Beijing and Phnom Penh. Cambodia suspended its joint Angkor Sentinel exercise with the United States in 2017, after the last drills in 2016. Following efforts by both sides to improve military relations, the exercise is set to resume next February.
Beijing has helped fund an expansion of the Ream Naval Base on Cambodia’s southern coast, raising concerns it could become a strategic outpost for the Chinese navy in the Gulf of Thailand. Cambodia has repeatedly denied any agreement granting China special privileges or the establishment of a foreign military base.
Cambodian leaders have said warships from all friendly countries are welcome to dock at its new upgraded facility, provided they comply with certain conditions. In January this year, the U.S. warship USS Cincinnati arrived at Ream, marking the first time a U.S. Navy warship has docked at the facility since its Chinese-funded renovation was completed in 2025.
According to Cambodia's state broadcaster TVK, three Chinese vessels arrived at Ream earlier this week to take part in the Golden Dragon exercise. The opening ceremony was presided over by Cambodian Defense Minister Tea Seiha and Rear Adm. Liu Sumin, commander of China's Guangzhou Naval Base.
Tea Seiha said the exercise does not aim to threaten or provoke the security of any third country, but is purely for the purpose of strengthening global security and humanitarian relief. Liu Sumin echoed the point, saying through an interpreter that “Its content does not target any third party, nor is it related to the regional situation or any specific security issues.”

The craze for fairness is more than skin-deep, and the trade-off can be costly. Inferior cosmetic products can end up harming your vital organs.
A 17-year-old girl in Keralam’s Malappuram developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, according to the doctors treating her.
The incident came to light after the authorities at the hospital that treated the teenager, who was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, held a press conference on Friday. Lab tests had confirmed 1.25% mercury in the cosmetic product, according to the hospital sources.
Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early.
Lack of awareness
Warning against following social media beauty trends and using topical creams seen online or bought over the counter without a prescription, M.M. Faizal, former president of the Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists, says people lack awareness of how topical applications can enter the bloodstream.
“People are obsessed with fair skin. We have observed a rise in the number of people buying steroid creams that are easily available over the counter and applying them to their faces. Such steroid-based applications and creams containing heavy metals such as mercury can damage your kidneys easily. The government needs to bring in some mechanisms to control this,” he says.
Vulnerable group
A rise in the number of teenagers relying on spurious beauty products has forced the Keralam Drugs Control department to launch awareness campaigns targeting students in Classes XI and XII, an age group particularly vulnerable to online campaigns. Frequent inspections are carried out in marketplaces to confiscate spurious cosmetics.
State Drugs Controller K. Sujith Kumar says raising awareness about such spurious cosmetic products is the only way forward.
“We have seized cosmetics that have high mercury levels from offline markets. But there is no way to track or regulate online marketplaces,” he says.
Prolonged use of such creams can lead to kidney damage, says former secretary of the Nephrology Association of Kerala, Jayant Thomas Mathew, who has come across a few cases of kidney disorders among users. The condition could be detected early because the patients were aware of the symptoms.
“The patients had used fairness creams and noticed symptoms related to kidney disorders. They probably had membranous nephropathy, and since they sought medical help at a very early stage, treatment was possible,” says Dr. Mathew.
The symptoms
Swelling in the legs and face and frothing in the urine are some of the signs people need to be wary about, the doctor adds.
Much has changed in the beauty industry, with social media driving trends, says Liji Coleenz, a make-up artist and salon owner in Kochi with 20 years of experience.
“Even teenagers fall prey to the beauty aspirations set on social media. Our fixation with fairness is troublesome. We can never aspire to have Korean skin and need to be comfortable in our skin,” she maintains.

According to a survey by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), severe anaemia was observed in less than 2% of people in the majority of age groups. The Survey for Assessment of Markers of Population Health, Activity, Diet and Anthropometry (SAMPADA) 2023-2025 was released on Monday (November 23, 2026).
It showed that children aged 12-59 months had 42% anaemia prevalence, adolescent girls aged 10-19 years had anaemia prevalence of 46%, adolescent boys aged 10-19 years and men aged 20–59 years had 22-23% anaemia prevalence, whereas women of reproductive age had 56% prevalence.
The survey also found that mild anaemia constitutes a substantial proportion of the overall anaemia burden.
“SAMPADA provides nationally representative estimates of anaemia across children, adolescents, adults, pregnant and lactating women and older adults, together with detailed information on micronutrient deficiencies to evaluate potential causes of anaemia. It is encouraging that prevalence of anaemia is lower in SAMPADA compared to previous national surveys. The comprehensive anaemia profiling in the SAMPADA survey provides an evidence base to strengthen the ongoing national efforts towards Anaemia Mukt Bharat,” said Rajiv Bahl, secretary, Department of Health Research.
The report noted that about half of anaemic women, including pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls, and children, have mild anaemia, indicating considerably lower risk of serious health consequences than moderate or severe anaemia. Anaemia prevalence is much lower among adolescent boys, adult and older men, and even among those affected, three-fourths have only mild anaemia, said the release issued by the Union Health Ministry.
SAMPADA represents one of the largest and most comprehensive nutrition surveys undertaken globally. The survey covered more than 2 lakh individuals from over 81,000 households across 183 districts in 35 States and Union Territories. More than 1.7 lakh blood samples were analysed for haemoglobin estimation across different age, sex, and physiological groups.
“A major strength of SAMPADA is the use of gold standard method of venous blood sampling and automated analysers for haemoglobin estimation, providing greater accuracy and reproducibility. In a sub-sample, the survey also assessed iron status, folate, vitamin B12, together with inflammatory biomarkers C-reactive protein (CRP) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) to obtain national level prevalence estimates,” the release said.
Iron deficiency accounts for about half of the anaemia cases in women, adolescent girls, and children, said the report.
The micronutrient assessment showed that although iron deficiency is the predominant contributor to anaemia in vulnerable population groups, it accounts for about half of the overall anaemia burden, highlighting the need to simultaneously address multiple nutritional and non-nutritional causes of anaemia, including infections, hemoglobinopathies, and inflammation related to chronic disease.
However, the prevalence of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency was similar in both anaemic and non-anaemic individuals across population groups, indicating a limited contribution of these micronutrient deficiencies to anaemia in India.
Iron deficiency is concentrated in specific life-stages and in moderate and severe cases of anaemia. SAMPADA findings show that iron deficiency is largely restricted to population groups including under-five children, adolescent girls, and women of reproductive age, while adolescent boys, men, and the elderly have a low prevalence of iron deficiency. Importantly, people with moderate and severe anaemia have a high prevalence of iron deficiency and need to be identified by testing for appropriate treatment and tracking till resolution as envisaged in AMB 2.0.
“These findings support more targeted, population-specific and life-course approaches to anaemia prevention and management. The evidence can contribute, while also identifying areas where further research and improved surveillance are required,” said Bharati Kulkarni, director, ICMR-NIN.

Apple iPhone assembler Foxconn Technology Group’s India unit is facing an insolvency petition from BCD Emprasa LLP, which is seeking nearly ₹143 Cr (around $15 Mn) in alleged unpaid dues, interest, service charges, and damages. BCD filed the petition before the Chennai bench of the NCLT in August against Foxconn Hon Hai Technology India Mega Development Pvt Ltd, Bloomberg reported, citing the filing. The claim, calculated as of July 8, relates to alleged defaults on rent and utility payments for accommodation leased to house employees working at Foxconn’s Bengaluru facility. The petition comes amid reported payment delays affecting about half a dozen local vendors working with Foxconn’s India unit. Queries sent by Inc42 to Foxconn and BCD Emprasa remained unanswered till the time of publication. The story will be updated on receiving their responses. Employee Housing Dispute Under an agreement signed in April 2024, BCD leased 700 residential units to accommodate Foxconn’s female employees. The agreement required rent to be paid regardless of occupancy and included a lock-in period extending until July 2026, according to the filing cited by Bloomberg. BCD alleged that Foxconn failed to clear an invoice due in May 2025 and did not agree to appoint an arbitrator to resolve the dispute. In a response to Bloomberg, BCD said the alleged defaults caused significant financial and commercial losses, adding that the matter was sub judice before the NCLT. Other Vendors Await Payments Beyond BCD, at least four other vendors have reportedly been waiting for several months to more than a year for Foxconn to clear their dues, the report said, citing sources. Several of these vendors were engaged in construction-related work at the company's Bengaluru facility and had been working with the iPhone manufacturer for the first time. The departure of certain non-Indian employees also reportedly slowed down the processing of payments to local contractors. The disputes come amid Foxconn’s continued investment in its Indian manufacturing operations. In June, its Singapore subsidiary invested $37.2 Mn in Foxconn Hon Hai Technology India Mega Development. The company has also been expanding its component manufacturing ambitions. In May last year, it infused nearly $1.5 Bn into its Tamil Nadu-registered entity Yuzhan Technology (India). It subsequently explored setting up another unit in the state to manufacture iPhone enclosures.

The Duchess of Sussex’s father Thomas Markle has been formally charged by a grand jury in Los Angeles with two counts of possessing child sex abuse images, court documents have indicated.

Authorities found items including slides, film negatives and books that all contained suspected child sex abuse material.
Last week, he was deemed psychologically fit to stand trial after being accused of possessing child sex abuse material, including images of himself with naked young girls.

Markle is currently in custody in Florida. He had initially been released on conditional bail but was detained just days later after removing his electronic monitoring tag.
A psychiatric assessment was ordered after his arrest at a senior care centre in Florida.
During a 90-minute interview, he reportedly denied the allegations against him and blamed his son for his legal troubles, according to a 15-page report.
“Why I am here? What have I done?” she quoted him as saying. “I don’t have any child porn. I have no pictures of naked kids.”

The Japanese Association of Metal, Machinery and Manufacturing Workers (JAM) has decided to call for a pay scale increase of at least ¥17,000 ($107) per month in the 2027 shuntō (spring wage negotiations), sources said Tuesday.
JAM, the fifth-largest industrial labor group in trade union confederation Rengo, has about 1,900 member unions, mainly from small- and medium-sized manufacturers, with a total of some 390,000 workers.
The 2027 pay scale hike demand matches the record-high figure from the last round of negotiations, reflecting the association’s goal of reducing the pay gap between large and small companies.
Including the pay scale increase, JAM will call for total monthly pay increases of ¥21,500 or more. This compares with Rengo’s call for small unions to seek total pay hikes of at least ¥20,000.
JAM is set formally adopt its pay increase demands in January.
The association also plans to stress the need to secure funds for pay increases by appropriately raising the prices clients pay, as the business environment for small firms has become increasingly severe in part due to rising raw material and energy costs stemming from conflict in the Middle East.
